div.head: Pennsylvania's Forests
div.p: Forests cover nearly 60 % of Pennsylvania (PA) and provide citizens with an array of values including clean water, clean air, climate change mitigation, recreation opportunities, wood products, and habitats for thousands of plants and animals. Sustaining these values for future generations requires a shared vision and coordination among many stakeholders, including agencies, landowners, forest industry, natural resource professionals, conservation organizations, community leaders, and policymakers.

div.head: Forest Action Plan: Purpose and Organization
div.p: The purpose of this Pennsylvania Forest Action Plan is to assess the condition of Pennsylvania's forests across all ownerships and establish a framework of strategies to achieve long-term forest sustainability. The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources' (DCNR) Bureau of Forestry (bureau) receives funding from the USDA Forest Service for Forest Stewardship, Urban and Community Forestry, Forest Health, and Wildland Fire programs. Completing this 10-year Forest Action Plan is a requirement of the federal Farm Bill (Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018, 2018 H.R. 2, 115 H.R. 2), which helps ensure continued funding of these critical programs for the bureau and its partners that rely on Federal funding. These plans were first compiled in 2010, so the 2020 Forest Action Plans represent the second cycle of this national forest planning effort. In addition to meeting the Federal requirements, the bureau is utilizing this process as an opportunity to undertake a holistic, long-term evaluation and strategic planning effort for Pennsylvania's forests. The completion of the 2018 Farm Bill requirements by December 31, 2020 is the first step of this longer-term endeavor that will culminate in the creation of a new Strategic Plan for the bureau, replacing the bureau's current strategic plan: Penn's Woods, which was developed and adopted in 1995.
Strategies developed for Pennsylvania's Forest Action Plan (see Chapter 3) are related to USDA Forest Service -State and Private Forestry National Priorities set forth in the Farm Bill.

div.head: State and Private Forestry National Priorities:
div.p: 1. Conserve and manage working forest landscapes for multiple values and uses.
2. Protect forests from threats.
3. Enhance public benefits from trees and forests.

The Priority Issues in Chapter 3 are a result of the input received as part of a long-term planning process that included all the consultations and feedback mechanisms listed in Appendix A which we used to inform both this Forest Action Plan, as well as the DCNR Bureau of Forestry's Strategic

Planning that is ongoing. There is significant overlap between the Bureau of Forestry Strategic Plan and this PA Forest Action Plan, and the plans complement one another. However, the priorities, purposes, and themes of each plan are slightly different. Natural resources management and social issues surrounding it are intertwined in complex ways that do not lend themselves to hierarchical plans. Topics within and between plans are related, although they have been partitioned into discrete "Issues".

For clarity throughout this plan: when referring specifically to the 2.2-million-acre system of state forests managed by DCNR Bureau of Forestry, the term "state forest land" will be used. When referring to the forest resources of the entire Commonwealth of Pennsylvania across all ownerships, the term "forests of the commonwealth" will be used.
This Forest Action Plan is organized into the following chapters:

• Chapter 1 -Introduction Chapters 2-4 are described further below. Each chapter pulls information from numerous sources and institutional knowledge. A list of "Additional Resources" are provided at the end of each chapter and/or subsection to provide the reader with reference material to delve deeper into various subjects mentioned or used to create the text of this plan.

div.head: Chapter 2 -Conditions and Trends (Assessment)
div.p: Understanding and documenting forest conditions and trends is a critical part of developing longterm strategies for sustainability. Using the Northeast-Midwest State Foresters Alliance's Criteria and Indicators for sustainable forestry, this chapter documents current conditions and future trends of the commonwealth's forest resources and provides an assessment of sustainability for each of 18 indicators. The intent of the chapter is to present in a concise format, relevant data and the bureau's interpretation of the data related to sustainability.

At the conclusion of each indicator, a "Sustainability Meter", similar to the one pictured below, is presented as a visual interpretation of the indicator. The image below reflects our overall assessment of Pennsylvania's forests related to that given indicator. Our forests face many challenges and threats including land use change and development, forest health concerns, ownership demographics, detrimental management decisions, and uncertainties of shale gas development and climate change.

The evaluation of many indicators resulted in Sustainability Meter readings on the green or "Sustainable" side, but with many causes for concern. Overall, there are considerable concerns about the future sustainability of Pennsylvania's forests.

div.head: Overall Sustainability Indicator Chapter 3 -Priority Issues
div.p: Considering the sustainability analysis (Chapter 2), existing programs, future directions, and stakeholder input, the bureau identified 11 priority issues for forests of the Commonwealth: For each issue, key threats and opportunities related to that issue are provided. Then, relevant data and an assessment of each issue are discussed, setting the foundation for establishment of long-term strategies. The Forest Action Plan long-term strategies are presented in a table at the conclusion of each issues sub-section, wherein linkages are made to State and Private Forestry National Priorities.

div.head: Chapter 4 -Priority Areas
div.p: Pennsylvania's forests occur in diverse landscapes ranging from urban park and street trees to scattered woodlots in highly developed or agricultural areas to the heavily-forested PA Wilds. These landscapes are influenced by many factors, including geology, spatial arrangement and sizes of forested tracts, and local development patterns. Understanding geography and landscape variability helps policy makers and program leaders tailor programs to meet local, specific needs while working within a broader statewide context.

Developing regional or landscape-level programs is not a new concept in Pennsylvania. Several models and programs already occur, though implementation among the state's 2,560 separate municipalities poses a significant challenge. The intent of this Chapter is to acknowledge and build upon existing landscape-level approaches while identifying additional areas for future consideration.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Pennsylvania State Constitution, Article 1, Section 27, adopted in 1972, states "The people have a right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment. Pennsylvania's public natural resources are the common property of all the people, including generations yet to come. As trustee of these resources, the Commonwealth shall conserve and maintain them for the benefit of all the people."

The obligation to conserve and maintain these resources for all people is foundational to the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR). The mission of DCNR's Bureau of Forestry is to ensure the long-term health, viability, and productivity of the commonwealth's forests and to conserve native wild plants. The forests of Pennsylvania provide many benefits and services to citizens of, visitors to, and the businesses and industry of the commonwealth. Pennsylvania forests offer wood products, energy resources, watershed values, recreation opportunities, plant and wildlife habitat, and are valuable in the mitigation of climate change. Pennsylvania's forests offer varied services to a diverse population. With proper management and sound conservation leadership, the commonwealth's forests have and will continue to sustain these benefits over time. This law states that one of the purposes for which the state forest system was created is "... to furnish opportunities for healthful recreation to the public."

Pennsylvania is a time-honored outdoor destination. Visitors to, and citizens of, the Commonwealth have enjoyed traditional outdoor pursuits like fishing, hunting, hiking, camping, and boating across generations. The Allegheny and Clarion rivers are both part of the National Wild and Scenic River System, as designated by Congress, and they provide unique recreation opportunities. Forests spanning the Allegheny and Appalachian Mountains cover two-thirds of the state and provide endless opportunities for outdoor experiences, recreation, and solitude.

Pennsylvanians today benefit from a proud history of natural resource conservation, despite periods of intensive resource degradation and destruction in the 19 th century. Unsustainable logging practices, followed by land abandonment, uncontrolled fire, and soil erosion left a grim landscape. Concerned conservationists began to organize themselves to demand action and resources to establish higher standards for land management and stewardship for the forest resources of the commonwealth. Forestry and conservation pioneers from the late 19 th century, such as Joseph Rothrock and Mira Lloyd Dock established a foundation upon which may others have built through the 20 th and now into the 21 st century. Public ownership protects over two million acres of state forest land, one-and-a-half million acres of game and wildlife lands, the half-million-acre Allegheny National Forest and 121 state parks. Many private forest landowners also allow recreational pursuits such as hunting and hiking on their properties and many have purchased properties specifically for recreational pursuits, such as hunting clubs. Research consistently shows that Pennsylvanians place a high value on outdoor places and activities from the standpoint of personal benefit, viewing these resources as an important component of maintaining quality of life. Forestlands serve as incubators for stewardship and facilitate meaningful outdoor experiences for all who appreciate the history, science, and natural beauty within.

The Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP), which is revised every five years, is an important tool to help guide recreation planning and related land management across all of Pennsylvania. The 2020-24 SCORP can be found at this link: https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/Recreation/PAOutdoorRecPlan/Pages/default.aspx

Recreation may begin as soon as one walks out the door and enters the community. Street trees and urban forests are often forgotten about in discussions regarding benefits of forests, but these urban forests may be the only outdoor setting some people experience, especially in fast-growing urban and suburban areas of the Commonwealth.

Traditionally, Pennsylvania's liability statutes have limited recreation potential on private lands. However, the following recent efforts have helped expand these opportunities. The commonwealth has worked to secure easements and provide recreational access through some private lands. Additionally, some statutes have been amended to ease liability costs on landowners. One example is the Recreational Use of Land and Water Act Pa. Stat. Ann. tit. 68, § 477-1 et seq., (RULWA). RULWA limits landowners' liability for personal injury and property damage if they make their land available to the public for recreational use, free of charge. The purpose of the law is to encourage landowners to allow recreational users onto their properties by limiting the traditional duty of care that landowners owe to entrants upon their land. Although private landowner liability is a current topic of discussion, forest recreation for most people nevertheless remains relegated to public lands.

Recreational opportunities on state forest land are aimed at those forms of dispersed forest recreation that are not being provided by other land uses or ownerships and that are compatible with the forest ecosystem. Some people seek the peace and solitude that forests provide in order to promote mental and physical fitness. Others enjoy more physical activities to achieve the same outcome. There are those who prefer traditional forms of recreation such as sight-seeing, hiking, hunting, fishing, horse-back riding, cross-country skiing, and others who find state forests ideal places to hang glide or geocache or to ride ATVs, snowmobiles, mountain bikes and dog sleds.

There is an abundance of land and wildlife available for hunters and trappers to enjoy with almost all Pennsylvania state forest land open to hunting, along with State Game Lands, many private forestlands, and much of the Allegheny National Forest. Specially designated areas of state forest are also open to persons with disabilities to aid in their forest recreation experience. This includes allowances like use of powered mobility devices for transport and access to areas otherwise closed to the public.

Pennsylvania's forests also have an abundance of streams, ponds and lakes that supply opportunities for cold-water and warm-water fishing. Forests throughout Pennsylvania have some of the most pristine waters in the commonwealth and they support abundant fish life, including over 16,000 miles of naturally-reproducing trout streams, according the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission.

There are also many other great opportunities for water activities in Pennsylvania including canoeing and kayaking rivers and streams, motorized boating and use of personal watercraft in lakes and rivers. For non-motorized boaters, there is an extensive system of water with guides available from partner groups (responsible for establishment of water trails) to make users aware of important things such as water access points and hazards.

DCNR's Bureau of Forestry has management responsibilities over all river islands in Pennsylvania that remain "vacant and unimproved" or "unpatented and unimproved". These islands offer excellent recreational opportunities. Today, DCNR collaborates with several volunteer groups that design, develop, and maintain river islands trails throughout the commonwealth. These volunteers also serve as trail stewards for maintenance, monitoring resource impacts and tracking public use, and many of these river island groups produce maps and brochures describing the trail, explaining access, and camping opportunities.

The forests of the commonwealth also provide the necessary and beloved backdrop for passive activities like wildlife watching and nature observation. The National Audubon Society has designated certain areas of forestland with unique or rare bird species as Important Bird Areas (IBA- https://www.audubon.org/important-bird-areas/state/Pennsylvania). These areas have particularly large and unique habitats for rare bird species of conservation concern. State Forest Natural Areas and Wild Areas are exemplary places for passive recreation, as they are managed with little direct human intervention and prioritize preservation of the natural resources and wild character. The entire 2.2-million-acre state forest system provides expansive landscapes for publicly-accessible outdoor recreation. Nature photographers and artists also find an abundance of subjects in the natural settings of the commonwealth's forests.

There is an almost endless list of personal recreational pursuits enjoyed by citizens of, and visitors to, Pennsylvania's forestlands. These forests provide the necessary resources for rock climbing and rappelling; they provide the perfect setting for geocaching expeditions and for vast numbers of campers; and they offer the perfect winter setting for downhill skiing, tubing, and snowboarding. The forests of Pennsylvania also offer over 12,000 miles of trails for hiking, biking, horseback riding, crosscountry skiing, snowmobiling, and riding all-terrain vehicles. Pennsylvania ranks first nationally in rail-trail projects, boasting 24 National Recreation Trails, and housing one of the longest multi-use trails in the nation with the Great Allegheny Passage, Pennsylvania is a national leader when it comes to trails, and its forests are certainly instrumental to outdoor recreation.

div.head: Water Conservation
div.p: Forested watersheds improve water quality, protect water sources, and help communities avoid the high costs of treating contaminated water and stormwater overload. Approximately two-thirds of the water that fills streams and replenishes groundwater flows from forested lands. Forests provide higher quality water than other land uses. They provide a steadier supply of water, gradually filtering and continually releasing clean water; and forest vegetation not only intercepts some precipitation to help manage storm runoff, but vegetation on the ground protects soils from eroding due to the flow of water.

Riparian forest buffers (trees along banks of waterways) further protect streams and waterways by acting as a filtering system and provide shade to streams which is critically important to maintaining cold water temperatures, especially important for wild trout. As water flows toward drainage areas, soil particles and other contaminants are filtered through this vegetative buffer before entering the waterway. Sediment and nutrients are trapped in the roots and matter of streamside vegetation, and thus kept out of waterways. This keeps the water quality high for public drinking supply purposes and also for aquatic life dependent on clean, flowing waters. Streams with forested buffers have higher nutrient-processing capabilities, helping to filter pollutants that are already in the water. In conjunction with forested buffers, establishing meadows instead of turfgrass can have significant positive impacts on water quality and ecosystem functions in certain areas.

Pennsylvania has over 602 public surface water supply systems that provide drinking water to approximately 10.2 million people. Northcentral and northeast Pennsylvania boast forestland with great ability to produce clean drinking water. Out of 104 drainage basins in Pennsylvania, 95 are used as sources of public water systems.

In addition to providing clean drinking water and lowering water treatment costs, forests protect Pennsylvania communities from flooding and other issues due to excessive stormwater flows. Municipal stormwater systems face overloading after large storm events which can cause flooding and contaminated water supplies, among other problems. A forested ecosystem decreases storm runoff by the interception of precipitation by trees and vegetation, and by the slowing and filtering of water through the organic matter on the surface of the ground.

Watershed health begins to decline as forest cover drops below 65-75% (see Goetz et al. 2003& Booth 2000). Currently, according the USDA Forest Service Forests to Faucets data, approximately 55% of Pennsylvania's small watersheds meet the threshold of 65% forest cover.

Water quality decreases as forests are converted to other uses, and so the importance of forest cover is evident. The USDA Forest Service recommends planting trees in urban and agricultural-based watersheds to recharge groundwater, reduce soil erosion and sediment in streams, and to improve water quality.

div.head: Wildlife and Biodiversity
div.p: William Penn first established the tradition of protecting the natural diversity of the commonwealth in the mid-1600s. In keeping with this stewardship ethic, Pennsylvania adopted Article 1, Section 27 as part of the Pennsylvania Constitution in 1972. The ecological rights described embody the very natural diversity William Penn recognized as important centuries ago.

Maintaining biodiversity is critical to ensure function and resiliency of forest ecosystems. Lifesustaining processes such as nutrient cycling, photosynthesis, decomposition, soil creation, climate regulation, removal of pollutants, and insect control, are all dependent on functional forest systems that can withstand stressors and continue to provide habitat and unique ecological services.
Maintaining biodiversity is key in conservation efforts regardless of the ecosystems of interest.

Forest biodiversity can be preserved by the provision and protection of various habitat types and retaining functional and healthy ecosystems. Notably, upland forests support 30% of Pennsylvania's Species of Greatest Conservation Need (PGC-PFBC 2015, Chapter 2 https://www.pgc.pa.gov/Wildlife/WildlifeActionPlan/Documents/SWAP-CHAPTER-2.pdf). The greater the diversity of habitat types in the forest, the greater the diversity of plant and animal life that will coexist in the forest. Reducing forest fragmentation will help to protect important habitat for many species that are unable to spread without continuous forestland. DCNR uses and supports thirdparty-certified sustainable timber harvesting practices that mimic natural occurrences and conserve natural resources, and that protect sites from pollutants by use of best management practices (BMPs). These BMPs also promote desired tree growth and composition of tree species in the forest. Proper planning and site management help to maintain the level of biodiversity, and sometimes even increase biodiversity in Pennsylvania's forest ecosystems.

Other strategies used to promote the natural biodiversity of forests are to control the establishment, growth, and spread of non-native invasive species. Invasive species are any organisms thriving where they are not native, and usually interfering with natural processes and function of the native ecosystem. They may be introduced on vehicles or equipment, via birds or other wildlife, may have spread from nursery stock imported from other areas, or be released by humans or escape from agricultural operations. These non-native or introduced species have the potential to out-compete native species for food or habitat and can thus have detrimental impacts on the forest system.

The biodiversity of the forest attracts many visitors, such as hunters, anglers, bird watchers, wildlife photographers and naturalists. Pennsylvania forest land has an abundance of streams, ponds and lakes that supply opportunities for cold-water and warm-water fishing. The State Forest system has some of the highest-quality waters in the commonwealth, supporting abundant fish and other aquatic life. The Department of Environmental Protection classifies 22,248 miles of waterways as High Quality and 3,875 miles of waterways are classified as Exceptional Value. In addition, the Fish and Boat Commission classifies over 16,000 miles as naturally-reproducing trout streams.

Biodiversity is also a benefit to forest visitors as it adds to the natural beauty and changing scenery enjoyed by so many outdoor recreation enthusiasts. Citizens and visitors alike appreciate the aesthetic benefits of a diverse forest system. Urban forests offer refuge and solitude to people and wildlife near population centers, while also creating small, but complete, ecosystems.

Looking deeper into the benefits to humans, many species of plants and fungi are gathered and sold for economic value and require proper habitat to thrive. Many plants also have medicinal properties that humans benefit from, not to mention the potential of our plant and animal kingdom to hold the secrets to yet undiscovered medical breakthroughs.

div.head: Climate Change Mitigation
div.p: The burning of non-renewable fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas introduces pollutants into the earth's atmosphere, most notably the greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel combustion occur directly from residential, industrial/commercial, or transportation sources.

Climate change mitigation includes any actions taken to reduce greenhouse gases, a root cause of for steady increases in the earth's temperature and subtle changes in weather patterns. To residents and visitors of Pennsylvania's cities and suburbs, trees also reduce emissions and energy consumptions by shading nearby homes and businesses. Large forest systems, as well as smaller urban forests, have the ability to sequester carbon dioxide and other pollutants from the atmosphere through absorption in the soil, trees, and other vegetation.

Climate change mitigation activities on forest lands can include management strategies adopted with the purpose of enhancing forests' natural ability and capacity to sequester and store carbon. Forests, including the soils, trees, and all plants have the capability to sequester and store carbon. When a forest is sequestering more carbon from the atmosphere through photosynthesis than it is releasing through respiration it is considered a forest sink. Currently, Pennsylvania forests are functioning as carbon sinks and absorbing carbon produced by greenhouse gas sources, thus reducing environmental or climatic impacts.

Forest systems are beneficial carbon storage pools, and their capacity to sequester and store carbon can be directly influenced by human activity. With proper management, the capacity of forests to sequester and store carbon can be increased while considering the other important resources, uses, for top quality furniture and cabinets or to be pulped for paper products. Pennsylvania exports some of the highest-quality hardwood in the world. By-products such as sawdust, can be utilized as a source of woody biomass material for pellets for burning in heaters, for example.

Along with timber production, Pennsylvania remains one of the top producers of anthracite and bituminous coal and is the state with the second-largest exports of coal to foreign markets. However, the share of Pennsylvania's electricity from coal is dropping: about 21% of the commonwealth's electricity in 2018 was from coal, which is less than half the percentage when compared to 2010, according to estimates from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA 2019). Oil and gas production from sources under Pennsylvania forests have been in play since the mid-1800s, with the most recent boom over the past decade with shale-gas development. In 2018, Pennsylvania was the nation's second-largest natural gas producer after Texas (EIA 2019). From 2010 to 2018, Pennsylvania's share of electricity generated from natural gas more than doubled to 36% (EIA 2019). An estimated 350,000 conventional oil and gas wells have been drilled in Pennsylvania since the first commercial well was developed in 1859, and 11,000 unconventional wells were drilled over the last decade aimed at developing the Marcellus Shale in Pennsylvania (PA DEP website: https://www.dep.pa.gov/Business/Energy/OilandGasPrograms/OilandGasMgmt/Pages/default.aspx).

Since 1947, DCNR has managed the leasing of state forest land for natural gas extraction in a way that minimizes negative environmental impacts. By the end of 2019, approximately 1,056 conventional and unconventional oil and gas wells were drilled and in production on approximately 254,000 acres of DCNR lands leased for oil and gas development. Proceeds from State forest oil, gas and mineral leases are used to fund conservation efforts throughout the Commonwealth.

With resources as significant as timber, oil, and natural gas within the forests of Pennsylvania, it is easy to forget about the vast amount of less significant, but still valuable products. These products all have some worth to people, whether as heat/energy sources, food products, herbal remedies, or sources of income (if sale of products is permitted). Using state forest lands as the example, it is possible to obtain nursery stock as permitted, and gathering permits are available for fuelwood, landscaping stone, and for certain plants used for food or medicinal purposes, like certain fungi and ginseng.

Spending on the recreational pursuits available in the forests of the commonwealth generates money to state and local economies. Many individuals and businesses provide land for activities like hunting or hiking or offer goods and services like guided trips or recreation equipment rentals and sales.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The value of Pennsylvania's natural resources of for some may be found in the timber, or in the natural gas reserves. Others may find value in the opportunities the forests create to engage in traditional or modern recreational pursuits. Environmental values of natural biodiversity and the provision of clean air and water promote ecosystems and communities that are vibrant and healthy. Sensory benefits arise from the peace and serenity found within the commonwealth's forests, given credit for benefiting mental health. Physical health improves with outdoor activities for which forests are the desired setting as well.

Sound, science-based management, with objectives for sustainable product yields and conservation of the natural resources within the forests, is the best means by which the commonwealth can ensure the productivity of the forests for future generations, including usability by people and industry. Proper and careful management, based on sound science, research, and experience will secure the health and vitality of the forests of Pennsylvania now and into the future, allowing for continuity of services and benefits for generations to come.

div.head: Overview
div.p: The concept of sustainability refers to the forest's ability to produce the full suite of ecological, economic, and social benefits and services for both current and future generations. In an effort to measure and track global progress toward achieving forest sustainability, an international seminar held in 1993 Montreal, Quebec resulted in the Montreal Process Criteria and Indicators for sustainable forestry. The Montreal Process includes a set of seven criteria and 67 indicators for assessing sustainability. To help make the process relevant on a regional scale, the USDA Forest Service Eastern Region, in cooperation with the Northeast-Midwest State Foresters Alliance, developed a set of seven criteria and 18 indicators for the Northeastern U.S. (Table 2-1).

What follows is an analysis of Pennsylvania's forests relative to these eighteen indicators of sustainable forestry. For each indicator we briefly describe what the indicator, present and discuss relevant data, and provide a conclusion regarding sustainability. Sustainability Meters were originally used in Pennsylvania's 2010 Forest Action Plan. To update the Sustainability Meters for the 2020 PA Forest Action Plan, bureau staff considered the following factors:

1. changes in resource conditions affecting the indicator, 2. management capacity to address the indicator, 3. funding availability to address the indicator, and 4. new or updated information about where the meter should be.

To show the movement of the meters from 2010 to 2020, a faint grey arrow has been included on the gauges to represent the 2010 "reading" along with a black arrow that indicates the 2020 assessment level.

div.head: Sustainability Meters CRITERION 1: CONSERVATION OF BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY
div.p: Indicator 1. Area of total land, forest land, protected forest land, and forest ownership

Maintaining forest cover is fundamental to providing the full suite of resources and values that Pennsylvanians enjoy from their forests, including clean water, recreation opportunities, wood products, and habitats for plants and animals. Pennsylvania's public and private forest landowners have extremely diverse sets of objectives, capacities, knowledge, and resources for managing their land-understanding these dynamics is critical to evaluating overall forest sustainability.

Pennsylvania contains close to 16.8 million acres of forest, covering approximately 60% of the commonwealth (Figure 2.1-1). For comparison, agricultural lands comprise about 22% of Pennsylvania, non-forest natural areas almost 5% and developed areas account for about 12% of Pennsylvania acreage (Figure 2. [1][2]. US Forest Service Forest Inventory & Analysis (FIA) data suggest that on a statewide basis, Pennsylvania's forestland area has remained relatively stable since around the 1960s. However, a closer look reveals that some parts of the state are gaining forests, while other parts are losing forests. Counties surrounding the metropolitan areas of Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Harrisburg have experienced losses in forestland over the past 10 years while counties such as Potter and Tioga have seen some increases in forestland. Urban forests and urban tree cover are increasingly important, given that over 75% of Pennsylvania's population reside in urban areas. Urban trees provide myriad benefits, including reduction of building energy use, carbon sequestration, and air pollution removal. Tree canopy cover on urban land is estimated at 40.7% across the state (Nowak & Greenfield 2018). Most tree canopy goals are set around 40%. It is important to note that, while our overall urban tree canopy estimate is currently reasonable, the actual tree canopy of various cities varies greatly. While some forests are being converted to other land uses, Pennsylvania is fortunate to contain over 5 million acres of public lands protected from development. Major public owners include DCNR (State Forests and Parks), the PA Game Commission (State Game Lands), and the USDA Forest Service (Allegheny National Forest). While each of these agencies has a specific mandate, they share overarching visions rooted in long-term conservation. Each agency manages for multiple

div.head: Non-forest Natural
div.p: Pennsylvania Acreage values, which can include recreation, timber, wildlife, water, and oil and gas while also designating portions of their land base for special uses such as Wild/Wilderness Areas, Natural Areas, and National Recreation and Scenic Areas. Protected land bases and mandates, long-term management plans, and professional, multi-disciplinary staffing provides for sustainable futures for Pennsylvania's public forests. Much of this public forest occurs in Northcentral PA and along the major ridges that form the Appalachian Mountains. These large, contiguous public ownerships serve as a backbone for biodiversity and other conservation values. Since 2010, the Pennsylvania Game Commission has added over 72,000 acres of State Game Lands and the Bureau of Forestry has acquired over 59,000 acres of state forest land, often leveraging partnerships with NGOs for purchases of key tracts. In addition to public conserved lands, many private forests are protected via conservation easements (held mostly by non-profit conservation organizations) with over 40,000 acres under conservation easements across the commonwealth.

The most recent Penn State landowner study suggests that over 738,000 entities own Pennsylvania's nearly 17 million acres of forestland (Metcalf et al. 2012). Private forest landowners' control around 70 % of the forest while public entities own the remaining 30 % (Figure 2.1-1).

Family forest owners hold an estimated 8.5 million acres (51%) of forest land in Pennsylvania (Table 2. . That total, combined with an estimated 2.4 million acres (13 %) owned by corporations and an estimated 721,000 acres (5 %) owned by other private owners (including conservation organizations and hunting clubs), places around 11.6 million acres of Pennsylvania forest land in private hands (Table 2.1-1). forest landowners often cite objectives such as wildlife, solitude, and enjoyment, few have professionally-developed management plans to guide on-the-ground decisions. Ownership patterns are quite revealing (Table 2. [1][2] and indicate that 64% of the state's private forestland is already carved into parcels that are 99 acres or smaller. Another troubling trend is timber investment organizations with large forest land holdings are divesting themselves of ownership, potentially resulting in parcelization and development. In addition to the increasing number of forest landowners, the demographics of existing forest landowners has implications as well. With the average age of Pennsylvania forest landowners at 61 (an increase of two years from the previous analysis-Butler et al. 2020), it is likely that private forestlands will, of necessity, change hands over the next two decades. Anecdotal evidence indicates that most harvesting and parcelization takes place during ownership exchanges. Therefore, further subdivision, and perhaps development, of privately-owned forestland are very possible. Smaller, non-contiguous parcels are more challenging for natural resource professionals to manage and less conducive to maintenance of ecosystem functions. Subdivision of forestland into smaller acreages and subsequent increases in the number of private forest landowners have profound implications for the future of Pennsylvania's forestlands, complicating outreach and assistance efforts. Education and incentive-based programs will have to continue to adapt and will likely become more resource-intensive to encourage forest stewardship among a growing number of private forest owners and across increasingly sub-divided forests. Additionally, implementation of regulations for sustainable forest management may become necessary in the future to maintain the intact, functional forests found within the commonwealth that provide the ecosystem services universally enjoyed by Pennsylvanians (and beyond).

While the amount of forestland has been stable on a statewide basis over the last 10 years, and public ownerships form a solid foundation of conserved forestland, there is significant cause for concern in urban and suburban counties experiencing heavy growth and resulting forest conversion While the challenges associated with private forest management are plentiful, opportunities exist to improve and increase forest management, such as statewide partnerships, woodland owner associations, certification systems, emerging carbon market opportunities, conservation easements, and new approaches for fostering stewardship. Even with the increased efforts to leverage these opportunities, landowner trends, forest health threats, and ecological complexity ensure that sustaining Pennsylvania's forests will be a major challenge.

Although there is significant and relatively-stable amount of forested acreage, the challenges and trends mentioned above resulted in the meter reading down one notch from the 2010 reading of the forest land area and same as the 2010 forest ownership reading. Indicator 2. Forest type, size class, age class, and successional stage Forest characteristics can be described and summarized at various geographic scales (forest communities, landscapes, and ecoregions). Maintaining health and diversity across these various scales ensures Pennsylvania forests will continue to provide diverse plant and animal habitat, human-derived values such as wood and clean water, and resiliency to insects, diseases, and other disturbances.

Pennsylvania's forests contain remarkable diversity-the latest USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program inventory recorded over 100 species of trees alone. Oak/hickory and northern hardwood forests dominate Pennsylvania's landscapes-each containing unique plant communities. Oak/hickory forests contain primarily oaks, maples, and hickories and commonly have understories with mountain laurel and blueberry. Northern hardwood forests (called maple/beech/birch in USDA Forest Service FIA data) contain primarily black cherry, maples, American beech, and birch with understories of ferns, striped maple, and beech brush. Hemlock and Eastern white pine are common to both forest types. Both forest types provide valuable wood products, hard and soft mast for wildlife, and contain diverse plant communities. Though acreages of the forest types have been relatively stable, recent US Forest Service data suggest that the composition of our forest communities is changing. Red maple, black birch, and white pine are becoming more common while sugar maple, hemlock, beech, ash, and the oaks are declining. These species shifts raise serious questions about the future composition of our forest, including their ability to provide food for wildlife with potential reductions in mast species such as beech and oak. Recent FIA data show only 59 % of sampled stands have adequate native tree regeneration to develop into high quality and productive forests (FIA, 2016).

Except for areas that have been recently harvested, much of Pennsylvania's forests originated between 90 and 120 years ago, reflecting the widespread clearing and harvesting that occurred to fuel the industrial revolution. As a result, most forest stands, especially on public forestland, are relatively uniform in age and, therefore, structure, and are dominated by large diameter ("sawtimber-sized") trees (Figure 2.2-2). Careful consideration is needed to examine the appropriate landscapes wherein early-successional habitat can be promoted, such that the mosaic of habitat is functional and distributed in a way that promotes resilience and minimizes fragmentation of other critical forest communities.

Many experts agree that Pennsylvania is experiencing a shortage of both early-successional habitat and habitat exhibiting old-growth characteristics. Although acres of large-diameter trees are increasing, forests with dynamics and traits of 'old-growth' are scarce. On publicly owned lands, many areas of true old-growth forest are protected from harvest via special designations (such as Natural Areas on State Forests). However, old-growth forests on private forest lands may be at risk due to lack of awareness of the unique features and needed protections at these sites. Conversely, the area of young, early successional forest continues to decline, and it is estimated there is less than 1.5 million acres of forest (8%) in small diameter (seedling/sapling) stands . As the overall age class average continues to increase, there is a growing need to balance age class distribution to create diversity and improve resilience to stressors across the landscape. Awareness of old-growth areas in need of protection is important in identifying the most appropriate and effective locations for treatments to establish early successional forests, such that both unique habitat types are maintained and promoted.

Acknowledging this general lack of habitat diversity, the Bureau of Forestry, for example, has developed explicit goals in its State Forest Resource Management Plan for achieving a balanced forest age-class distribution across the state forest, and is currently within the second decade of implementing these goals. Regenerating stands through timber harvesting is the primary means to achieving these long-term goals. Regeneration difficulties related to white-tailed deer browsing and competitive native and invasive plants, along with significant pests and pathogens affecting hemlock, sugar maple, ash, and American beech cause concern for both early-and late-succession habitats. Lack of diversity in age classes and successional stages, changing overstory species composition, threats from biotic and abiotic vectors, as well as poor management practices reduce the health and resiliency of the forest and produce poorer habitat for native species. Pennsylvania's forests contain a wide breadth of forest types, but pressures from climate change, lack of or poor management, and other forest threats lead to a growing concern about the long-term sustainability of the commonwealth's forests. Pennsylvania's largest public land managers, such as DCNR's Bureau of Forestry, have recognized and are addressing these issues in long-term management plans. However, the majority of the forestland remains in private ownership and few of these landowners have management plans or the resources to implement such plans. Landowner education will continue to play a vital role in the future of Pennsylvania's forest resources, as well as programs that provide assistance to private forest landowners.

Because of these continued threats and additional uncertainties, the overall assessment is that Pennsylvania's forests are trending toward an unsustainable condition in terms of maintaining diversity of forest characteristics (age, size, forest type and successional stage) and therefore, the reading has dropped one notch on the sustainability meter. The process of converting forests to other land uses or dividing them into smaller units significantly undermines sustainability by limiting overall ecological functions. Conversion means that a forest is cleared and converted to another use such as housing, commercial/industrial development, or agricultural uses. Fragmentation refers to breaks in forest cover, or openings created by roads, utility corridors, gas well sites, and housing developments; resulting in a loss of interior forest habitat. Parcelization refers to landowners dividing their properties into smaller parcels that are then owned by other individuals or entities. Parcelization may or may not result in fragmentation or conversion, but generally, smaller ownership acreage increases the likelihood of conversion and decreases potential for connectivity, management, and sustainability.

div.head: Conversion
div.p: Forest conversion is occurring at alarming rates in certain parts of Pennsylvania and represents an unsustainable situation in these locations. Most of the development in recent years, according to the National Land Cover Database (NLCD), is found in the SW, SE, and NE regions of the state. Between 2011 and 2016, per NLCD, Pennsylvania gained more forest acreage statewide than it lost. However, losses were primarily in the categories of deciduous and evergreen forest cover, while gains were in mixed forest and woody wetlands (as expected, because forest gains occur as young forests age and cultivated land reverts). The same data show a decrease in agricultural lands, but a significant increase in developed areas. These gains could be a result of older agricultural lands reverting back to forests (for example, gas revenues have allowed some landowners to let their agricultural land to revert to forest), or from increased efforts to reforest riparian areas, especially within the Chesapeake Bay watershed.

Between 2009 and 2014, it is estimated from USDA Forest Service FIA that PA lost 320,778 acres, or an approximate rate of 175 acres/day, to development, deforestation, or conversion. Approximately 153,000 acres of forest were lost to development . Fortunately, forest gains exceeded forest losses during that period . However, recent data suggest that the balance may be tipping towards forest loss outpacing gain at the statewide scale. In the years leading up to 2018, it is estimated from USDA Forest Service FIA that PA lost 386,000 acres of forest land to development, deforestation, or conversion. Approximately 193,000 acres of forest were lost to development. Losses of forest land were offset by some gains in forest acreage (217,000 acres), resulting in a net loss of 169,000 acres . These trends are emerging and will be monitored closely as FIA plots are revisited and sampled. Regardless of the statewide ratios of gain and loss, strategic and collaborative approaches are required to protect forest land and minimize conversion, fragmentation, and parcelization across the commonwealth.

div.head: Fragmentation
div.p: Fragmentation of the forest is difficult to quantify and depends on the definition of a fragmenting feature. The resulting size and spatial arrangement of forest blocks define areas as interior forest and edge forest. While a certain amount of forest edge creates habitat beneficial to some wildlife, larger quantities of forest edge are problematic for species requiring expanses of unfragmented, interior forest. Fragmentation generally decreases integrity and function of core forest attributes. Forest fragmentation also creates conduits for the introduction and spread of invasive species. Pennsylvania already contains an abundance of roads and other fragmenting features, with the exception of large blocks of public forests in northern Pennsylvania. Over the last decade, aspects of Marcellus shale gas development have contributed to fragmentation of interior forest areas of northern Pennsylvania. A recent GIS core forest analysis layer was performed by DCNR Bureau of Forestry to show the fragmentation of forest across the state, using roads, gas wells, pipelines and electric lines, and other infrastructure to provide an understanding of where large areas of core forest are being fragmented (Fig. 2.3-2). The core forest analysis was based on the density of fragmenting features within a half mile of any given point, with fragmenting features including roads, pipelines, well pads, certain large rivers (large enough to show up on NLCD), etc. Where possible, such as on state forest land, this information can be used to reduce further fragmentation by using existing corridors for newer infrastructure when feasible. generations, there is a steady trend toward smaller parcels. For holdings greater than 10 acres, the average size for a private family forest is 46 acres. As forested parcels are subdivided and sold, new owners are often confronted with decisions regarding their forests. Whether new owners choose to develop their newly acquired land, or their management objectives simply differ from their neighbors, continuity of forest cover is jeopardized. Landscape-level management with a focus on overall sustainability is extremely difficult with larger numbers of landowners with wide-ranging management objectives. A recent study (Metcalf et al. 2012) estimates that Pennsylvania has 738,000 forest landowners, with an aging demographic, suggesting the potential for an increased rate of parcelization in the near future. The study estimates that half of Pennsylvania's private forests will change hands in the next two decades. In another study, researchers found that the next generation of landowners have varying viewpoints of forest ownership, thus raising additional uncertainty of future management and stewardship.

div.head: Summary
div.p: Forest conversion, fragmentation, and parcelization are separate but highly related phenomena, individually contributing to an increasing cause for concern as forest ownership continues to change hands and become divided into smaller, less contiguous units. With continued urban and Forest and woodland communities experience shifting conditions for a variety of reasons. An impact to one species can have resulting effects on other species within a community. For example, eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), a vital component in many riparian areas, influences processes affecting stream quality and site conditions and provides habitat or food to a wide range of plants and animals. The non-native insect pest, hemlock wooly adelgid, threatens these forest communities as infested hemlocks will die without intervention. The loss results in an unhealthy forest system, creating a ripple effect of impacts to processes and species, such as Pennsylvania endangered checkered rattlesnake-plantain (Goodyera tesselata) that depend on hemlockdominated site conditions. Stream chemistry process is changed by loss of hemlocks as well, causing a ripple effect in aquatic communities. The loss of ash trees due to the emerald ash borer is another example of far-reaching impacts. Many species of moths and butterflies use ash trees as larval host plants. Without this critical resource, larvae may not survive, and rare species may become extirpated.

Forest and woodland communities represent 20% of Pennsylvania's natural communities recognized by the Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program (PNHP). Statewide, there are 7 rare forested natural communities assigned a state rank by PNHP of S1 "critically imperiled" (extremely rare, often 5 or fewer occurrences in the state) to S2 "imperiled" (restricted range or very few populations, often 20 of fewer). There are also seven rare woodland natural communities ranked as critically imperiled to imperiled in Pennsylvania. None of these woodland or forest communities have been assigned a global rank. There are two globally-ranked (G3 "vulnerable," relatively few populations, often 80 or fewer globally) communities in Pennsylvania, both are forms of wetlands: cottongrass poor fen and sparsely vegetated vernal pool community.

Changes in regulatory protections can provide insight into the health of special concern species in Pennsylvania. Between 2010 and 2019, special concern species have experienced a mixture of declines and improvements in regulatory status (Table 2. . Some caution should be taken when reviewing this information. More scientific information has become available for many species, including improved sampling techniques and increased sampling areas. More scientific information has become available for some species, including sampling techniques and increased sampling areas. This has led to the discovery that some species were rare, but cryptic and difficult to sample for, particularly fish species such as bowfin, Ohio lamprey and mountain brook lamprey. In addition, taxonomic and genetic research has become more accessible and many plant species have been discovered to be non-native or not as rare as previously thought, not necessarily "recovered." Nevertheless, it is accurate to state that several species thought to be rare have been documented to be secure, which is an improvement. Plant species make up the majority of this list since DCNR updated their list of classified plants in 2018, a task that had not been done for over twenty years.

The Pennsylvania Wildlife Action Plan (PA WAP) was comprehensively reviewed and revised in 2015 (PGC-PFBC 2015). It includes 664 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), composed of 90 birds, 19 mammals, 65 fishes, 18 amphibians, 22 reptiles, and 450 invertebrates. The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat and Game Commissions developed and administer the PA WAP, a non-regulatory, proactive conservation blueprint to prevent SGCN from becoming endangered. It can be seen as the wildlife-and habitat-based counterpart to this Forest Action Plan.

All plant and wildlife species experience many different threats. Some threats have emerged or intensified since 2010, and others are ongoing. Diseases and pests, climate change, invasive plants, and habitat fragmentation, degradation and destruction are among the greatest issues. Hemlock wooly adelgid and emerald ash borer have continued expansion across the state, along with a suite of established plant diseases and pests that impact forests and woodlands. Spotted lanternfly is a new invasive pest that impacts forests and woodlands, and the species that depend upon them.

Wildlife diseases have devasting impacts on species across Pennsylvania (see Issue 8 below for more details). For example, chronic wasting disease, which impacts deer and elk, was first detected in Pennsylvania in 2012 and now (2019) confirmed in 13 counties. White-nose syndrome, a disease caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans, has caused severe declines in several hibernating bat species in Pennsylvania and nationwide. Reptiles and amphibians experience diseases including ranavirus, Chytridiomycosis, and snake fungal disease. Increased development continues to fragment and degrade forest communities. Impacts of development are compounded by invasive plants, which follow fragmentation corridors, allowing further spread. As invasive plants continue to expand into forest landscapes, the capacity for land managers to detect and eradicate novel populations becomes more limited. Limited funding, personnel and competing priorities are obstacles for benefitting forest and woodland special concern species.

Amidst the threats and declines, there have been some successes. Northeastern bulrush (Scirpus ancistrochaetus), a federally endangered plant whose population center is in Pennsylvania, is now being considered for removal from the federal list. Part of this success is due to the conservation work in Pennsylvania forests, such as protection and daylighting of vernal pools. Another success story is the Timber Rattlesnake, which was removed in 2016 from Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission's Candidate Species list. Recovering numbers were attributed to successfullyimplemented protective measures and regulations. Novel cooperative alliances, technologies, and approaches have emerged to assist in conserving forest and woodland species. For example, DCNR's Bureau of Forestry and Bureau of State Parks, the Pennsylvania Game Commission, and US Fish and Wildlife Service have developed a Bat Habitat Conservation Plan that will allow for continued and new activities that are beneficial to bats and their habitat.

Another cooperative approach that is used to benefit forest and woodland special concern species is the Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program (PNHP), a partnership among the DCNR and the PA Fish and Boat Commission, PA Game Commission, and the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy, in cooperation with the US Fish and Wildlife Service. PNHP conducts inventories and collects data for use in guiding conservation work, land-use planning, and land development. One way in which forest and woodland special concern species are identified and conserved across the commonwealth is through PNHP's Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory (PNDI) tool, an online platform for environmental review of special concern species. Since 1988, use of this tool has become routine in most environmental reviews. In 2018, PNHP launched a new web interface that combined PNDI environmental review screening and conservation planning, called the Pennsylvania Conservation Explorer. The Explorer provides significantly improved access to species information, habitat location, and conservation measures allowing users to more effectively avoid impacting rare, threatened, or endangered species when planning projects.

Additionally, the web-based Conservation Opportunity Area tool, launched in 2019 by the Pennsylvania Game Commission and Fish & Boat Commission, facilitates delivery of the 2015-2025 Pennsylvania Wildlife Action Plan. In the Conservation Opportunity Area Tool, users can find information on Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), habitats, conservation actions, and more, and can be used to explore statewide features or seek information in a user-defined area of interest (https://wildlifeactionmap.pa.gov/).

The sustainability meter for Indicator 4 moved down two notches towards unsustainable. The rationale for this is because while some species have seen some improvements, overall, the status of forest communities and their associated special concern species have declined or are at risk (e.g., hemlock, ash, etc.) due to compounding factors that include disease, invasive species, and habitat degradation. As defined by the US Forest Service, timberland is "forest land producing or capable of producing crops of industrial wood (more than 20 cubic feet per acre per year) and not withdrawn from timber utilization by statute or administrative designation. The statutes and designations apply only to publicly owned land. Timberland, formerly known as commercial forest land, may be "nonstocked" so long as no natural condition or human activity prevents or inhibits the establishment of tree seedlings." Timberland is an important economic indicator as it provides a measure of accessibility to the commonwealth's valuable hardwood resource. Land that is permanently withdrawn from wood product utilization by statute or administrative designation is known as "reserved forest land" in this inventory. "Other forest land" includes understocked areas and low-productivity forest land, which cannot produce at least 20 cubic feet of growing stock per acre annually under natural site conditions (such as sterile soil, dry climate, poor drainage, high elevation, steepness, or rockiness) .

Pennsylvania contains 16.1 million acres of timberland, representing over 96 % of the state's forest acreage. While the proportion of timberland to total forestland has decreased slightly since the 1950s, it has remained relatively constant for the past two decades. The decrease results mostly from public agencies designating areas off-limits to timber harvesting, such as State Forest Wild and Natural Areas and Wilderness and Roadless Areas on the Allegheny National Forest. Forest land conversion noted in Indicator 3 also contributes to a small decrease in total forest land acres estimated by FIA (see Figure 2.5-1). In addition to acreage alone, it is important to consider social and environmental variables that affect "access" to timber. Anecdotal reports suggest that it is becoming more difficult to procure quality timber for mills, despite adequate acreage of timberland and wood volumes in Pennsylvania. Certain biophysical constraints (steep terrain, riparian corridors) or access issues (lack of roads) can make harvests increasingly more expensive and complex. Variability in markets for forest products can affect the willingness to harvest or limit economic incentives for certain harvest types. Certain local ordinances make the forest management more complicated and further discourage timber harvesting on private land.

Although USDA Forest Service data indicate timberland in Pennsylvania is relatively stable over the long-term, recent studies and anecdotal evidence from the forest industry suggest that access to timber is highly-complicated, variable, and could become limited in the future. Acreage alone may be an oversimplification of the issue The meter remains the same, but emerging trends may reveal additional areas of need to maintain sustainability. The complexity of procuring the timber resource in certain areas may present obstacles for sustainable and timely harvest. Pennsylvania forests supply raw materials to a global industry producing a wide range of products from paper to hardwood flooring to high-end furniture and cabinetry-with black cherry, oak, and sugar (hard) maple currently being most desired. The forest products industry is an important component of many rural economies. Timber provides an important economic value to forestlands that is increasingly competing with other land uses like housing and commercial development. Sustainable production of quality forest products is critical to both Pennsylvania's economy and working forest landscapes.

A basic measure of timber sustainability is the comparison of wood volume removed to net tree growth. If net growth equals or exceeds the amount of wood removed, then theoretically, the forest is sustainable. According to USDA Forest Service FIA data, net tree growth in Pennsylvania's forest currently exceeds removals, at a ratio of about 2.3:1. On an annual basis, for every cubic foot of volume harvested our forests are growing another 2.3 cubic feet. On this measure alone, PA's forests are sustainable.

div.head: Net Growth (gross growthmortality) Removals
div.p: Net Change (net growthremovals) Northwest including species composition, tree quality, and regeneration trends. Recent FIA data (2018) indicate that the top species groups harvested in recent years are as follows: red oak (15.9%), soft maple (15.6%), white oak (11.7%), ash (9.3%) and beech (5.2%). Similarly, the 2016 Timber Products Output survey placed red oak, white oak, maples, and ash as the top species harvested across the commonwealth. Looking at regeneration trends, however, mesophytic and shadetolerant species, such as red maple, beech, and birch, are becoming more prevalent in the emerging cohort. These trends, coupled with further poor management practices and myriad regeneration challenges described in this plan, could lead to stands that contain trees of lesser quality, have a different species composition within the stand, or regenerate to a different forest community than was harvested. This suggests the mix of species available for harvesting in the future will be different. It is not clear if and how society's product demand will shift to match the changing forest composition, or if growing stock productivity will be equivalent to current or past conditions.

Further, as described in Indicator 5, the willingness of private landowners to harvest for wood products and manage responsibly is changing and management decisions across ownerships will affect the future sustainability of the timber resources in Pennsylvania. Finally, the current tree species mix provides a critical source of food and cover for wildlife, with the prevalence of preferred mast species declining, unknown impacts throughout the ecosystem may emerge leading to another critical, unanswered question of sustainability.

Based on the ratio of tree growth to removals, Pennsylvania's forests are sustainable, so the reading remains the same as in 2010, above the midpoint. Considering the holistic suite of variables, threats to forest health, and changing composition of the forest, overall future timber sustainability is not a given and trends should be monitored.

div.head: Indicator 6. Annual removal of merchantable wood volume compared with net growth
Sustainability Meter
