div.head: CRITERION 3: MAINTENANCE OF FOREST ECOSYSTEM HEALTH AND VITALITY Indicator 7. Area and percent of forest land affected by biotic and abiotic processes and agents
div.p: Considering the large list of potential "damaging agents," including forest insects and diseases, invasive plants, white-tailed deer browsing, weather events, excessive moisture, drought, climate change, air pollutants, poor management decisions, and wildfire, nearly every acre of forest in Pennsylvania has been affected by a damaging agent. While the stressors have been ubiquitous both across the landscape and throughout history, Pennsylvania's forests have proven resilient and diverse, but have not escaped unscathed.

At the broadest level, Pennsylvania has fewer acres of forest now than it did 200 years ago, and forest conversion to other land uses is occurring in some parts of the commonwealth. Diseases have essentially extirpated the American chestnut and American elm from their natural habitats though American elm in recent years has begun to increase. Hemlock woolly adelgid and elongate hemlock scale, beech bark disease, beech leaf disease, emerald ash borer, Asian long-horned beetle, spotted lanternfly, and sudden oak death threaten to do the same to other host species. In addition, native and non-native insects such as forest tent caterpillars and gypsy moth become problematic when combined with drought, deer browsing, and other stressors. Gypsy moth populations have impacted Pennsylvania forests cyclically for over 40 years . Over the past decade, the trend has been very low populations in the years between outbreaks, although impacts from previous mortality events are still impacting forests and their recovery in certain parts of Pennsylvania. Recent US FS FIA inventory data indicate that 83% of sampled plots had medium or high levels of deer browse impact (Albright et al. 2017). Invasive plant species abundance and occurrence are increasing, with the southern portion of Pennsylvania showing more impact that the north. Increased moisture due to more frequent weather events over the past ten years has caused new problems with root diseases, increased stress from too much moisture over shorter periods of time enabling secondary insect pests and diseases to attack the stressed trees. Such instances of compounding impacts and disease complexes may prove to be more problematic as abiotic stresses, such as extreme weather events, changing growing seasons, and other factors change the resilience of Pennsylvania's forests. Exacerbation of decline complexes is expected, and examples of synergistic impacts of pathogens and abiotic factors related to changing climate are documented, such as in black cherry decline (Royo et al., in review). The "green veneer" covering much of the state hides the fact that trees are dying, forest types are changing, diversity is declining, and overall forest health is a serious concern . The list of damaging agents is large, while preventative measures and controls are expensive and challenging over large landscapes. Despite these challenges, recent development of an ash management plan, hemlock conservation plan, DCNR Invasive Species Management Plan, Pennsylvania Invasive Species Management Plan, a national HWA Initiative, and development of host resistance and tolerance to various forest pests have provided forest managers methods to conserve and restore threatened tree species and landscapes. More collaborative alliances and landscape-scale partnerships, such as Pennsylvania Invasive Species Council, Allegheny Forest Health Collaborative, and Cooperative Invasive Species Management Areas, are forming to tackle these issues that cross ownerships and require an integrated and strategic approach to management, control, and mitigation. 0 1,000,000 2,000,000 3,000,000 4,000,000 5,000,000 From a holistic perspective, the health of Pennsylvania's forests is approaching an unsustainable condition in the face of a growing list of damaging agents (see Table 3.2-1 in Chapter 3). However, tools exist to address the most damaging agents. Even though progress is being made on several damage-causing agents, the Sustainability Meter Indicator remains the same as it was in 2010 as gains are offset by impacts due to spread and novel introductions.

div.head: Indicator 7. Area and percent of forest land affected by biotic and abiotic processes and agents
Sustainability Meter CRITERION 4: CONSERVATION AND MAINTENANCE OF SOIL AND WATER RESOURCES Indicator 8. Soil quality on forest land
div.p: Soil is defined by the Soil Science Society of America as: the unconsolidated mineral or organic material on the immediate surface of the earth that serves as a natural medium for the growth of land plants. Pennsylvania's native soils are generally well-suited to growing trees, as forests historically covered nearly the entire state. Pennsylvania has an extremely diverse set of soils ranging from sandy soils in the extreme southeast, to deep and fertile limestone valley soils in the central region, to a near absence of soil on rocky ridge tops, to the glaciated soils on the Allegheny Plateau famous for growing the prized black cherry. The four dominant soil orders in Pennsylvania are: Inceptisols, Ultisols, Alfisols, and Entisols.

The USDA NRCS defines soil quality as the capacity of a specific kind of soil to function within natural or managed ecosystem boundaries to: sustain plant and animal productivity, maintain or enhance water and air quality, and support human health and habitation. Soil quality relates directly to the site class of forest stands, which denotes the quality of the site for timber production. Soil quality also relates to the functioning of non-timber ecosystems such as wetlands, barrens habitats, and riparian areas necessary for diverse plant communities and associated wildlife. Soil quality is critical to growing plants and trees, and thus sustainable forests. In addition, soils play a critical role in carbon sequestration, with an estimated 420,629,873 metric tonnes (or 34.4% of total forest carbon in PA) found in soils (USFS FIA data, 2018; See also Indicator 11).

Forest soils are composed of an assortment of materials and organisms that, when viewed in whole, function as an ecosystem. The physical, chemical, and biological properties of Pennsylvania's forest soils have changed throughout history and continue to change-having the potential to affect conditions for plant and tree growth and ecosystem functions. Agents of change have included:

• Long-term climate change • Glaciation • Acid deposition • Acidified soils: lower pH, lower base cation concentrations, and greater aluminum availability leading to poor Ca:Al ratios • Accelerated erosion • Compaction
• Equipment, trails, and oil, gas, and mineral extraction • Exotic species :changing flora, fauna and resulting soil chemistry and structure
• Potential reduction in nutrient cycling from unsustainable biomass harvesting • Disruption of the soil profile of soil organic material at abandoned mine lands and gas development sites

Best management practices (BMPs) designed to protect soils from erosion have been developed and are generally widely accepted and followed across Pennsylvania. Forest regeneration in some parts of Pennsylvania is difficult to obtain and has been attributed to "soil quality," but little scientific data exist to characterize the situation with certainty. Other complicating factors such as changing chemistry and impacts of invasive flora and fauna raise additional questions about soil quality in the commonwealth. However, substantial progress has been made in reducing acid deposition since the 1991 Clean Air Act amendments with some National Acid Precipitation Monitoring Program numbers showing substantial decreases in nitrogen in precipitation samples.

There is a need for more information to fully understand the existing soil conditions and trends, and to develop practices and policies that address the entire soil ecosystem, which includes bacteria, algae, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, arthropods, earthworms, insects, small vertebrates, and plants, as well as physical and chemical properties of the soil. Some actions have improved the sustainability of soil health, such as improvement in air quality (and therefore reduction in nitrogen deposition). The impacts of these improvements on ecosystems are not yet fully understood. However, new impacts emerge and change, such as soil effects from invasive species or compaction and erosion due to increased development or forest activities. Some of the legacy impacts from acid deposition may require intervention to mitigate, even with less pressure from those systems (i.e., acid deposition has decreased, but base cations have already leached out of the system and may require lime supplementation to restore).
Because the widespread implementation of soil management BMPs, the meter remains slightly above the midpoint, despite historic and emerging impacts and the need for additional data.

div.head: Indicator 9. Area of forest land adjacent to surface water, and forest land by watershed
div.p: Pennsylvania contains 86,000 miles of streams, 4,000 lakes, reservoirs, and ponds, and over 400,000 acres of wetlands. Forests adjacent to these water bodies, commonly referred to as riparian forests or riparian forest buffers, are critical to providing clean water for humans and quality aquatic habitats for plants, animals, and fish. Riparian forests help to reduce the impact of upland land uses by providing overhead shade to cool the water and by trapping and filtering sediment, chemicals, and excess nutrients from agricultural operations and other human activities. Riparian forest buffers in urban settings help slow stormwater runoff and filter pollutants from sources such as lawn fertilizers. Forest cover also helps to ease the burden on municipal storm water systems. Additionally, riparian forests are a source of large woody material, a critical component to stream and floodplain habitats. Numerous studies have documented the benefits of riparian forests and for maximum benefits, 70 % or more of the length of streams in a watershed should be protected by a forested buffer. Statewide in Pennsylvania, about 65% of stream miles are buffered by a forest more than 100 meters wide (USFS).

Although riparian forest cover appears adequate at a statewide level, it matters enormously where the unbuffered streams are located, and the dynamics of forest cover benefits vary greatly at a local level. For example, unforested watersheds flowing through agricultural operations and in urban areas allow for greater runoff of nutrients and sediment into streams and rivers. Forest buffers are especially critical on small-order headwater streams to help keep water clean and cool, and to reduce the potential for flooding impacts further downstream. Generally speaking, headwater areas in Pennsylvania are well-protected with intact forests. As a whole, Pennsylvania streams and rivers have a high percentage of forest buffer coverage, but certain regions have critical need of more forest buffers, especially on small streams (Figures 2.9-1 and 2.9-2).

Threats to existing forest buffers include exotic pests such as hemlock woolly adelgid and emerald ash borer. These insects have led to the decline of many hemlock and ash riparian areas. Invasive plant species also pose a threat to existing and new forest buffers. Another major threat includes deforestation by private landowners who wish to clear the land for other purposes.

Beyond the amount of forest immediately adjacent to streams, overall forest cover within a watershed is another measure of watershed health. Water quality decreases as forests are converted to other uses, such as agriculture, or commercial and residential development. In general, research has demonstrated that watershed health begins to decline as forest cover drops below a range of 65-75% forest cover (see Goetz et al. 2003& Booth 2000). According the USDA Forest Service Forests to Faucets data, about 55% of Pennsylvania's 1451 small watersheds meet the 65% natural cover threshold. Small watersheds are the hydrologic unit code 12 (HUC12) delineations defined by the US Geological Survey; in Pennsylvania, HUC12 watersheds range from 1,834 -47,304 acres, with the average size being 21,412 acres. Balance between maintaining forest cover for water quality with necessary development can be found by keeping backyard woodlots, establishing urban canopy cover, and incorporating agroforestry techniques, such as riparian forest buffers, windbreaks, and hedgerows, into farming operations. The Chesapeake Bay cleanup efforts have been a major driver of riparian forest buffer reforestation and other watershed efforts in Pennsylvania. Half of the land area of Pennsylvania drains to the Chesapeake Bay from four major river basins, and Pennsylvania comprises 35 % of the entire Chesapeake Bay Watershed. The Susquehanna River is the largest tributary to the bay, providing 90 % of the freshwater flow to the upper bay and half of the total freshwater flow to the bay. Simply stated, the water quality of the Chesapeake Bay cannot be restored without Pennsylvania's support. But even more important, water quality in Pennsylvania must be restored. On December 29, 2010, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established the Chesapeake Bay Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL). This TMDL includes accountability features to guide sweeping actions to restore clean water in the Chesapeake Bay and the region's streams, creeks, and rivers. In addition, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires Pennsylvania and its neighbors in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed (Delaware, the District of Columbia, Maryland, New York, Virginia, and West Virginia) to reduce a suite of pollutants by specific amounts by 2025. Pennsylvania's targets are:

• Nitrogen: Reduce by 34 million pounds per year • Phosphorus: Reduce by 0.7 million pounds per year • Sediment (soil): Reduce by 531 million pounds per year Even with increased attention and resources given to riparian forest buffer projects, continued support and substantial expansion of efforts are needed to reach the TMDL goals. Riparian forests are critical to reaching pollution reduction targets in Pennsylvania, as forest buffers are an incredibly efficient pollution reduction measure. Annually, one acre of forest buffer can remove up to 100 pounds of total nitrogen, 8 pounds of phosphorus, and 2,483 pounds of suspended sediment in an average agricultural setting (Chesapeake Bay Program factsheet). Buffer width and placement are key factors affecting buffer efficiency-buffers planted at least 50 feet wide on smaller, headwater streams are the most efficient, but riparian forest buffers planted along any water course will have positive impacts on water quality (see WeConservePA for convenient guide). In Pennsylvania, within the Chesapeake Bay watershed alone, approximately 86,500 more acres of riparian forest buffer plantings are needed in order to meet stated water quality standards (Chesapeake Bay Program buffer goals for PA; PA's Phase III WIP).

Overall, heavily forested areas of Pennsylvania are at a sustainable condition relative to this indicator, while areas containing smaller amounts of forest cover, areas with a robust agricultural history, and areas experiencing heavy growth and development are unsustainable, as forests are converted to other land uses or lack forest cover for other reasons. State and federal programs exist to promote streamside tree planting and riparian forest protection. Pennsylvania is ramping up efforts to increase funding and efforts to plant new riparian forests across the commonwealth, but resources are still woefully inadequate to realize outlined goals for planting additional riparian forest buffers.

Because the significant work required to address the challenges and inadequate resources to implement, the meter was dropped one notch toward unsustainable. It still remains above the midpoint toward Sustainable, but attention and resources are needed to ensure the downward trend does not continue.

div.head: Indicator 9. Area of forest land adjacent to surface water, and forest land by watershed
Sustainability Meter Indicator 10. Water quality in forested areas
div.p: Forested watersheds are key components of a public infrastructure that provides clean drinking water to millions of Pennsylvanians. Three-hundred and five surface water supply systems provide drinking water to 7.5 million Pennsylvanians, while the remaining population obtains its drinking water from groundwater systems which are hydrologically linked to surface waters (Fig. 2.10.-1). The quality of the water from these watersheds is of obvious interest, not only as drinking water sources for human populations, but for the health of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Forested watersheds produce higher quality water than non-forested watersheds and the relationship between length of unimpaired streams is directly correlated to the amount of forested cover within a watershed (Fig. 2-10-2). Recent nationwide analyses of watershed importance identified all but 2 of the HUC12 watersheds in Pennsylvania as "target watersheds" for prioritizing in water conservation. Target watersheds are those that have a municipal ground water supply and a Forests to Faucets importance index of >30. The index of importance to surface drinking water includes areas important for providing water (water supply), areas where drinking water is removed for use (water demand), and lands that connect the water supply and demand (Fig. 2.10-3). When considering the location of watersheds with the greatest forest cover and the locations of watersheds ranked highest in this analysis of surface water importance, the relationship is roughly inverse, with the watersheds with the highest importance index occurring where there is lower percentage of forest cover (Figure 2.9-2 vs. Figure 2.10-3). Recognizing that water quality at any point is affected by a large land base that encompasses far more than just the immediately surrounding watershed, it is important to note that much of the headwater areas of major water systems in Pennsylvania originate from well-forested and protected lands, such as state forest land. The complexity of water issues is readily apparent, with many factors and contributing variables. In general, efforts for establishing riparian forest buffers should focus on areas where streamside forests are absent or minimal. Areas with established forest should be maintained as forest cover to ensure the highest quality of water throughout the system. While our forested watersheds help to provide clean water, Pennsylvania still has many serious water quality and aquatic ecosystem issues, especially in areas where forest cover and riparian buffers are lacking. Statewide, major issues include increased water temperature due to lack of shade, abandoned mine drainage (AMD), sedimentation, excess storm water runoff, industrial spills, acidified streams due to acid deposition, fragmentation that limits aquatic organism passage (AOP), and fluctuations in seasonal water quantity. Threats to forests in general, especially riparian forests, impact water quality, such as hemlock wooly adelgid, emerald ash borer, invasive plants, and climate change. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) has listed 17,498 miles of streams as impaired for aquatic life. Abandoned mine drainage (AMD) is also a leading source of impairment. Current stream crossing assessments using the North Atlantic Aquatic Connectivity Collaborative (NAACC) protocol indicate that 27% of stream crossings allow for full AOP, 41% allow reduced AOP, and 32% have no AOP. Efforts to improve water quality and mitigate the effects of pollutants are underway, but face serious challenges such as increasing development, inadequate treatment through combined storm and sewer systems, and a highly modified environment that includes legacy sediments, channelized streams, and impervious surfaces. With general acceptance and implementation of erosion and sedimentation BMPs, forest management activities do not represent a threat to water quality in forested watersheds. Roads associated with forest activities, however, can impact connectivity of aquatic ecosystems. Ground and surface water impacts from shale gas development (drilling activity as well as increased infrastructure and road traffic) is also a major concern; however, recent monitoring efforts have not detected water quality impacts directly related to the shale gas development activities (https://mdw.srbc.net/remotewaterquality/assets/downloads/pdf/continuous-water-qualitytrends-susquehanna-basin-2016.pdf; https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/Conservation/ForestsAndTrees/NaturalGasDrillingImpact/ShaleGasMonit oring/Pages/default.aspx).

Pennsylvania's special protection waters are classified by the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) into several categories indicating water quality, with exceptional value (EV) and high quality (HQ) being the top two categories. Currently, there are 22,248 miles of waterways classified as High Quality and 3,875 miles of waterways are classified as Exceptional Value. Many of the HQ and EV streams in Pennsylvania occur in forested settings on both public and private land, placing great importance on the management decisions of private landowners and public land managers alike.

The Pennsylvania Fish & Boat Commission also classifies streams based on trout reproduction and biomass. Class A trout streams are considered the best trout streams in Pennsylvania based on trout biomass. As of the writing of this document (2020), Pennsylvania has over 16,000 miles of naturally reproducing trout streams statewide (31% Public, 69% Private), and over 2,500 miles of Class A trout streams (38% Public, 62% Private), with 79% of the Class A trout streams are found within watersheds with >65% forested cover.

Due to the daily importance of clean water, this is one of the most significant indicators to Pennsylvania citizens. Our forested watersheds have proven their ability to provide clean water and with proper management and BMP implementation will continue to do so. However, impaired streams remain and additional threats loom in the future. Water quality needs to remain a priority issue for natural resource managers and associated stakeholders.
For now, the meter remains the same as the 2010 reading, as abundant forested watersheds remain to protect the headwaters.

div.head: CRITERION 5: MAINTENANCE OF FOREST CONTRIBUTION TO GLOBAL CARBON CYCLES Indicator 11. Forest ecosystem biomass and forest carbon pools
div.p: Worldwide, promoting sustainable forests has been recognized as a key strategy for mitigating potential climate change impacts. Sustainably managed forests can store carbon for decades, while also providing associated co-benefits such as improved water quality, plant and animal habitat, wood products, and recreation opportunities. Durable wood products generated from harvested timber are an important and recognizable source of long-term sequestration, with a smaller carbon footprint compared to other, more energy intensive building materials, such as concrete and steel.

Pennsylvania's forests sequester (remove from the atmosphere and store) significant amounts of carbon annually, with carbon flowing in and out of identified carbon pools for a number of reasons-all related to disturbance events such as insect and disease mortality, wildfires, storms, and harvesting. Overall, our forests capture and store carbon when new growth of trees exceeds total removals. The carbon pools are live trees and plants (above and below ground), dead wood, plant debris litter on the forest floor, and soil organic material, which results from the decomposition of plant material. The US Forest Service estimates that between 2007 and 2017, on average Pennsylvania's forests sequestered an additional 7 million metric tonnes of carbon each year (USFS FIA 2018). Estimated total carbon stored in all carbon pools to 1.2 billion metric tonnes in 2017 (Figure 2.11-1), a 2.9% increase from 2012 (FIA 2018). The majority of the sequestered carbon is found in the live above ground plant material, followed by soil organic material . The forest's capacity to sequester carbon is directly tied to its health and overall management-the healthier the forest the more carbon it can sequester. Disturbance events that cause tree mortality release carbon into the atmosphere, thus reducing sequestration rates. Considering the status of Indicator 7 (damaging agents), this indicator could be rated similarly if insects and diseases, invasive flora and fauna, loss of forestland, and other impacts are not appropriately addressed.

However, based on net tree growth (Indicator 6), which is the primary measure of carbon sequestration capacity, this indicator receives a sustainable rating. Timely monitoring and threat suppression programs are vital to accounting for and maintaining the positive carbon balance of Pennsylvania's forests.

div.head: CRITERION 6: MAINTENANCE AND ENHANCEMENT OF LONG-TERM MULTIPLE SOCIOECONOMIC BENEFITS TO MEET THE NEEDS OF SOCIETIES
div.p: Indicator 12. Wood and wood products production, consumption, and trade

Pennsylvania's working forests, both public and private, contribute significantly to local and statewide economies while providing a suite of other values and services. Pennsylvania produces some of the finest hardwoods in the world and is well known for its cherry, oak, maple, and ash. In 2016, harvest levels were estimated at 1.3 billion board feet with annual sales of $21 billion and a total economic impact of $37 billion (see also Indicator 16). According to the Timber Products Output (TPO) survey for production year 2016, top species by volume processed in Pennsylvania were red oak, mixed hardwoods, white oak, ash, and red/soft maple. The TPO survey also indicates that 66% of volume was in Lumber/Dimension, 30% in Pulp/Chips, and Exports accounted for 4% of the volume processed (Fig. 2.12-1). path for collaboration and partnership in outreach and promotion of quality Pennsylvania forest products. However, since the spring of 2018, global timber markets have peaked and taken a significant downturn, primarily due to a slowdown in the Chinese economy and the tariff dispute.

Even with a trade resolution, the effects will likely continue from the slowdown in the Chinese economy. The US market share of wood products is shrinking due to the recent trade dispute, as other countries are fulfilling Chinese timber demands. It may take decades to regain this share as a source for US forest products.

Steady and thriving markets for wood products are essential to forest management. When markets are good and demand for forest products is high, land managers can readily sell timber and create healthy young forests via timber harvest. Additionally, income from selling timber provides landowners with incentives to keep their land forested and provides funding for forest management activities, such as wildlife habitat improvements or invasive species control. In addition, having a variety of market options, including markets to sell low-grade material (pulp, biomass), is critical in management of lower quality sites. Conversely, as markets slow, it is more economically difficult to regenerate forests and create early successional forest habitat. Poor markets can begin a chain reaction in which harvesting decreases, which means decreases in availability of work for loggers and mills, which then increases the likelihood of closures and loss of professionals and facilities available to do work, making industry recovery even more difficult.

Careful monitoring of the timber products output is essential to formulate policies and programs that support the wood economy of Pennsylvania. To bolster efforts to evaluate ongoing trends, the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry has re-invigorated efforts to conduct a Timber Product Output (TPO) survey on a regular basis (every 4 years). This survey assesses trends in harvest and production, in terms of region, volume, species, product type, among other myriad demographics that provide insight into the current status of wood-products industry across the commonwealth. Surveys were completed for 2012 and 2016 production and reports can be found online (https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/Business/ForestProducts/Pages/default.aspx). In addition, the USDA Forest Service also compiles statistics from primary wood processing facilities which can be used in conjunction with the bureau's TPO and compared across states and regions in the US.

In addition to the social impacts on wood products production, consumption, and trade, natural threats can have major influence on the availability and consumption of certain products. The rapid proliferation of the emerald ash borer has decimated ash populations across all of Pennsylvania. While current harvest and processing estimates reflect an uptick in ash production, much of this represents salvage efforts to remove dead or dying ash before it is unusable. Other insects, diseases, and species declines could lead to reduction of quality or quantity of those major highquality hardwood products for which Pennsylvania is known, such as declines in black cherry health and mesophication of oak forests. Deer over-population and invasive plant species are a continued threat to forest health overall.

The production of high-quality hardwoods appears sustainable in the short-run, while long-term sustainability depends on the health of the forest and robustness of the industry to operate in a global marketplace. Emerging markets such as carbon, biomass, and non-timber forest products (NTFPs) all have the potential to be additional sources of revenue and leverage points for sustainable management. While production, expansion, and consumption of PA wood products has steadily expanded since the 2008 recession (although still not achieving pre-2009 harvest levels), and PA producers continue to diversify into various market streams and export markets, the current tariff conflicts loom large, as China was the single largest importer of Pennsylvania hardwood logs and lumber.

Domestic demand and demand from a few other smaller countries remains positive for now. While significant gains in NTFP marketing and education have helped this small niche industry and the landowners growing these products, as well as carbon markets gaining more attention with climate change pressures increasing, the overarching issues with global trade, consumption, and likely decreasing production of wood products are cause for concern. With the recent downturn in global wood product markets and the decline that is projected for 2020 and 2021, the sustainability meter has been set slightly lower than in 2010.

Indicator 12. Wood and wood products production, consumption, and trade Land management agencies and numerous volunteer organizations spend considerable time and money maintaining facilities and planning events to support this excellent level of recreation opportunities. Pennsylvania boasts more than 6,300 miles of trails providing opportunities for hiking, biking, and ATV, snowmobile, and horseback riding. Two thousand miles of water trails provide canoeing, kayaking, and camping opportunities along streams and rivers. Recent planning efforts have identified gaps in recreation trails and efforts are underway to fill the gaps and provide connections through greenways and other corridors, and efforts to develop railroad beds into functional recreational trails continue to garner support. Survey data show that trails are consistently the top facility/infrastructure that is of concern to recreators.

div.head: Sustainability Meter
div.p: The value of the recreation economy has risen sharply in the last decade. The outdoor recreation industry contributes $29 billion to the commonwealth's gross domestic product (SCORP 2020-24), and a recent study by the Center for Rural Pennsylvania put the total estimated annual expenditures at $400 million for recreational trips to State Forests alone (report from Center for Rural PA, 2018).

Since the last revision of the PA Forest Action Plan, outdoor recreation opportunities have diversified and use levels have intensified for most opportunities. According to the 2020-24 State Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP), Pennsylvanians revealed that over 50% of respondents participated in outdoor recreation at least once a month. Most public opinion polls place outdoor recreation at or among the top use values for public forest lands. In the same public poll conducted as part of the SCORP, 65% of Pennsylvanians agree that parks, trails, and open space are an essential part of the healthcare system. The top five outdoor recreation activities for Pennsylvanians are hiking, walking/running, visiting historic sites or nature centers, scenic driving, and camping (SCORP 2020-24). While less popular than in the past, hunting and fishing still engage many outdoor enthusiasts. In addition to expanding use, broad planning efforts and crossownership cooperation have increased to strategically address recreation needs and challenges, most notably 2 Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plans have been completed (2014,2020). Currently, the COVID-19 global pandemic is increasing the number of visitors to parks and forests to unprecedented levels, as outdoor recreation is of the few available options for socializing and getting exercise. While new expanded use introduces potential new advocates and stewards of parks and forests, carrying capacity and resource impacts must be carefully balanced against providing opportunities for outdoor recreation.

Current infrastructure needs across PA Parks and Forests are estimated at over $500 million (PPFF Infrastructure Study, 2017). Aging infrastructure and special infrastructure requirements for new recreational pursuits may put additional strain on funding and maintenance, especially as interest and use increases. Increases in visitation necessitate the funneling of additional resources into certain measures, such as sanitation and erosion/sedimentation control.

With attention and support garnered by the recently completed Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan, outdoor recreation opportunities appear sustainable in Pennsylvania's near future. Current budget shortfalls, increasing infrastructure use, and potential impacts from shale gas development are causes for concern. Climate change has the potential to create significant challenges in maintaining infrastructure. Concerns for the future also include carrying capacity issues for some popular recreation destinations, challenges with infrastructure maintenance with decreasing budgets, and ensuring recreation opportunities are inclusive and accommodating to all Pennsylvanians.

Because of the significant increases in use and threats, without adequate resources to ensure sustainability of infrastructure and natural resources, this meter has dropped one notch since the 2010 plan. Although still in the 'sustainable' category, vast investments are needed.

div.head: Indicator 13. Outdoor recreational participation and facilities
Sustainability Meter
div.p: Grey arrow=2010 reading and marketing, and forest health all help to dictate an informed future in understanding and sustaining forest health, management, and productivity for society. However, federal agencies, including the USDA Forest Service, have seen a significant reduction in support for research. Concerns exist with the recent variability of the timber market and gas market, increasing costs for contractors, as well as invasive species movement, deer herbivory on native plants, climate change effects, and staffing to meet these challenges. Government agency budgets continue to be lean, especially in light of the current economic downturns resulting from the global pandemic. Some of these concerns are perpetual, others will likely ebb and flow over the coming decade.

Because the investments have been met with new challenges and obstacles, as well as stagnant or decreasing availability of funds for management and research efforts, the meter reading has moved down one tick to the midpoint in the yellow. Targeted and effective investments are needed to support these areas and sustain forest health, management, research, and wood processing

div.head: Indicator 15. Forest Certification
div.p: The emergence of third-party certification grew out of a joint effort by environmental groups, forest industries, and other nonprofit economic development organizations. The goal of certification was to arrive at a consensus on numerous criteria for sustainable forest practices and to establish a process to certify forest products as sustainably-produced per these criteria. Organizations, landowners, foresters, or industries could have their forest products certified as sustainably produced, through a third-party audit process. The primary entities for certification in Pennsylvania are FSC, SFI, and American Tree Farm. Each system has a set of management standards that landowners must follow and are evaluated against during audits of management practices.

Pennsylvania was one of the first states to have the entire state forest system certified as sustainably-managed. Pennsylvania State Forests have been certified continuously by Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) since 1998 and gained additional certification by Sustainable Forestry Initiative (SFI) in 2018. This certification assures the citizens of the commonwealth that their forests are managed with the most up-to-date and sustainable practices and are reviewed by an outside entity. It also sets an example for other landowners of the benefits of certification, as well as assisting the wood products industry by providing a steady flow of certified wood. Currently, there are over 2.5 million acres of FSC certified acres in Pennsylvania, including both public and private ownerships. Pennsylvania now has over 2.3 million acres certified to the SFI Forest Management Standard, 22 companies that hold SFI Certified Sourcing certificates, and 68 companies that hold SFI Chain of Custody certification.

Certification of private forests is growing within Pennsylvania. In the past, costs to landowners were prohibitive, but in recent years, more affordable options have arisen. In 2017, the State Tree Farm committee initiated a membership fee to cover the cost of certifying Tree Farms. Currently (2019) there are 193 Tree Farms with a total of 44,600 acres being managed to the 2015-2020 Standards of Sustainability for Forest Certification as endorsed by the Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification (PEFC). Participation in the third-party certification requires landowners to be audited every 5 years to ensure their compliance to the sustainability standards.

In addition to forest certification, two programs assess communities' adoption of standards and guidelines for managing trees in community settings, the USDA Forest Service Urban and Community Forestry Program (through its Community Accomplishment Reporting System (CARS)) and the National Arbor Day Foundation (through its Tree City USA Program and related programs). For the federal fiscal year ending September 30, 2019, DCNR reported that 250 communities in PA have active, "managing" urban and community forestry programs, while another 560 have programs classified as "developing," according to the CARS standards. Additionally, Pennsylvania has 139 communities, campuses, and companies participating in Arbor Day Foundation programs that set and track standards annually for participating entities (2020 calendar year: 111 Tree City USA, 18 Tree Campus USA, 7 Tree City USA Growth Award, and 3 Tree Line USA).

The Bureau of Forestry's Urban and Community Forestry Program, also known as TreeVitalize, is a statewide partnership made up of a variety of public, private, and non-governmental stakeholders. Participating stakeholders span from federal and state agencies to local level community groups. The TreeVitalize program seeks to educate citizens and increase quality of life for Pennsylvanians in communities across the rural to urban gradient through tree planting, tree care, and tree planning. TreeVitalize helps citizens understand the myriad benefits of planting trees, the importance of keeping existing trees in the community healthy, and the value of sufficient tree canopy. Common benefits of trees that are a focus of the program include air pollution reduction, shade and cooling, property value growth, storm water control, and community beautification. The program also encourages-and provides outlets and grant funding for citizens and municipalities to improve their urban and community forests. Internal staff and external partners conduct trainings for volunteer Tree Tenders (Tree Tenders is a registered trademark of the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society) across the state. TreeVitalize team members work across the commonwealth to:
1. Guide, manage, and support the TreeVitalize program and its partners, providing leadership and coordination to stakeholders and communities engaged in urban and community forestry;

2. Enable communities and TreeVitalize partners to set, achieve, and track tree canopy goals; support communities with technical assistance in urban and community forestry practices; FSC which may disallow certain entities from maintaining certification while completing the management required on their forests. Costs of certification continue to be restrictive for many landowners with small tracts, but new systems and opportunities, such as American Tree Farm System, are emerging to provide a more accessible option for certification of these smaller private forests. It is critical that markets for certified products are promoted and maintained to incentivize the cost and commitment of certification for landowners. In addition to formal third-party certification systems, support programs are in place to assist in adoption of broad guidelines and best practices for communities, such as Tree City USA and TreeVitalize.

Because there is increasing interest in certification and additional opportunities for landowners with smaller parcels, this meter is set slightly above the midpoint toward sustainable. To ensure forest certification efforts remain sustain in Pennsylvania, continued work is needed to incentivize and promote certified products, as well as provide affordable options to private landowners.

div.head: Sustainability Meter
div.p: Note: this metric was not used in 2010 so no previous meter reading is available.

div.head: Indicator 16. Employment and wages in forest-related sectors
div.p: Sustainable management of our forests depends on a community of professional resource managers working in partnership with a robust and vibrant forest products industry. Pennsylvania is a state rich in agriculture and natural resources. One major sector of the Pennsylvania agricultural industry is the forest industry. Because this sector is quite different from most traditional agricultural sectors, it is often overlooked when considerations are being made for economic development efforts. Pennsylvania is the largest producer of hardwood lumber in the United States and is known for its high-quality hardwoods. Currently, imports of finished goods outweigh exports, which suggests the opportunity to increase demand for domestically-processed finished goods. The forest products sector is also a major source of employment for the state with potential for growth, especially in secondary processing and manufacturing.

The Pennsylvania forest industry generates value by starting with raw materials (trees) from its vast forests, which cover 16.8 million acres, and harvesting them through logging and timber companies. Once harvested, the trees pass through primary manufacturers, or processing mills, including pulp mills, plywood & veneer mills, and sawmills. Next, the materials from these manufacturers go through secondary manufacturing processes, including paper, wood paneling, pallet, and furniture manufacturers. Additional products, including sawdust, mulch, pellets (biomass energy), biochar, and biofuels, are also created as part of the manufacturing process. These residual products are growing in importance in the value chain of timber. The finished goods are then sold through wholesale and retail distributers to consumers, construction companies, and other manufacturers.

Exports of raw materials, particularly to China in recent years, make up a large part of the economic impact of the forest sector. Unfortunately, due to differences in labor and manufacturing costs to turn raw materials such as logs into finished goods such as furniture, much of the secondary processing portion of the value chain is completed outside of Pennsylvania.

Employment data are sourced from Pennsylvanians Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages. Forest related employment is based on four sectors; forestry/logging, wood product manufacturing, paper, board and fiber, and furniture related products.

In 2009, Pennsylvania employment estimates forest-related sectors placed total employment at around 66,000 workers, with an estimated total economic impact of $25 billion. In these sectors, "Paper, Board, and Fiber" category was the largest source of employment, followed by "Wood Product Manufacturing", "Furniture and Related Products", and "Logging and Forestry" (Table 2.16-1). In 2019, the same data source estimated the employment for the forest-related sectors over 65,000 employees. Although this is fewer employees working than in 2009, the estimated total economic impact is now estimated to be $37 billion, which is up from $25 billion in 2009. This $12 billion increase in economic impact is far ahead of inflation rates over this same time. The distribution of the workers since 2009 has changed somewhat, with "Wood Product Manufacturing (Sawmills)" now being the largest source of employment and "Paper, Board, and Fiber"-related jobs experiencing a decrease (Table 2.16-1).

The forest products industry, land managers and related government agencies, and professional consulting firms provide good sources of forest-based employment in all parts of Pennsylvania. Long-term employment sustainability ties to both the ecological condition of the forest and the overall economic climate. As discussed in Indicator 12, Pennsylvania industries are operating in a highly-competitive global market with many forces at play. Alternative energy initiatives such as biomass could provide additional employment opportunities. Overall, the forest-related employment sector appears stable for now but has much room to grow. Concern arises about the sustainability of the employment and recruitment to the profession if wages do not keep up with inflation. Other concerns are the high cost of workers compensation insurance and the lack of new loggers and foresters. 1,000 less workers in this same time span. The decrease in total number of workers could be due to increased mechanized equipment in timber harvesting and manufacturing and the decline in the paper/board/fiber sector. Most wages have increased over the last decade, but some have stayed below the inflation rate. There continues to be much concern over the volatility of export markets, and the lack of domestic markets for wood products.

Although growth continues, uncertainty and volatility remain and therefore the meter remains at the same location as in the 2010 plan. SILVAH is the computerized implementation of a systematic approach to silviculture, in which current conditions are identified through a systematic inventory of overstory and understory. These conditions are evaluated using an objective set of research-based standards and the constraints and objectives of the land-manager. Then a prescription is recommended to move the stand closer to the manager's objectives. SILVAH provides managers with consistent, science-based decision-making tools that help ensure sustainability. The sustainability of SILVAH and the associated training sessions as tools for organizing research results to support sustainable and adaptive practices is threatened by substantial disinvestments of federal funding to support such work (discussed also in Indicator 14).

div.head: Forest Certification
div.p: Third-party certification systems (covered in more detail under Indicator 15) also provide a standardized framework of broadly-accepted best management practices that factor in the multifaceted nature of forest management. The number of certified acres and opportunities for certifications are growing in Pennsylvania.

div.head: Education Resources
div.p: Several organizations and agencies work to provide education and outreach to forest landowners and a host of other audiences in rural and urban settings.

div.head: Forester Certification
div.p: In Pennsylvania, there is no requirement for professional certification of foresters, such that anyone can legally claim to be a forester or forestry consultant, regardless of training, certifications, or experience. Private landowners must carefully choose the specialists they hire to plan and implement forest management on their property.

div.head: Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory Environmental Reviews
div.p: The Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory (PNDI) is a collection of natural heritage information used to identify potential impacts to threatened, endangered or rare plants, animals, natural communities, and geologic features throughout Pennsylvania. PNDI is used to conduct environmental reviews for various projects that have potential to impact these resources. Pennsylvania forest owners have a wealth of effective standards and guidelines addressing a broad spectrum of resource management issues and interests at their disposal. Public lands are effectively managed through state and federal laws, certification systems, data-driven analysis programs, public involvement, and resource plans. These processes are updated with new information and science to yield the best possible resource management strategies and outcomes. Despite the challenges of staffing and budget reductions, funding for research facilities, and lack of adoption by some owners in the private landscape, Pennsylvania continues maintain and enhance working forest management standards and guidelines for sustainable forest practices.
Despite the challenges with implementation, the standards and guidelines continue to increase and facilitate cooperation. This meter has improved toward sustainability since the 2010 reading.
Indicator 18. Forest-related planning, assessment, policy, and law

div.head: Forest Planning
div.p: Forest planning guides decisions that aim to achieve long-term ecosystem sustainability while obtaining the benefits and services society currently needs and desires. Comprehensive planning includes inventories and resource information, public input (for public lands) and landowner objectives and is adaptive to incorporate changing conditions and research findings.

Planning in Pennsylvania occurs at multiple scales ranging from statewide to individual tree care in the State Forest Resource Management Plan (specific to state forests), the Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan, the State Wildlife Action Plan, the State Water Plan, the Pennsylvania Greenways Action Plan, and the Pennsylvania Invasive Species Management Plan. These plans provide a statewide context and help to set priorities for funding projects aimed to achieve state-level goals and objectives. Intermediate-level planning includes eco-regional and landscape-level plans such as: DCNR's eight Conservation Landscapes; watershed planning, including the Chesapeake Bay Initiative; and regional councils of government. In addition, several topic or species-based plans have been developed in recent years, such as the Hemlock Conservation Plan, Ash Management Plan, and Guidelines for Administering Oil and Gas Activity on State Forest Lands.
County comprehensive plans, municipal planning, and local zoning and ordinances occur at the local level and are highly variable considering that Pennsylvania has 2,560 municipalities.

Property-specific planning comes in many forms including Forest Stewardship, Conservation Activity Plan 106 (CAP 106) and Tree Farm Plans, in addition to custom plans developed by consultants, and plans tied to conservation easements. DCNR and other organizations have adopted and support a common template (developed by WeConservePA, formerly the Pennsylvania Land Trust Association (PALTA)) for developing conservation easements in Pennsylvania. Most experts agree that forest planning guided by resource professionals is lacking for most of Pennsylvania's private forests and that helping landowners think of themselves as part of a larger landscape is particularly needed to achieve effective, ecosystem-based outcomes.

Accurate and timely inventory information is a foundation for any planning effort. Several natural resource inventories exist on a large scale in Pennsylvania, including the USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA), State Forest and State Game Land inventories, Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory, and County Natural Areas Inventories. On State Forests and State Game Lands, each of the respective agencies have conducted their own Continuous Forest Inventory to supplement the USDA Forest Service FIA data, and answer questions specific to the needs and goals each land management agency. Numerous other inventories exist across the commonwealth, from widespread water monitoring networks to forest pest monitoring to communities that inventory their street trees. Inventories conducted across ownerships and across agencies offer unique opportunities to collaborate and tackle issues at scales appropriate for management actions. Resource managers continuously cite inventory and monitoring as an overall need for improvement.

Federal lands in Pennsylvania have their own plans as well as connections to related plans with partner agencies. Allegheny National Forest and military installations each have resource management plans that outline goals and objectives specific to their land base and management goals.

div.head: Forest Policy and Law
div.p: Well-designed and properly administered policies and laws can help to conserve forest resources. It is important for governments to acknowledge the importance of forest values and accordingly develop policies sufficient to ensure the protection of public benefits, such as wildlife and clean water, as well as sustainability for future generations. In Pennsylvania, several state agencies have jurisdictional responsibilities over natural resources (Table 2.18-1). All federal regulations are also applicable and overseen by their respective federal agency, such as the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), or Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). The intent of these statutes is to make it easier to carry out forestry activities by limiting the scope of zoning. Given this broad legislative mandate, municipalities that regulate forestry activities will have to craft ordinance provisions that are based on sound forestry principles and practices. The statute does not define "unreasonable". If a zoning ordinance prohibits timber harvesting in zoning districts with significant forests or makes timbering a special exception or conditional use subject to many burdensome and time-consuming requirements, the ordinance is subject to challenge by landowners and loggers alike. There have been several forestry-related cases filed through the ACRE law that have been successful. ACRE is a way for complaints about ordinances that restrict agricultural operations to be lodged. Forestry-based suits have been brought by landowners and industry against ordinances that were seen to be overly-restrictive related to the right to practice forestry listed in the MPC. In order to be successful, the PA Attorney General must agree with the assessment of the ordinance and then will take up negotiations with the offending municipality. This often results in successful rewrites of ordinances but could also result in a lawsuit in which the Attorney General files against a municipality and it would be heard in a court. This approach has been successfully used several times in forestry-related cases.

At the local level, regulations vary but fall into a few general categories. First, some municipalities have enacted local ordinances to control timber harvesting to some extent through the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code. However, the Right to Practice Forestry provision prohibits local governments from using a zoning ordinance to unreasonably restrict forestry activities. Local municipalities also enact land use, road bonding and street tree ordinances. Local municipal regulations concerning earth moving, timber harvesting, and other activities associated with forest management vary considerably. Therefore, it is advisable for earth movers, landowners, resource professionals, and timber harvesters to become familiar early in the planning stages with codes and ordinances currently enforced by the municipality in which work is anticipated. Working with Pennsylvania's 2,560 individual municipalities represents a formidable challenge when working to establish comprehensive, well-informed policies for managing natural resources.

Certain taxation laws also have implications for the forest products industry as well as communities that depend on forests. For example, sales tax exemptions, such as those afforded to agricultural industries have recently been extended to certain logging operations equipment, communities are receiving higher payments for public lands in their jurisdiction, and tax relief for landowners keeping their land as forests was revised to ensure equity. From the Green Ribbon Task Force Report: Considering the assessment of other indicators and in the absence of major changes, the current framework for planning and policy is questionable for ensuring the long-term sustainability of Pennsylvania's forests. The work of collaborative groups and cross-boundary planning efforts have offset the relative lack of new laws to enforce best practices. The meter remains slightly above the midpoint, relying heavily on the continued work of forestry leaders and cooperative groups.
Indicator 18. Forest-related planning, assessment, policy, and law
