div.p: Grey arrow=2010 reading

div.head: Summary: Overall Sustainability
div.p: Pennsylvania contains a vast and diverse forest resource that provides numerous societal benefits for humans and invaluable ecological services to thousands of species. To quantify and measure the condition of this resource is a daunting and complex task and is extensively detailed in myriad research, reports, and informational outlets. As an overarching snapshot of the current situation to provide context for the issues and strategies outlined in this plan, the Criteria and Indicators developed by the Montreal Process and adapted by NMSFA for the northeastern United States were used. The sustainability meters and their associated text provide a broad summarization of critical considerations for each of these factors and forces working to advance or hinder achievement of sustainability in each realm.

The challenges identified herein are numerous and appear to multiply and expand with growing human population, climate change, and increased demands on our forests. However, the awareness and resources allotted to finding solutions and strategies are also significant. Collaboration, new technology, and novel approaches to these problems bode well for the conservation of Pennsylvania's forests and all natural resources of the commonwealth. Since 2010, there have been many changes to forest resources of the commonwealth, from introduction of spotted lanternfly to new forest landowner education opportunities to the establishment of groups that promote the utilization of Pennsylvania wood products. Species have recovered and species have declined. Additional acres of forest were certified as well-managed, and new resources have become available for outdoor recreation. Focus on urban forestry and tree cover in our urban communities has gained interest and relevance. While some factors have worsened, and others have improved, the overall sustainability meter for Pennsylvania's forest resources remains at the same reading as in 2010. This reading is an average of the 18 meters and represents the broad trend of progress counterbalanced by challenges for sustainability in general. Continued conservation will require diligence of resource managers, landowners, and all stakeholders and new approaches to existing and upcoming challenges.

div.head: Overall Assessment of the Sustainability of Pennsylvania's Forest Resources
Sustainability Meter
div.p: Chapter 3: Priority Issues

Priority issues are topics that emerged as common themes of concern, focus, or efforts and resources in current forest conservation and planning in Pennsylvania. These topics serve as a way to organize data, strategies, and discussion, but, unsurprisingly, there is significant overlap among the Issues. In order to select which subjects should be featured in this plan, a review of a multitude of feedback from previous and ongoing efforts was reviewed, including SWOT analysis performed by Bureau of Forestry staff and external advisory committees, public feedback from recent planning efforts involving public meetings and online polling, and ongoing stakeholder consultation as components of the plan were compiled (see feedback summary in Appendix

div.head: Issue Discussion
div.p: Sustaining Pennsylvania's forested land is fundamental to conserving the array of resources and values our forests provide. Pennsylvania's landscape has changed dramatically over the past several decades in certain parts of the state as forests and farms are converted to residential and commercial developments. While economic growth is critical to improving our quality of life, poorly planned development negatively impacts natural systems and causes permanent forest loss. Retaining and restoring functional, diverse forest systems are critical to ensuring long-term sustainability of Pennsylvania's natural resources and the services they provide.

div.head: Forest Distribution
div.p: Patterns in forest cover can be seen from satellite imagery (2017). Large, contiguous patches of forest extend across the Allegheny Plateau in the northcentral portion of the State. In central Pennsylvania, forest-land distribution follows the topographical contours of the ridges that divide agricultural valleys. Smaller, more fragmented blocks of forest land are noticeable in more urban and agricultural regions, especially across southern-tier counties. Pennsylvania's forested landscape consists of urban and woodlot forests surrounding and within metropolitan centers, the expansive 'Big Woods' region in the northcentral region that makes up one of the largest contiguous blocks of forest land in the northeastern U.S., and the ridge and valley region that is characterized by forested ridgetops and agricultural valleys.

The northwest part of Pennsylvania, anchored by the city of Erie, is characterized by small parcels of forest land. The French Creek watershed boasts some of the most productive and diverse fisheries in the Northeast U.S. (Smith & Crabtree 2005), and some of the richest plant diversity and abundance of rare plants in the state. This region is influenced by Lake Erie and glacial topography and has the highest acreage of lakes and ponds in the commonwealth.

The northcentral part of Pennsylvania is characterized by its rural communities and high proportion The southeast region is greatly influenced by Pennsylvania's most populated city, Philadelphia. This region is characterized by fertile agriculture lands interspersed by small patches of woodlot forests and suburban communities.

div.head: Forestland Loss and Gain
div.p: Although no significant net change has occurred in Pennsylvania's total forest area over the past decade, both losses and gains in forest continue at various scales. In such a dynamic, the total acreage of forest area may remain the same while shifts occur in certain areas of the forest-land base. Therefore, characterizing this base as having "no net change" may not accurately represent actual changes in forest distribution, character, and composition.

div.head: Urbanization
div.p: Urbanization of forest land is the process of increasing urban (versus agricultural) development, either replacing or coming into increasing proximity to forest land. Urbanization of the wooded landscape significantly affects the amount of forest land and also its species composition, health, and overall sustainability. Population gains tend to coincide with areas of forest loss due to development.

div.head: Ownership
div.p: According to 2014 USDA Forest Service data, there are 16,916,190 acres of forested land in the commonwealth. This forestland is distributed among ownerships and across the landscape as per the following chart: Twelve million acres (70%) of forestland in Pennsylvania is under private ownership. These lands pose special challenges for sustainability and good forest management:

• The average age of a Pennsylvania landowner is currently 61, indicating that a large shift in landowners is likely to occur in the near future. Unsustainable timber harvesting and subdivision is more likely to happen around ownership change.

• Many landowners bequeath their property to a child or, often, multiple children, which often leads to property subdivision. Oftentimes, heirs are not interested in owning forestland, or cannot agree on how to manage the property and it ends up being sold to a new owner or developer in order to liquidate and fairly distribute assets.

• The increasing parcelization of private lands creates challenges for forest managers, in many cases resulting in additional work for potentially smaller income. Tracts that once contained enough wood volume to sustain commercial timber harvests are broken into smaller acreages on which harvest operations are not financially viable. Subdivision that leads to housing development is a larger issue than just land division. Small wooded housing lots make logging extremely difficult and with more potential to be contentious, if one's neighbors are opposed to the harvesting.

• Most landowners indicate that they do not own land for the purpose of harvesting timber (Metcalf et al. 2012). Most landowners do not have a background in forestry and therefore often lack knowledge of sustainable forest management principles.

• Though most landowners do not own land for its timber value, many can be swayed by seemingly large financial offers for their timber or may feel forced into an unsustainable harvest due to pressing financial obligations. Promotion and support of markets for small-diameter and low-grade wood will ensure more income sources (and therefore management options) are available for landowners with various forest conditions on their property.
• The increasing parcelization of private lands creates challenges for forest managers trying to manage wildlife, invasive pests, or invasive plants.

The diversity of ownership of Pennsylvania's private forests poses several challenges to achieving overall sustainability. While private forest landowners often cite objectives such as wildlife, solitude, and enjoyment, few consult with professional natural resource managers and few have professionally-developed management plans to guide on-the-ground decisions. Ownership patterns are quite revealing (Table 3. [1][2][3] and indicate that 64% of the state's private forestland is already carved into parcels that are 99 acres or smaller. Another troubling trend is that timber establishments with large forest land holdings are divesting themselves of ownership, potentially resulting in parcelization and development. Losses of forest land to development can fragment remaining forest lands into smaller patches that are farther apart, decreasing the chance that remaining wildlife populations are sustainable. As the amount of direct interface or "forest edge" increases, interior or core forest areas are lost, increasing the chances for invasive species to be introduced and reducing the amount of habitat available for interior forest species. Fragmentation also limits migration opportunities for many wildlife species, a concern that will continue to grow with the impacts of climate change. See Wildlife Action Plan Chapter 1, Threats to Species section (starting on page 1-26) and Chapter 2 for information on the proportion of edge to interior forest patches across physiographic provinces (https://www.pgc.pa.gov/Wildlife/WildlifeActionPlan/Pages/default.aspx).

To characterize relative forest fragmentation across the commonwealth, a core forest analysis was performed as part of the 2016 update of the DCNR Bureau of Forestry State Forest Resource Management Plan. The results of this analysis are displayed and described below. The core forest analysis was based on the density of fragmenting features within a given area, which includes roads, pipelines, well pads, certain large rivers (large enough to show up on NLCD), etc. As expected, all of state forest land across the state scored very high relative to more developed areas of the state. Forests in the northcentral region contain the highest proportion of core forest and also the least amount of fragmentation. Not surprisingly, the region hosts the largest forest-patch sizes. The Allegheny National Forest and State Forests contain the largest patches in Pennsylvania. Forest land in the southeastern region is the most highly fragmented, with small patches and minimal core forest.

div.head: Forestland Protection and Conservation Efforts
div.p: The commonwealth has a rich history of land conservation that includes early heroes of the conservation movement in the United States, such as Gifford Pinchot, Joseph Rothrock, Mira Lloyd Dock, and many others. These pioneers had the foresight to purchase land for the public during a time of extensive forest clearing, giving today's Pennsylvanians one of the premier state park and forest systems in the country, which has continued to grow (Fig. The tradition of forestland conservation in Pennsylvania is alive and vibrant today. In addition to public lands owned by the PA DCNR and PA Game Commission, various local municipalities, educational institutions, and non-profit organizations -particularly land trusts -have played an active role. WeConservePA (formerly Pennsylvania Land Trust Association (PALTA)) inventories indicated 5,800,891 acres of protected land in the commonwealth in 2018 . Today's conserved landscape has expanded to include lands on which conservation-related entities hold the development rights via conservation easements.

div.head: USDA-NRCS Programs
div.p: In the area of Forestry, the major 2018 Farm Bill adjustments include: The USDA Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) in Pennsylvania is authorized to provide technical and financial assistance for both agriculture and forestry conservation practices to address resource concerns. Some of the programs offered to non-industrial private forest landowners are as follows:

Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP): This program provides financial assistance to eligible non-industrial private forest landowners to implement conservation practices on forestlands that address resource concerns such as plant condition, wildlife habitat, or water quality. Available conservation practices include wildlife habitat improvements, riparian buffer establishment, invasive/noxious plant treatments, and forest stand improvement. A very important practice offered under EQIP is the development of a Forest Management Plan. Known as a Conservation Activity Plan (CAP) 106 (forestry), this plan is developed by a qualified technical service provider for the landowner with financial assistance from NRCS to provide a document that guides the management of their forest.

Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP): This NRCS program offers a five-year contract that aids landowners by helping them increase their level of forest stewardship. CSP offers non-industrial private forest landowners and managers an opportunity to enhance their operations by adopting conservation enhancements that can advance the conservation of natural resources including improving forest health, increasing wildlife habitat, and improving water quality.

Working Lands for Wildlife Initiative: NRCS assists eligible non-industrial private forest landowners in creating and maintaining desirable habitat for golden-winged warblers in the Appalachian region. Focus is on encouraging the growth of desirable trees, such as oak and hickory, developing early successional habitat, and controlling invasive species in the understory. This initiative is part of the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP).

Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP): This program promotes coordination of NRCS conservation activities with partners that offer value-added contributions to expand the collective ability to address on-farm, watershed, and regional natural resource concerns. Through RCPP, NRCS seeks to co-invest with partners to implement projects that demonstrate innovative solutions to conservation challenges and provide measurable improvements and outcomes tied to the resource concerns they seek to address. In 2020, a grant of nearly $10 million was awarded to the Kittatinny Ridge Conservation Landscape Partnership through the RCPP. The funds will support the partnership's work to target the long-term protection of farmland and forests in the Kittatinny Ridge landscape that falls within Chesapeake Bay watershed.

National Water Quality Initiative (NWQI): NRCS provides financial and technical assistance to farmers and non-industrial private forest landowners interested in improving water quality in priority watersheds with ag-impaired streams.

Healthy Forests Reserve Program (HFRP): This voluntary working forest easement program helps landowners restore, enhance, and protect forestland resources on non-industrial private forestlands through easements and financial assistance. HFRP aids the recovery of endangered and threatened species under the Endangered Species Act, improves plant and animal biodiversity and enhances carbon sequestration.

Agricultural Conservation Easement Program (ACEP): This program helps landowners, land trusts, and other entities protect, restore, and enhance wetlands, grasslands, and working farms and ranches through conservation easements. Under the Agricultural Land Easements (ALE) component, NRCS helps state and local governments and non-governmental organizations protect working agricultural lands and limit non-agricultural uses of the land. Under the Wetlands Reserve Easements (WRE) component, NRCS helps to restore, protect, and enhance enrolled wetlands through the purchase of perpetual wetland reserve conservation easements.

The Wetland Reserve Enhancement Partnership (WREP): NRCS signs agreements with eligible partners to leverage resources to carry out high priority wetland protection, restoration, and enhancement and to improve wildlife habitat. It is part of the Agricultural Conservation Easement Program (ACEP).

div.head: Other Federal Programs
div.p: The Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF): On March 12, 2019, the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act (formerly known as the Natural Resource Management Act) was signed and permanently reauthorized the Land and Water Conservation Fund allowing for up to $900 million annually. The allocation for the State and Local Assistance grant (state-side) program is determined based on a formula set in the LWCF Act. Total apportionments for Pennsylvania in fiscal year 2019 were $5,430,820 (source: https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1207/secretary-bernhardt-announces-170-6-million-to-support-stateparks-and-outdoor-recreation-through-the-land-and-water-conservation-fund.htm). In August 2020, the Great American Outdoors Act was signed into law and provides for full and permanent funding of the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

The Highlands Conservation Act Grant Program: The Highlands region spans 3.4 million acres across Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. In an effort to conserve natural resources in the region, the Highlands Conservation Act was passed in 2004, founding the Highlands Conservation Act grant program. This grant program is among the many that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service administers to help partners conserve an array of plants, fish, wildlife, and their habitats. Grant funding also supports states, non-governmental organizations and other conservation partners working to sustain key landscapes in the Highlands region for the benefit of both people and wildlife. Since the passage of the Highlands Conservation Act in 2004, more than $20 million in federal funds, matched by $44.3 million in non-federal funds, have been awarded to permanently protect 9,405 acres of land. Projects supported by the Highlands Conservation Act grant program are led by state agencies and address lands that support key conservation objectives outlined in the Highlands Conservation Act such as clean drinking water, healthy forests, thriving wildlife populations, productive agriculture, and abundant recreational opportunities.

div.head: Conclusion and Future
div.p: This snapshot of Pennsylvania forestland in 2019 shows several clear trends. Overall, total forestland acreage across the state is holding steady as losses in urbanizing areas are counterbalanced by afforestation, primarily of agricultural lands. Recent expansion of natural gas drilling in the state and pipeline and overhead transmission line expansion for energy conveyance may accelerate forest fragmentation at higher rates relative to the decades prior to shale gas development. Forestland ownership patterns are changing even more rapidly. Half of private forestland acreage may change ownership in the upcoming years, with increased opportunity for harvesting as well as parcelization and fragmentation. Increasingly, smaller ownerships may mean fewer opportunities for timber harvest. While private landowners' reasons for ownership have not changed in recent years, there are many more landowners, making planning and forest-resource decision-making more difficult and resource-intensive. Finally, the limitations of state-level programs and federal funding to conserve forestland through fee-simple or easement acquisition means current funding cannot keep pace with the need or demand for forestland conservation in the state.

Despite the lack of resources for forestland conservation, there are a number of promising programs and approaches that bode well for future efforts in the state. These include multi-state (regional) approaches, new sources of federal funding and policies, state-level initiatives, and county and local efforts to maintain and expand the forest land base of the commonwealth.

div.head: Strategies
div.p: These strategies are supported by the following USDA Forest Service Program Areas:

• Forest Legacy Oaks continue to be at risk from gypsy moth, oak wilt, and sudden oak death (caused by the pathogen Phytophthora ramorum). This fungus could devastate oaks, as understory hosts of the pathogen are prevalent in Pennsylvania's mixed-oak forests. Beech bark disease continues to expand and, combined with other stressors such as drought or too much moisture, could increase beech mortality. Beech leaf disease, discovered in 2016 in northwestern Pennsylvania, is an emerging threat to beech. The causal agent is believed to be a nematode and is causing mortality to all age classes of beech. Threats to oaks and beech are especially important because they are the most important sources of hard mast for wildlife, since the demise of the American chestnut.

Hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA), introduced into Pennsylvania in 1967, continues to spread westward and is affecting the important hemlock resource in the commonwealth (Figure 3.2-1). Continued monitoring will be critical to research and management efforts aimed at understanding and ameliorating the impact of this insect pest. Three counties in western Pennsylvania (Greene, Mercer, & Crawford Counties) have not yet had HWA detected, likely due to limited hemlock found there. A national HWA Initiative and Strategic Plan guides national and regional efforts to manage this pest. In addition, the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry released the Hemlock Conservation Plan in 2019, which lays out strategies for conservation of this keystone species in Pennsylvania. The purpose of this plan is to provide a sustainable conservation strategy for eastern hemlock, integrating all available information regarding the species and its associated threats into a comprehensive and science-based approach. Although it was compiled by the DCNR Bureau of Forestry, the information provided is not solely meant for State Forests and is equally applicable to public and private land. The emerald ash borer (EAB) was detected in Pennsylvania in 2007 and has been detected in all 67 counties (as of October 2017). It is a serious threat to ash trees in both the forest and urban communities throughout the commonwealth including a state special concern species, pumpkin ash.

It is also a threat to the ash seed orchards managed by the DCNR Bureau of Forestry Prioritizing forests based on susceptibility to damage and vulnerability to mortality is a key piece of information that needs to be developed to better manage the forests and to focus future efforts in forest management. div.head: Sub-Issue: Over-abundant Deer Populations
div.p: White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), as a wild, native ungulate, is an integral part of the evolutionary history of Pennsylvania's forest ecosystems. The extirpation of large predators, land use changes, and the status of the whitetail as a game animal under regulatory protection have all profoundly changed the population dynamics and thus the level of influence that foraging by whitetail deer has on species abundance and composition of forest plant and animal communities.

Pennsylvania forests have sustained deer population densities high enough to cause impacts to forest vegetation since the 1920s (Kosack 1995). Researchers have studied the effects of deer on forest ecosystems for many years, and the impacts of deer on the forest are well established in decades of scientific literature. Through selective browsing of native plants, shrubs, and trees, they influence the vegetation that grows in the forest. By preferring certain species over others, they can effectively diminish the presence of certain species in the forest while allowing less preferred species, such as striped maple, to thrive. In the most severe cases, deer can completely browse desirable tree seedlings over time thereby eliminating the ability of the forest to renew itself.

In some areas of the state, deer over-browsing has eliminated the understory -the lower vegetation layer that includes young trees, shrubs, and other plants. Deer feed extensively on many herbaceous plants such as wildflowers and other low-growing plants and even fungi. Some forest plants that deer prefer include large white trillium, bluebead lily, Canada mayflower, and numerous orchids. Because they never outgrow the reach of deer, plants that grow on the forest floor are continually vulnerable to deer impacts. Hobble bush and Canada yew were historically very common but are rarely found today due to their high palatability to deer.

In Pennsylvania, deer management is the responsibility of the Pennsylvania Game Commission. On DCNR Bureau of Forestry lands, the mission is to ensure the long-term health, viability, and productivity of the commonwealth's forests and to conserve native wild plants.

div.head: Issue Discussion
div.p: The sustainable management of rural and urban forests, both public and private, is a significant topic of discussion, innovation, and action for the commonwealth's natural resource managers and citizens alike. Managing the approximately 2.2 million acres of third-party certified state forest in the commonwealth is a challenge, where carefully balancing a wide variety of sometimes competing uses on the land is paramount to success. The commonwealth's natural resource managers work to strike this balance -from working with industry to satisfy societal demand for wood products and energy needs; to opening the land to the public for various types of outdoor recreation.

Whether the land is publicly or privately owned, Pennsylvania's natural resource managers are facing many challenges in the management of forested landscapes within the urban to rural continuum. Beyond biotic factors, such as forest pests and diseases, issues that create difficulty in sustainable management include fragmented forests and parcelized ownership (discussed under Issue 1), unsustainable timber harvesting practices, variability of markets for forest products (discussed under Issue 9), and lack of funding and practitioners to assist landowners in implementing best management practices. However, there are opportunities to expand and leverage existing efforts to ensure sustainable management, such as the continued monitoring of forest conditions, promotion of third-party certification, expansion of landowner assistance, improving and expanding outreach and education to private landowners and communities with forested land, and leveraging emerging markets, for non-traditional products, such as biomass, carbon credits, and non-timber forest products (NTFPs). Because Pennsylvania is nearly 60% forested, these challenges and opportunities affect a significant land mass area of the state. Apart from the health of the forests, the management of these landscapes is integral to the health of the commonwealth's waters and directly affects all its citizens. The state must continue to use current successful strategies, expand on these strategies, and formulate additional creative ways to ensure the sustainability of its forests.
This chapter is organized by sub-issue. The sub-issues to be discussed are:
• Unsustainable Timber Harvesting

div.head: Sub-Issue: Unsustainable Timber Harvesting
div.p: The vast majority of the current forest land in Pennsylvania was harvested by 1920 during the major timber boom in Pennsylvania. The current forests regenerated from that industrial logging or became reestablished on land abandoned by mining or agricultural. Over the years, weather events, deer, invasive plants, insects, diseases, and logging have disturbed these forests. These impacts have led to changes in species composition and, in some areas, declining timber quality and quantity.

The removal of trees for economic purposes that does not address the future biological diversity, value, and productivity of the forest is a concern for sustaining all the values Penn's Woods currently offers. Logging practices that do not consider the future productivity of the forest, such as those that take the highest value trees from the forest, leaving low-quality, low-value and damaged trees, are The effort is large and a sufficient description of every partner, each one offering vital resources to the whole, is not feasible to include in this document, especially since the partnership has continuously added new interested entities frequently since the effort kicked off at the end of 2018.

The energy of the group continues to rise and there is much excitement that this partnership, which is focused on a set of "unifying principles," will be able to move the needle on the challenging issue of unsustainable timber harvesting and a host of other challenges faced by private forestlands and their owners. The group is set up with co-leadership, so that it is not seen as the enterprise of any one entity. The current co-leads are (alpha order by last name):

• Ryan Davis, Alliance for the Chesapeake Bay In addition to SFI's focus on the logging community, they provide educational outreach to forest landowners, the public, the wood manufacturing industry, and other resource professionals. A variety of techniques are used, including newsletters, workshops, informational displays, partnerships, and more to promote the benefits of sustainably managed forests and the value of the forest industry in Pennsylvania.

div.head: Unsustainable Timber Harvesting Summary
div.p: Good stewardship requires that landowners consider the future consequences of their decisions and that resource professionals and harvesters recommend sustainable forest management practices. However, the cost of carrying timber through a long rotation is so high that landowners are often pressured to liquidate their timber when selling land. Timber not harvested at that time is often unsustainably harvested by the new buyer to help pay for the property transaction and many landowners do not seek professional assistance in planning their management strategy for their forest. Education, awareness, and strong incentives are also needed to improve harvesting practices on private lands. Advances in carbon and other ecosystem markets, as well as expansion of forest certification efforts, may also help curb these unsustainable practices.

div.head: Sub-Issue: Certification Systems
div.p: Forest Certification is a market-based, non-regulatory forest conservation tool designed to recognize and promote environmentally-responsible forestry and sustainability of forest resources. The emergence of third-party certification grew out of a joint effort by environmental groups, forest industries, and other nonprofit economic development organizations to arrive at a consensus on numerous criteria for sustainable forest practices and to develop a process by which organizations, landowners, foresters, or industries could have their forest products certified as sustainably produced, through a third-party audit process. The primary entities for certification in Pennsylvania are the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), the Sustainable Forestry Initiative (SFI), and American Tree Farm System (ATFS). Each system has a set of management standards that landowners must follow and are evaluated against during regularly-occurring audits of management practices. These standards address social, economic, and environmental considerations. The FSC and SFI are two of the main standards operating in North America for larger ownerships. ATFS is the largest certification system available to small private landowners. Green Tag, a program of the National Woodland Owners Association, also offers certification for small private landowners. Currently in Pennsylvania, there are over 53,000 acres certified under ATFS, 2.5 million acres of FSC certified acres (both public and private ownerships), and over 2.3 million acres certified to the SFI Forest Management Standard. Twenty-two companies hold SFI Certified Sourcing certificates, and 68 companies hold SFI Chain of Custody certification.

Certified wood may be preferentially selected by consumers due to "green conscience". Certification reassures consumers and environmental watchdogs that the forestry practices by which the product was obtained was sustainable and held to broadly-accepted standards. SFI certification is gaining traction and value since the Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification (PEFC), which is a major certification in European markets, has endorse their standards. The SFI certification will open more markets in Europe because of the PEFC.

div.head: Certification of State Forest Land
div.p: Pennsylvania was one of the first states to have its entire state forest system certified as sustainably-managed. This certification assures the citizens of the commonwealth that their forests are managed with the most up-to-date and sustainable practices and are reviewed by an outside entity to ensure such. It also sets an example for other landowners of the benefits of certification, as well as assisting the wood products industry by providing a steady flow of certified wood. Since 1998, Pennsylvania's management of its approximately 2.2-million-acre state forest system has met or exceeded the FSC certification standards for long-term ecological, social, and economic sustainability. In 2018, the state forest system added a second certification program by becoming certified under SFI standards as well. These independent scientific review processes scrutinize timber resource sustainability, forest ecosystem management, and financial and socioeconomic considerations. Each year, a third-party audits management of state forest to ensure that FSC and SFI standards continue to be achieved. The certified public forest base provides a sound foundation for certified product production and marketing in Pennsylvania.

div.head: Certification of Private and Industry Lands
div.p: Certification of private forests is growing within Pennsylvania. Costs to landowners, that were prohibitive in the past, have been made more affordable through several programs, namely the ATFS.

Wide-spread third-party certification would engender better stewardship and management of the commonwealth's forested land, but because the direct and indirect costs to a landowner for entering into such an agreement are sometimes prohibitive, one of the challenges will be discovering how to motivate landowners to go through the certification process and then maintain their certified status into the future. The ATFS has a relatively minimal cost to participate, making it an attractive certification option for smaller, non-industrial landowners. Landowners with as few as For landowners with larger properties, The Nature Conservancy's (TNC) Working Woodlands program combines certification with active participation in carbon markets. Working Woodlands allows landowners to manage their forestlands sustainably, with no upfront costs. Landowners are aggregated under TNC and certified by FSC while also meeting the criteria for trading carbon credits.

Landowners agree to manage their forests sustainably in return for conservation and management assistance, including assessments of the forest, a customized 10-year management plan, and certification by the Forest Stewardship Council. Revenue generated by FSC-certified products from these enrolled properties goes directly to the landowner and the majority of revenues from carbon credits as well. In Pennsylvania, the property must encompass at least 1,500 acres to be eligible.

Financial incentives are needed to gain any widespread acceptance of certification by nonindustrial, private woodland owners. In addition to those mentioned above, opportunities for tax incentives and other creative assistance programs should be explored. While sound community forestry management can provide numerous benefits, there are certainly numerous challenges associated with the planting and maintenance of trees in urban settings. Concerns that are particularly challenging are placing the right trees in the right places, accommodating for stressful conditions such as poor soil quality, dealing with excess salting of roadways, and accounting for future resources such as maintenance money for pruning to ensure the safety of people and property. Because of these special concerns, the management of trees in urban settings takes specific training and planning. To date, Pennsylvania's premier tree planting and educational program, TreeVitalize, has trained over 7,000 citizens and municipal officials across the state in proper planting and maintenance of urban trees via the Tree Tenders™ program (a registered trademark of the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society). Financial assistance through grants is available to aid communities in the myriad challenges associated with maintaining and restoring urban tree canopy.

div.head: Sub-Issue: Urban and Community Forestry
div.p: An additional concern in Pennsylvania is to ensure that we work with communities equitably and in a way that benefits all Pennsylvanians, regardless of access to resources. According to the PA Department of Environmental Protection, "environmental justice embodies the principles that communities and populations should not be disproportionately exposed to adverse environmental impacts … [and] ensures that everyone has an equal seat at the The partnership between DCNR and Penn State Extension Urban Foresters is key to the success of the state's Urban and Community Forestry Program. These staff members, whose positions have been funded by pass-through federal grants for nearly 30 years, continue to offer high quality workshops and stellar technical assistance on a variety of subjects relative to urban forestry throughout their regions. The DCNR emphasis on TreeVitalize since 2004 has consumed a considerable amount of their time.

Partnerships are vital to the TreeVitalize program. The strong partnerships forged with partners in the large metropolitan areas (Cities of Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, the PA Horticultural Society, the Western PA Conservancy, TreePittsburgh, Allegheny County Parks) are crucial to the overall work, as well as partners that are more locally-based throughout PA's many municipalities.

div.head: Current Status
div.p: Presently there are an estimated 254.4 million trees in Pennsylvania's urban areas; these trees provide an estimated benefit worth over $1 billion in ecological services (Nowak and Greenfield, 2018). The services these urban trees provide are even more crucial, considering that impervious surfaces now occupy over 17.9% of the urban land in the state, or nearly half a million acres. A single mature tree is estimated to take up 4,000 gallons of water per year--recharging the water table, reducing pollutants entering streams, and cooling the air through both transpiration and shading. It has been estimated that for every 5% increase in canopy cover, stormwater drainage is reduced by 2%.

Pennsylvania is carved into over 2,500 municipalities that house 12.7 million people (per the 2010 Census). The DCNR Bureau of Forestry, with the help of its partners, has made good progress toward establishing urban forest management programs in communities throughout the state.

Current figures show 250 communities as "managing," accounting for 5.3 million people; and another 560 communities, representing 3.1 million people, are considered to have "developing" urban forestry programs, according to the criteria established by the USDA Forest Service through its Community Accomplishment Reporting System. "Managing communities" are those that have record of a community forestry management plan, utilize in-house or contracted professional staff, maintain a tree-related ordinance, and have a tree board or advocacy organization. "Developing communities" meet at least one of these criteria, but not all four.

Combined, the state program has reached over 800 communities, and 8.4 million people, no small feat. At the same time, though, more than 2/3 of the state's communities have received no service, and only a small minority of communities follow any sort of written management plan to ensure the sustainability of the urban forest.

The Bureau of Forestry employs approximately 35 Service Foresters, representing 25 full time Service Forester equivalents (some Service Foresters also have duties on state forest land). These individuals are available to assist municipalities as well as forest landowners with various forestry practices, but the majority of their time in the field is spent providing rural forestry assistance. Only approximately three full time equivalent service foresters are dedicated solely to urban and community forestry work. Additionally, the bureau hopes to hire one program specialist who will focus on incorporating equity and environmental justice principles into the TreeVitalize program, as well as work directly with environmental justice communities on urban and community forestry work. This incremental change in service forester and program specialist work has been essential to the growth of the TreeVitalize program.

The urban and community forestry program also relies heavily upon five urban foresters employed through Penn State University Extension Service, with funding from the US Forest Service provided through the Bureau of Forestry. The vast majority of urban forestry information, education, and technical assistance in the state is provided through Penn State. Available funding fluctuates from year to year, depending on US Forest Service appropriations to the state.

Though not often discussed, the ownership issue affects the commonwealth's urban and community forests as well. Grant funding is generally available for use on public land or "quasipublic land" only. This includes parks and greenways; a narrow strip along roadways within the public rights-of-way; and sometimes on school grounds, churchyards, and cemeteries. While much can be accomplished toward increasing tree canopy cover by better utilizing public space available, the majority of property is privately-owned. This heightens the importance of urban planting and educational efforts, such as Pennsylvania's TreeVitalize Program, that can engage average homeowners and motivate them to plant on their own property.

div.head: Needs
div.p: The overall benefits from increasing tree canopy cover in urban areas are substantial, welldocumented, and fairly easy to calculate using benefits calculators from the iTree suite of software.

If we are to provide assistance equitably to the state's communities, the DCNR Bureau of Forestry and its partners need to dedicate more financial and personnel resources towards the TreeVitalize program. For example, the Bureau of Forestry employs only 25 full-time equivalents in service foresters to cover 67 counties, over 700,000 private landowners, over 2,500 municipalities, and more than 12 million citizens. There is an enormous amount of work, and even more potential work on the horizon. Further employment of service foresters or other partner staff in both the field and offices to focus on urban and community forestry issues is key to expanding the program's breadth and depth, which provides benefits to all Pennsylvanians.

In addition to service foresters, Pennsylvania's TreeVitalize program depends heavily upon the knowledge and expertise of urban foresters employed through Penn State through the use of federal funds. The success of the TreeVitalize program will depend upon the securing of permanent funds for the Penn State Extension urban foresters, while also maintaining a steady flow of funds to support urban and community forestry project implementation.

While only a small percentage of the state's land area is classified as urbanized, the large majority of the population resides in urbanized areas or in smaller communities. Community trees are readily accessible to all Pennsylvania residents, while rural forest land may be less accessible to many people. A large majority of urban residents, and even many rural residents, are completely unaware that trees affect their lives and that forestry assistance is available. TreeVitalize is working to close that gap. Providing assistance to community shade tree programs is one efficient way to introduce the Bureau of Forestry and its partners to the majority of the population. Opportunities to assist in the development of conservation-wise local ordinances increases when a relationship is established with these local communities.

div.head: Sub-Issue: Monitoring Conditions
div.p: Forests are dynamic systems and are constantly changing in some fashion. Trees grow, die, expand, or contract their range and presence in any of the number of situations that were covered in this chapter, from forestland in the "wilds" to the street trees within neighborhoods. It is extremely important for natural resource managers to have quality information on these dynamics in order to make informed decisions and effectively implement programs that aid in maintaining and sustaining the health and vitality of the forest resource. This section will provide an overview of those programs.

div.head: US Forest Service -Northern Research Station -Forest Inventory & Analysis
div.p: The following text provides an excellent overview of the The purpose of the CFI is to provide basic biological data on plants, shrubs, trees, tree growth and mortality, forest stand structure, volume, and change on state forest land. Inventories are a continuous process to provide data for developing periodic updates to resource management plans, as well as for long range planning and monitoring.

Prior to 1996, the CFI was mostly a timber inventory, with monitoring the components of growth and yield as the primary objective. This inventory was conducted on 15-year cycles. The last of these 15year inventories began in 1985. At that time, personnel from each of the state forest districts collected all inventory field data. The release of the bureau's strategic plan in 1995 advanced a policy of employing ecosystem management concepts for managing state forest land. As a result, the CFI was redesigned to include monitoring of herbaceous plants, woody shrubs, mid-canopy trees, tree regeneration, and coarse woody debris. With the decision to shorten the resource management planning process to 5-years, it became necessary for a more rapid monitoring cycle of forest ecosystems. The Bureau of Forestry's Resource Inventory and Monitoring Section currently manages the CFI.
As of 2018, the bureau has completed four inventory cycles of the CFI along with numerous inventories focused on designated Natural Areas.

div.head: Urban Forest Monitoring
div.p: The health of our urban areas is also of prime importance. DCNR and its partners are working to assess tree canopy in the commonwealth's metropolitan areas, but more monitoring of urban tree canopy/urban forest health is needed in order to evaluate what is occurring in our populated areas. This will help us target efforts to the places that need the most assistance as well as help us assess whether or not our efforts are making headway. Funding is a major issue in procuring and analyzing the appropriate imagery. One existing tool is PA TreeMap. This tool has been made available to PA communities at no cost, through grants from the US Forest Service. This tool allows communities to upload existing tree inventory data, or to collect it in the field. Communities can keep track of their trees over time, indicate maintenance needed and track actions taken.

div.head: Shale Gas Monitoring
div.p: Given the host of potential impacts of shale gas development to the state forest system and its associated uses and values, the bureau has established a Shale Gas Monitoring Program to track, detect, and report on the impacts of the activity. The program aims to provide objective and credible information to the public and inform and improve shale gas management efforts.

The bureau takes a three-tiered approach to its monitoring, recognizing that an effective, long-term monitoring program must be multifaceted. These tiers include: 1) an integrated and dedicated Shale Gas Monitoring Team; 2) related forest resource monitoring and on-the-ground management activities; and 3) research and external partner collaboration. These tiers form the foundation for the bureau's shale-gas monitoring effort.

The bureau has released two comprehensive Shale Gas Monitoring Reports and they can be found at the following links: http://www.docs.dcnr.pa.gov/cs/groups/public/documents/document/dcnr_20029147.pdf http://www.docs.dcnr.pa.gov/cs/groups/public/documents/document/dcnr_20033642.pdf

div.head: Monitoring of Conservation Easements
div.p: To ensure compliance, it is imperative that all conservation easements owned by the bureau be monitored at least once per year. As the DCNR forest conservation easement program grows, the bureau's capacity for easement monitoring will need to increase proportionally.

div.head: Other Monitoring
div.p: The Bureau of Forestry also monitors a subset of Forest Stewardship plans routinely to determine approximate compliance with the program.

div.head: Challenges
div.p: One of the greatest challenges in the monitoring arena is that there is a great amount of important work to be done, but very little support, personnel resources, or financial resources exist to complete it.

div.head: Strategies
div.p: These strategies are supported by the following USDA Forest Service Program Areas:
• Forest Legacy

div.head: Issue Discussion
div.p: Global climate change is a process driven by irradiative heat retention or loss in Earth's atmosphere. The process is influenced by the physical and chemical properties of Earth's atmosphere leading to alteration of global temperature and precipitation patterns that influence the integrity and function of terrestrial, aquatic, and marine ecosystems. The current period of global warming represents a confluence of natural and anthropogenic factors leading to a significant period of increasing temperatures. As a result, variable warming of ocean water and reductions in global ice sheets are affecting weather patterns and subsequent ecosystem composition, integrity, and function.

Over the past several decades there has been a groundswell of information and policy generated on the issue of climate change at the international, national, and state levels. The first action on climate change is recognized as the forming of the IPCC, or Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in 1988, with their first report issued in 1990 indicating that climate change was occurring. This was followed in 1992 by the Rio Earth Summit which produced the first international treaty on the issue, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). This established a nonbinding goal for industrialized countries to reduce their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Following the Rio Summit was the first binding agreement in 1997, the Kyoto Protocol, which set mandatory GHG reductions for participating countries. In 2016, the UNFCCC reached an agreement to "strengthen the global response to the threat of climate change by keeping a global temperature rise this century well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase even further to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Additionally, the agreement aims to increase the ability of countries to deal with the impacts of climate change, and at making finance flows consistent with a low GHG emissions and climate-resilient pathway". The United States entered into what became known as the Paris Agreement in 2016 via executive action. In 2017, however, the United States announced intent to withdraw from the Paris Agreement; a process that takes 3 years and will be finalized in 2020.

Climate change and GHG emissions have been brought to the forefront of politics resulting in a mountain of new actions and policies, led by various organizations, states, and some of the world's largest energy companies. This has spawned a number of emissions protocols; for example, The Climate Action Registry; and emission offset protocols, such as the Chicago Climate Exchange, the Climate Action Reserve, and the Voluntary Carbon Standard, to name just a few. In a similar vein, The Nature Conservancy's Working Woodlands program aims to help sequester carbon on private lands.

As the fourth-biggest carbon dioxide emitter of all the states, Pennsylvania is taking action to reduce GHG emissions. Many states have developed or are currently developing state level climate action plans. Pennsylvania's Climate Action Plan, required by Act 70, was completed in 2009, and was updated for the fourth time in 2018. In April 2019, Governor Tom Wolf announced that Pennsylvania would join the United States Climate Alliance, a bipartisan coalition of governors committed to reducing GHG emissions to levels required by the Paris Agreement. In October 2019, Governor Wolf directed the PA Department of Environmental Protection to join the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), a cap-and-trade collaboration between nine Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states to reduce GHG emissions. DCNR's Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Plan --developed with the Northern Institute of Applied Climate Science --outlines 123 action steps to be undertaken to make the commonwealth more resilient to potential impacts from a changing climate. During 2017, staff members from across all of DCNR's bureaus participated in a rigorous process to determine and prioritize the department's greatest climate change vulnerabilities and identify strategies to address them. The resulting plan includes objectives to prepare for and mitigate the risks associated with potential climate impacts to Pennsylvania, including higher temperatures and more extreme weather events, range shifts for wildlife and plant species, and an increase in invasive species. Although significant uncertainties exist regarding the extent and details of the changing environmental conditions in the coming decades, research has identified myriad practices can be implemented to benefit forests in under various scenarios and future conditions. The "Additional Resources" section below contains valuable resources that provide details of the significant efforts to compile recommendations and actions despite uncertainties.

Climate change is already beginning to impact Pennsylvania's forests, and in future years the need to adapt to these changes will grow as the impacts increase. According to Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection Pennsylvania Greenhouse Gas Inventory Reports, it is estimated that Pennsylvania's forests currently sequester about 10% of Pennsylvania's GHG emissions (see PA Greenhouse Gas Inventory Reports). Maintaining healthy forests in the face of climate change will be critical to the continuation of this sequestration. Additionally, there may be ways to increase sequestration of carbon within Pennsylvania's forests, which will also be critical in the oncoming decades. Considering the role forests play in carbon sequestration, appropriate management of Pennsylvania's forests is important on a global scale.

div.head: Current Impacts on Pennsylvania Forests
div.p: Pennsylvania has already seen measurable changes in temperature, precipitation, and storm intensity from climate change. As noted in the DCNR Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation plan, since the early 20th century, the commonwealth has seen a temperature increase of more than 1.8° F. Winter temperatures have risen even faster, increasing 1.3° F per decade from 1970 to 2000 in the northeastern U.S. The frequency of very hot days has also increased significantly. Record high temperatures in the U.S. in 2017 outnumbered record lows by 9:1, and by the middle of the century the northeastern part of the country is expected to see 20 to 30 more days above 90° F. Annual precipitation has increased about 10 % over the past 100 years, and heavy precipitation events also have increased significantly. According to the 2014 National Climate Assessment, the heaviest downpours, which are the number of days where the total precipitation exceeded the top 1 % of all rain and snow days, have increased by 71 % in the northeast.

It has also become evident that changes in phenology (the timing of biological events) have been occurring. Historic records indicate that many plants are blooming earlier, and in similar fashion many insects are emerging earlier. Changes in habitat conditions and prey availability appear to have impacted species as varied as the snowshoe hare and the purple martin (Butler-Leopold et al. 2018).

Statistics indicate that climate change is influencing many of the natural processes that impact Pennsylvania's forests. These include weather events such as droughts, floods, and heat waves, as well as biological stressors such as native or non-native pests, diseases, and invasive plants. Since these weather events and stressors occur regardless of climate change, it is difficult to tease out natural variability from the additional impact of climate change. However, research indicates that warming sea temperatures can lead to a magnification of storm intensity and therefore, increasing storm water events. Spatial modeling suggests many invasive plant species that currently have a range south of Pennsylvania will aggressively expand in temperate broadleaf and mixed forests of the northeastern U.S. due to climate change.

One analogy is that climate change has been 'loading the dice', increasing the likelihood or severity of these natural events and thus their impact on the state's forests. For example, significant losses of chestnut oak in southern Pennsylvania occurred after Pennsylvania received 67 inches of rain in 2018, significantly more than the normal rainfall average 40 inches. Pennsylvania also saw its first infestation from the Southern Pine Beetle (Dendroctonus frontalis) in 2017.

While current research has not shown any increased tree mortality in the eastern U.S. due to climate change, future studies may continue to tease out the present impacts from climate change on Pennsylvania's forests and ecosystems. As temperature and precipitation regimes continue to change, and carbon dioxide levels increase, it is possible that these stressors on forests will increase mortality to the point where it is measurably different and attributable to climate change.

div.head: Projected Impacts on Pennsylvania Forests
div.p: The impacts of climate change on forested ecosystems are currently the focus of a tremendous amount of research. There is a growing body of information on what the potential impacts on Pennsylvania forests may be over the next century and beyond. The exact amount of warming that will take place is unknown, due to the complexity of global feedback processes as well as the rate of GHG emissions over the next several decades. However, at current emissions rates, Pennsylvania's climate will certainly undergo significant changes, even as soon as in the next 50 years. Due to these changes, many of the state's current ecosystems will destabilize in their present locations, potentially leading to lower regeneration rates and higher mortality rates of many tree species. Climate change will increase the loss of species that already appear stressed, such as black cherry and sugar maple, and likely limit habitat for other northern hardwood species in Pennsylvania. Some species in the southern part of the state, such as oaks and hickories, may expand their range to the north. For a species-specific list of changes in probable habitat due to climate change, please see the Mid-Atlantic Forest Ecosystem Vulnerability Assessment and Synthesis.

Longer growing seasons and increased CO2 availability may increase forest growth rates, although this could be offset by future problems with mortality and regeneration rates. Nutrient cycles are also likely to be affected by climate change, although how these complicated effects will play out across ecosystems is not fully understood.

Changes in the frequency and intensity of natural disturbances are also projected to increase. Drought, wind, tornados, ice storms, fires, and floods may all occur more often and with greater impacts to Pennsylvania's forests in the future. These will likely increase mortality in Pennsylvania's forests or have a compounding effect on other stressors such as insects, diseases, and competition from invasive plants.

In general, climate change will likely lead to greater impacts on forests from insects, diseases, and invasive species. Higher winter temperatures and longer, warmer growing seasons may allow insect pests to increase their range, population size and number of generations per year. These factors could increase forest damage from native insect pests (e.g., elm spanworm, forest tent caterpillar, two-lined chestnut borer) as well as nonnative pests (e.g., gypsy moth, hemlock wooly adelgid, emerald ash borer). Some tree diseases, especially those that benefit from wetter conditions and warmer winters, will also likely increase.

Since invasive plants tend to quickly adapt and take advantage of disturbed sites, future climate impacts will likely favor these at the expense of native forest species. It is also likely that phenological changes will stress the relationships between plants, their insect pollinators, and animals such as migratory birds that depend on the insects for food. Other animals, especially amphibians, are likely to be adversely impacted by changes in precipitation and temperature. These changes will occur within a context of forest ecosystems that have already been subjected to major anthropogenic disturbances within the past two centuries and that continue to suffer from significant additional stressors today. The harvesting and fires of the late 1800s and early 1900s dramatically changed the species composition of Pennsylvania's forests, greatly reducing the extent of once common species such as white pine, hemlock and beech and increasing the dominance of oaks. Chestnut blight and other exotic diseases, including Dutch elm disease and beech bark disease, along with exotic insects, such as hemlock wooly adelgid, gypsy moth, and emerald ash borer, have been -and continue to be -stressors to the forest. Native plants compete with nonnative plants, including trees such as ailanthus and Norway maple; shrubs such as bush honeysuckle, multiflora rose, Japanese knotweed, and privet; and herbaceous plants such as Japanese stiltgrass and mile-aminute weed. Finally, atmospheric deposition has substantially altered the soil chemistry of at least some of the state's forest soils, and some species, particularly sugar maple, have been shown to be very sensitive to these changes (Horsley et al. 2000, 2008, Driscoll et al. 2001, Fenn et al. 2006). The state's forests also face other significant stressors, including forest loss and fragmentation due to development, parcelization into increasingly difficult-to-manage small ownership blocks, unsustainable harvesting practices and regeneration problems. Climate change can be viewed as just one more stressor within this increasingly challenging forest management context. Adapting to a changed climate will be complicated by many of these problems, and a changing climate will likely exacerbate others.

div.head: Adaptation Strategies
div.p: The impact of climate change on forests can be mitigated by international efforts to reduce carbon and other GHG emissions to the atmosphere, but Pennsylvania's climate is forecasted to change in the coming decades, affecting ecosystems across the commonwealth. Because the specific nature of these changes is uncertain, foresters and other natural resource managers should take an adaptive approach to addressing these impacts, by investing more in managing for healthy, resilient forests with a high degree of biodiversity. The 2018 DCNR Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Plan highlights major vulnerabilities of the state's forests to climate change, as well as actions to help adapt to these vulnerabilities.

div.head: Changing Forest Composition
div.p: Species composition is expected to change due to the decline of some species, increases in others, hybridization, and immigration of southern species. Adding to these stressors are forest regeneration failures compounded by previous land use changes and forest fragmentation that impedes the movement of species. As conditions continue to change, land managers must learn how to manage forests in new ways that include tree species that will thrive in both today's climate and in future climate conditions.

Forests should be managed for species, age, and functional diversity by selecting for species expected to adapt well to future conditions while permitting the establishment of species from across a greater geographic range. Natural resource managers and private forest landowners must also be educated and encouraged to implement similar management practices. In certain instances, it may be appropriate to implement assisted migration strategies for certain tree species. Such strategies must be approached thoughtfully and following appropriate science-based recommendations and monitoring.

div.head: Rare Species
div.p: Populations of rare, threatened, and endangered species, especially those near the edge of their range in Pennsylvania, are expected to decline faster and possibly disappear because of climate change and other stressors. Additionally, some species that are common now could become rare and new species may move into the state.

Adaptation strategies for this vulnerability include identifying, surveying, managing, and monitoring plant and wildlife species and other natural resources most vulnerable to climate change. At-risk ecosystems must be conserved through land protection strategies across a range of sites and conditions to increase ecosystem redundancy.

div.head: Forest Pests
div.p: More frequent, severe, and widespread forest pest outbreaks will result in more tree mortality, leading to increased management and treatment costs. Forest pests will influence forest composition, and the loss of some tree and understory species may reduce the diversity of the current forest. Controlling these pests increases a forest's ability to withstand and adapt to climate change.

High-value forests should be monitored closely for new and existing threats. Regeneration of a diverse composition of tree species through adaptive management and herbivory prevention can improve resilience to forest pests.

div.head: Invasive Plant Species
div.p: As the climate changes, new invasive plant species are expected to move into the commonwealth and those already here will increase in abundance. These invasives will further reduce the resilience of native ecosystems already experiencing the impacts of climate change and are projected to reduce native diversity and potentially contribute to species extirpation. In aquatic ecosystems, invasive species impair habitat for native species, and increase the potential for choked waterways, fish kills, toxic water, and harmful algae blooms. In terrestrial ecosystems, invasives disrupt succession as they outcompete native tree regeneration in the understory and influence fuel conditions and fuel loads for fires.

Invasive species should be prioritized for removal or control using existing protocols, while new methods of control, such as biocontrol agents, are considered. Partnerships with other stakeholders will allow for more monitoring of new species appearances and for the development of best management practices. Controlling invasive plants in forested settings across the commonwealth will require a significant increase in staff hours and funding.

div.head: Fragmented Habitats
div.p: Climate impacts are expected to vary across the landscape according to elevation, topography, aspect, slope, and other variables. Some areas will see significant impacts, while more resilient habitats will become increasingly important for conservation planning and may influence where and how conservation dollars are spent. This will necessitate changes in land conservation priorities to create an interconnected system of habitats that allow species to move north and to higher elevations in response to climate change.

Unique ecological sites and key tracts of land will be targeted for conservation through acquisitions, easements, forest landowner legacy planning, and stewardship plans to ensure habitat connectivity and potential migration corridors remain intact. Areas that have resisted or could potentially resist widespread climatic changes may be managed as refugia.

div.head: Natural Disasters and Public Safety
div.p: Increased frequency of flooding, wildfire, blowdowns, and other natural disturbances will create challenges for land management operations and public safety. Damage to trails and roads in state parks or state forests could result in stranded visitors, and repeated events may lead to long-term loss of access to some areas. Compared to the western U.S., fire has not been a major disturbance in Pennsylvania, but that is likely to change. There is already evidence of an extended fire season, with fires now happening year-round, not just in spring and fall. The demand for state resources to deal with emergency management, including assistance to the West and South Fire Compacts, is expected to increase.

Establishing protocols and detailed plans before disasters occur is critical. Wildland-urban interface locations (see Issue 7, and other high wildfire risk environments will be prioritized for fuel mitigation and preparedness plan development. More staff and volunteers must be trained and provided with resources to build the capacity for wildfire response and for prescribed fire implementation.

Flooding is already a growing and substantial threat in Pennsylvania. As the intensity of storms worsen from the effects of climate change, rural and wooded areas, as well as suburban and urban areas, will develop more problems as roads, bridges and flood plains become inundated damaging infrastructure and buildings. In some cases, repeated events may lead to long-term loss of access to some areas.

Maintaining and creating riparian forest buffers in floodplains that are currently unforested, as well as strategic plantings in urbanized areas, can mitigate some flooding scenarios caused by severe storms. Private landowners with the potential to create riparian buffers will continue to receive financial and technical assistance, as funding allows. The Bureau of Forestry has created Riparian Buffer Guidelines, providing guidance to bureau foresters and landowners seeking to minimize disturbance when working within buffers or near wetlands.

There is little doubt that Pennsylvania's forest ecosystems are going to be affected by climate change in the coming decades. However, by following these actions, there is much the state can do to adapt to these changes.

div.head: Carbon Sequestration
div.p: Forests can play a role in mitigating the factors causing climate change. Forests and their soils represent one of the largest terrestrial pools of carbon, and they actively sequester carbon from the atmosphere. According to estimates based on USDA Forest Service FIA data for Pennsylvania, 42% of the total carbon storage in Pennsylvania forests occurs in the live above ground woody material and 34% occurs in the soil organic material (see figure 2.11-2 in Chapter 2, Indicator 11.) However, the carbon sequestered by Pennsylvania's forests each year equals less than one tenth of the GHG emissions from the state (see PA Greenhouse Gas Inventory Reports). It may be possible to significantly increase the rate at which carbon is sequestered by the forests of Pennsylvania, but not without very large investments in forest management across both public and private forested lands.

On the other hand, forest clearing and development result in losses from the pool of carbon stored in the forests and their soils. Depending on what happens to the wood from harvested forest land and depending on the land use that replaces forest, much of the carbon stored in this pool can be emitted to the atmosphere. Thus, preventing the loss of forests can be an effective way to reduce carbon emissions. Globally, forest clearing is the second-most significant source of carbon emissions to the atmosphere, after the burning of fossil fuels. In the eastern US, and in Pennsylvania in particular, the pool of carbon in forests has increased over the past century. This trend may be reversed if forestland is increasingly cleared for development in light of declining growth rates and increasing harvest levels as the forest matures. Similarly, if climate change, or its effect combined with other stressors causes mortality to increase and regeneration to decrease, it is possible that Pennsylvania's forests may cease to sequester significant amounts of carbon. The most effective policy to ensure the continued contribution of Pennsylvania's forests to mitigating climate change is for them to remain healthy forests in the long term.

In general, it is possible to increase forest growth rates, and hence carbon sequestration rates, but in many forest systems, this requires a shift from natural forests to intensively managed plantations, which would generally involve planting conifers. Pennsylvania's climate and soils are not well-suited to this type of forestry, which is why such plantations do not currently exist in the state. Rather, Pennsylvania's forests have been managed for the state's native oaks and northern hardwoods, which are relatively slow growing, but produce high-quality, high value wood products, albeit over long rotations. The practice of silviculture in the state has focused more on increasing the quality of wood grown through improvement thinnings. Research indicates that, in some Pennsylvania forest types, thinning can increase forest growth rates and promote carbon sequestration. However, stand structure and thinning methods utilized affect the carbon sequestration rates, and whether the practice results in a net gain or loss in carbon sequestration (Hoover & Stout 2007;Hoover 2019).

Because nearly 70 % of Pennsylvania's forestland is owned by private citizens who infrequently involve a professional forester or other natural resource manager in their tree management decisions, much of Pennsylvania's forestland is not sustainably managed. Many timber sales are conducted using practices that only remove the trees that are most economically-valuable at the time of the harvest. This cutting practice typically leaves slower growing, genetically inferior, damaged, and economically less-valuable trees to become the remaining/future forest. Repeated application of this harvesting approach eventually degrades the woodland, allows for the establishment of invasive plants, and leaves the landowner with few financially-viable silvicultural options. Growth rates could be significantly increased in these forests, but in the degraded systems that lack adequate natural regeneration, the only viable option requires supplementing with planted trees to re-establish the forest. This management option is expensive and will not provide financial or significant carbon sequestration benefits for a decade or more. Nevertheless, because of the other ecological and social benefits provided by healthy forests, this could be a worthwhile investment from society's perspective.

Pennsylvania also has tens of thousands of acres of what are termed "marginal lands" that are not currently forested or have trees but at very low stocking levels. These include marginal farmland, land that is idle because of lack of management by the current owner, riparian buffers, and reclaimed mine lands. The planting of trees in these areas, a practice known as afforestation, will develop into a forested ecosystem that continually sequesters carbon as trees grow. This option does come at some expense, and the trees would eventually sequester significant amounts of carbon, but not for the first decade or so. Urban and suburban environments offer another important opportunity for increased carbon sequestration by trees that will also save on energy consumption by reducing cooling costs, absorb other pollutants, increase property values, calm traffic, and improve the aesthetics of urban and suburban environments. Because of these substantial co-benefits, planting urban and suburban trees is likely a cost-effective approach to sequestering carbon, but, again, compared to the total carbon emissions of our society, the amount of carbon that urban trees can sequester is relatively small. In areas where trees will not readily grow, native plantings of forbs and grasses can help increase the area of early successional habitat required by many species. Although the direct carbon sequestration of these lands may be minimal, they can help provide a boon to both conservation of early successional species and small gains to carbon sequestration efforts.

Mortality caused by native and non-native diseases and pests also significantly reduces the carbon sequestration rates of Pennsylvania's forests. As discussed above, climate change is likely to exacerbate these problems. Investments to mitigate these forest health problems can help to ensure that the state's forests continue to sequester carbon at their highest potential.

div.head: Woody Biomass and Wood Products
div.p: There may be market opportunities to use wood from Pennsylvania's forests to produce biofuels that can be used in the place of fossil fuels, thereby reducing net carbon emissions as the carbon released by burning is offset by the carbon that is sequestered by the trees when the wood is grown. Woody biomass has important advantages over other sources of biomass as it does not directly compete with food production, although this non-compete presumes that significant areas of land are not shifted out of agriculture into woody biomass production. Woody biomass is available in large quantities in Pennsylvania and the infrastructure for harvesting it and transporting it already exists. Markets for woody biomass could have the additional benefit of improving forest management by providing a way for landowners to sell low-value wood that cannot currently be harvested economically. This would make treatments such as improvement thinning more economically viable and reduce incentives to only harvest the high-value trees and leave low-value trees to dominate the future forest.
