o General habitats management recommendations to support each species. • Draft strategies for each forest district to protect, maintain, or enhance wildlife habitat features during forestry management activities.

div.head: Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program
div.p: The Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program (PNHP) is a partnership between the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR), the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission (PFBC), the Pennsylvania Game Commission (PGC), and the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy (WPC) in cooperation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Natural heritage refers to the collective biological diversity, including plants, wildlife, ecosystems, and geological structures.

PNHP gathers and provides information on the location and status of these important ecological resources in Pennsylvania and provides scientific information, expertise, and assistance to support the conservation of biological diversity.

PNHP collects and stores location and ecological information about rare plants, rare animals, unique plant communities, significant habitats, and geologic features in Pennsylvania. The PNHP database is Pennsylvania's chief storehouse of information with approximately 30,000 detailed digital occurrence records. Tracking biodiversity, combined with descriptions of the physical environment in which species are found, creates a comprehensive picture of the ecology of Pennsylvania. This information enables us to prioritize the most efficient and effective conservation and restoration actions within the context of statewide biodiversity conservation goals. PNHP uses information on the occurrences of rare species and unique natural communities gathered from PNHP biologists, as well as from museums, universities, colleges, and fieldwork by professionals throughout the state to identify the areas of highest biodiversity and significance across Pennsylvania. The program has since maintained a staff of between 50-60 people across the partnership, diversified its expertise and functions and become one of the most successful programs in the country.

div.head: PA County Natural Heritage Inventories
div.p: PNHP regularly performs inventories throughout Pennsylvania and reports on the critical biological resources that are found within Natural Heritage Areas (NHA). The County Natural Heritage Inventory (CNHI) reports resulting from this effort include an introduction to the ecology of the focal county; a description of methods used to collect data; and descriptions of each NHA in the county, including maps, images, lists of present species and natural communities, and conservation recommendations regarding their management and protection. CNHI reports are snapshots of the known biological information at the time of the inventory.

div.head: Pennsylvania Conservation Explorer
div.p: The information collected by PNHP biologists is maintained and accessible through the Pennsylvania Conservation Explorer. This online platform for accessing rare and endangered species and natural community information is a one stop shop for conservation planning and PNDI environmental review. The Explorer provides conservation information on biological diversity, protected lands, streams, and other natural resources for planning purposes and also allows users to screen a project area for potential impacts to threatened, endangered, and special concern species. The level of conservation information available to the public is unprecedented.

div.head: Pennsylvania Biological Survey
div.p: The Pennsylvania Biological Survey (PABS) is a nonprofit, all-volunteer organization whose purpose is to increase knowledge of, and foster the perpetuation of, the natural biological diversity of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Among other tasks, the PABS makes recommendations for determining the status (endangered, threatened, etc.) of wild species of animals, plants, and other organisms in the state. Its over 150 members are scientists from throughout Pennsylvania, representatives of state and federal agencies concerned with natural resource management, representatives of Pennsylvania's major natural history museums and scientific institutions, and other interested and knowledgeable individuals. PABS is governed by a Steering Committee that functions through technical and standing committees focusing on species groups or program areas.
The Survey's work includes (but is not limited to):

• Make recommendations to state agencies for the status of each wild species or subspecies of plant, animal or other organism known to occur in Pennsylvania, using uniform criteria, within a formal system of categories (endangered, threatened, etc.). For more information on this aspect of PABS's work, see the listing process.

• Providing advice and guidance to state and federal conservation and natural resource management agencies regarding the status and management of any or all species or subspecies of plants, animals and other organisms in Pennsylvania and the commonwealth's ecological communities.
• Facilitating and enhancing communication among Pennsylvania's natural resource scientists, educators, managers, and decision makers.
• Fostering the preservation of Pennsylvania's natural history collections.

• Fostering research that will increase and refine our knowledge of the biota of Pennsylvania, including the status and distribution of individual species or subspecies of plants, animals, and other organisms as well as ecological communities.

• Communicating the results of PABS's research and activities to appropriate audiences, including the scientific community, the public, state and federal agencies and legislative bodies. Chaired by the Secretary of Agriculture, the council members include Pennsylvania agency heads responsible for the conservation of agricultural and natural resources and the protection of public health along with public members representing agriculture and natural resource organizations and educational institutions conducting invasive species research and outreach, with the purpose to: "...minimize the harmful ecological, economic and human health impacts of invasive species through the prevention and management of their introduction, expansion and dispersal into, within and from Pennsylvania."

div.head: Pennsylvania Plant Conservation Network
div.p: The Council meets quarterly to discuss current and potential threats to Pennsylvania's agricultural and natural resources, interagency cooperation strategies, public outreach and education, and updates and recommendations for policy development. All meetings are announced prior to the date and are open to the public.

div.head: Wild Resource Conservation Program
div.p: The Wild Resource Conservation Fund was created in 1982 to among other things, aid in the conservation of the commonwealth's flora and non-game fauna. It set up the ability for citizens to support the management of wild resources by creating a contribution opportunity through a tax check-off and license plate program, furthering management and conservation.
Each year, these funds support the survey, research, management, and conservation of wild resources through DCNR's Wild Resource Conservation Program (WRCP).

WRCP identifies research and conservation needs on the commonwealth's native flora and nongame wildlife. The program provides grants and facilitates the flow of information between researchers, conservationists, and educators.
For more than 30 years, WRCP has helped to:
• Develop County Natural Heritage Inventories that locate and identify rare species and special habitats in all 67 Pennsylvania counties

div.head: Issue Discussion
div.p: Pennsylvania contains a vast and diverse forest resource. In addition to inspiring our state's name, these forests give many communities their sense of history and identity. Despite waves of clearance, development, and fragmentation, the forest land base still holds relatively steady, with approximately 60 % of the commonwealth (16.8 million acres) in forest. This forest resource supports a $21 billion forest products industry and many other jobs, directly or indirectly supported by the presence of the forest itself.

Jobs and forests are inextricably linked; Pennsylvania's forests supply the raw materials used to sustain the forest products industry and other non-timber, recreation, and restoration jobs. In order to maintain a vibrant forest products industry and myriad other uses for forest materials, we must also conserve and care for the forest.

In recent decades, numerous factors have begun to threaten forest-related values and reduce the number of forest-based jobs including: changing land-use patterns, declines in forest health, and the economic recession. Related to a strategic initiative on forests, at the direction of Governor Tom Wolf, DCNR and partners convened a Green Ribbon Task Force with experts from private industry, academia, marketing, forest science, economic and workforce development, and related disciplines to analyze current limitations to forest conservation and job growth and to develop an action plan to address both objectives. The Woods that Work Report was released in October 2016. Work groups composed of members of the task force and other partners are focused on implementation of the action steps. The topics and strategies outlined in this section draw heavily from that effort and report. https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/Business/ForestProducts/Pages/default.aspx Since 2008, the forest products industry has undergone one of the worst economic downturns in its history. With wood products strongly linked to housing construction, the Great Recession had an extreme impact on the Pennsylvania forest products industry, which contracted from 100,000 direct jobs prior to 2008 to about 60,000 by 2016. These job losses add to those of two decades ago, when the loss of furniture-industry jobs in the state in the late 1990s and early 2000s led to declines in overall forest products employment. By 2018, as the economy continues to recover, the industry was looking to expand again, grow new jobs, and modernize. This progress slowed as increased tariffs between the US and China in 2019 caused a decline in the exportation of wood, resulting in decreases in timber prices. Areas of job growth in the recreation, tourism, and restoration economies offer potential for forest-based jobs of a different kind. However, with uncertainties in the economy due to COVID-19, the future trends in the forest products industry are difficult to predict. In addition to economies and jobs that are related to the forest products industry, recreation and tourism are dependent on the abundant natural resources across the commonwealth.

div.head: Forest Products
div.p: With a $37 billion economic impact on Pennsylvania's economy, the marketing and economic development of products is very important to Pennsylvania's rural and statewide economy. In recent years, Pennsylvania's forest industry has focused increasingly on expanding and developing new overseas markets. However, as the decline of log and lumber exports has shown, the multiple factors affecting worldwide demand for Pennsylvania forest products make it hard to predict and harder to control. A reliable funding stream for the Hardwoods Development Council (HDC) can help address many industry concerns, marketing, sales, and local materials integration. One of the top 5 Economic Development and Products Recommendations in the Green Ribbon Task Force Report is increased funding for HDC. Consumers in Pennsylvania and beyond need to be more aware of the many timber and non-timber products derived from Pennsylvania forests. By purchasing Pennsylvania's forest products consumers are supporting local industries and jobs. Promoting locally grown Pennsylvania timber and non-timber products will also create a stronger constituency for better management and conservation of the forest in turn more Pennsylvania-based jobs. Education and awareness of forest benefits through forestry tours and demonstration areas will help demonstrate the values of forests to water quality and soil conservation.

div.head: Wood Products
div.p: Pennsylvania is known throughout the world as a leading source of high-quality hardwood products and is home to one of the nation's largest concentration of hardwood growing stock: high quality black cherry, northern red oak, red maple, sugar maple, white oak, poplar, and ash. Pennsylvania leads the nation in the production of hardwood lumber, accounting for about 10 % of the country's annual production. The state typically produces more than a billion board feet of hardwood lumber annually and ranks nationally in the production of value-added wood products such as millwork and flooring, kitchen cabinets, and pallets and containers. Wood products produced in Pennsylvania are diverse and include veneer; paper and consumer paper products; railroad, mine and landscape ties; housing timbers; engineered wood products; tool handles; baseball bats; wood fuel pellets; and landscape mulch.

The sale of timber provides private forest landowners with hundreds of millions in revenue annually, and industry purchase of timber from public lands also provides Pennsylvania taxpayers with tens of millions annually that helps support the operations and activities of DCNR and PGC.

Though producing a much smaller impact overall, the utilization of urban wood is worth mentioning. In urban settings, trees must be removed when they die, for safety reasons, or when development occurs. These trees often have unique characteristics that differ from forest-grown trees. These characteristics make the wood especially attractive for specialty or decorative items. Urban wood utilization looks to provide an avenue for the potential of "higher and better uses" for wood that must be removed from urban areas. This wood is generally utilized for high-end specialty furniture or other artistic products, but opportunities for other uses exist, with production of biochar being of particular note. Urban wood utilization is an area where growth is expected to occur, as there is growing interest in re-use of urban wood, sometimes called "story wood" due to the intrinsic value or novelty of a product due to the history of the source tree and its story. DCNR and the TreeVitalize program play a key role in the promotion of urban trees for the values they provide to communities. Promotion of products made from trees serves to complete the "life cycle" of these unique and vital part of Pennsylvania's forest resources.

The current economic climate poses significant challenges to the commonwealth's forest industry. Although it continues to be a driving force in Pennsylvania's economy, the last few years have brought significant business challenges. In recent years, Pennsylvania's hardwoods industry has focused increasingly on expanding and developing new overseas markets. However, as the 2016 price decline of native cherry has shown, the multiple factors affecting worldwide demand for Pennsylvania hardwoods are hard to predict and harder to control. Pennsylvania sawmills have seen major decline in log and lumber exports. Like the majority of the United States, Pennsylvania's wood processing facilities rely on lumber and log export to China. With increased tariffs on products exported to China and new fumigation regulations, lumber markets are struggling. Between 2018 and 2019, exports to China fell 43%. This major decline of log exports has caused the lumber market to dramatically fall to records lows. The prices for several key species that Pennsylvania is known for like red oak and black cherry have reached records lows. Prices have dropped so low that mills are sawing lumber at breakeven prices or selling lumber at below manufacturing cost. This has caused facilities to decide between producing and storing lumber or not to buy standing oak and cherry timber at all. Domestic demand for hardwood products continues to be below what was previously considered usual levels. Demand for low-grade lumber for pallets and industrial applications are outpacing the high-end species and grades. There is also anecdotal evidence that the certified wood products have moved from a niche product to a relevant part of the overall wood demand.

While demand and prices for their products have declined, sawmills and secondary processors experience higher energy, transportation, labor, and other production costs, impacting overall company profitability. Additionally, timber harvesting costs have not declined as fast as lumber prices, leaving a smaller profit margin.

The dynamics of the lumber market are hard to predict. The speed and extent of the market recovery will depend upon the demand for hardwood products, both domestically and globally, as well as the ability for Pennsylvania hardwood lumber and wood producers to remain competitive in the global marketplace.

A strong forest products industry is important to Pennsylvania's forest sustainability and to its forest landowners. The most viable economic models for biomass energy development require associated income derived from continued strong markets for hardwood sawtimber. Road construction, maintenance, and timber stand improvement work can be incorporated in a sustainable manner. This can only be accomplished through the aid of a strong forest products industry. It is also important to note that much of the sustainable management on state forest land is accomplished through the forest products industry. Without this industry, proper management of state forest land would be difficult. As evidenced by recent work of the Woodland Stewardship Partnership (see Issue 3, Sub-Issue: Urban and Community Forestry), there is broad-based recognition of the important role of the forest products industry plays in the ability to make sustainable forest management happen on the ground. In addition, supporting emerging markets, especially for low-grade materials, is important to ensure economic benefits and management options on lower productivity sites.

div.head: Non-timber Forest Products
div.p: Gathering Non-timber Forest Products (NTFP) is a cultural tradition in Pennsylvania, where landowners and others search our forests for the season's bounties, whether it is ramps in the spring, berries in the summer months, or mushrooms or medicinal plants in the fall. Many of these products are also wild-crafted, or collected for commercial markets. This practice is prohibited on state forest land, where these products may be harvested for personal use only. One exception is ginseng, which is protected and regulated under CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora). It is unlawful to harvest ginseng on any lands managed by the commonwealth. A significant challenge to both ecological and economic sustainability of forest systems is the fact that currently few of the goods and services provided by forests provide an annual or even short-term income, due to lack of developed supply-chains and markets for these products. With more interest and investment in the future, forest-based cultivation of ginseng and similar plants, and sustainable collection of non-timber forest products (NTFPs) are two practices with potential to create a growing annual income stream for private forestland owners.

In some cases, the interest and demand for NTFPs has led to overharvesting, which in turn, has threatened the sustainability of wild populations. Other threats include the loss of suitable habitat to land development, conversion, invasive species, or climate change. Many NTFP species have specific growth requirements and grow only in certain edaphic conditions. Finally, there is a need for plant conservation education among landowners, wildcrafters, TSPs, loggers, foresters, conservancies, and land managers to help them recognize and conserve suitable habitat and to protect vulnerable populations.

One approach to reducing removals from public lands is to encourage cultivation and management, or forest farming, of NTFPs on private lands, including farms and woodlots. In 2014, the bureau assisted in the establishment of the Forest Grown Verification Program, a voluntary third-party program designed to verify legal and sustainable harvesting of vulnerable species. Initially the program focused on ginseng but has since expanded to include other at-risk species such as goldenseal and bloodroot. This verification program has connected forest farmers with herbal markets that require sustainability certification of the products they sell.

Recently, DCNR has partnered with Penn State, agricultural organizations such as the Pennsylvania Association for Sustainable Agriculture, forest landowner groups, consulting foresters and others to host workshops to train resource professionals and managers how to manage and cultivate NTFPs. Forest farming, or actively planting or stewarding plants such as ginseng, goldenseal, ramps, and cohosh, can reduce the pressure on wild populations. Native plant nurseries can provide plants and seeds to producers, landowners, and gardeners to conserve native germplasm of NTFPs. A DCNR-led agroforestry team of researchers, natural resource professionals, farmers and landowners has formed to assist economic development for NTFPs. This includes exploring the development of coops, centralized processing or shared commercial kitchens and educational programs to help producers find markets and to develop value-added products to extend shelf-life and marketability. These activities will contribute to the economic and ecological sustainability of our native medicinal and edible woodland plants.

A Penn State study, completed in 2004 (Strong), surveyed both farmers and woodland owners to determine their knowledge of agroforestry and in their interest in establishing agroforestry practices on their land. One of the Strong's findings indicated that landowners would be willing to implement agroforestry on their land, if they had technical support and/or could visit demonstration sites to help them design their systems. Since then, DCNR and partners have received grants to provide agroforestry training to farmers, landowners, and technical service providers, as well as to locate and establish demonstration sites.

In 2015, the bureau and its partners received a USDA NE SARE Professional Development Grant to broaden the understanding, application, and outreach among technical service providers for agroforestry practices including forest farming, creating riparian forest buffers, establishing windbreaks, alley cropping, and silvopasturing. Of these practices, forest farming, creating riparian forest buffers, and silvopasturing have garnered the most interest among private landowners and farmers seeking to diversify their income streams as well as to enhance the ecological function of their land.

Building on the multifunctionality of agroforestry practices, DCNR developed a riparian forest buffer grant program, which includes funding opportunities for multi-functional riparian forest buffers, to assist land owners and land managers in establishing riparian forest buffers that not only protect water quality and enhance pollinator and wildlife habitat, but can provide edible, medicinal, and floral NTFPs for their own personal use or for sale to the public.

In 2020, DCNR partnered with the Pennsylvania Forestry Association, the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau, the PA Department of Agriculture and Kitchen Table Consultants to disseminate and analyze a survey. One purpose of this survey is to compare landowner understanding of agroforestry principles relative to the 2004 study and to gauge the efficacy of DCNR's outreach and education effort. Further, this survey was intended to discover what additional assistance landowners and farmers anticipate as their crops come into production. In addition to understanding the feasibility of the practice of agroforestry, this survey will assess landowner's willingness to enter into permanent conservation easements.

div.head: Carbon Markets
div.p: Carbon markets are an opportunity for forest landowners, public and private, to generate income through certain management practices that increase carbon sequestration and result in a carbon credit. A carbon market is a mechanism that allows industry and individuals to reduce or offset their carbon footprint by purchasing and retiring carbon credits. These carbon credits are created through projects that increase the amount of carbon sequestered from the atmosphere to off-set carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions elsewhere. For a carbon credit to be generated and made available for purchase, a GHG reduction project needs to follow the rules and requirements established by one of several carbon credit registries. These registries have their own accounting quantification methodologies to determine the generation, retirement, and cancellation of carbon credits. Typically, projects applying for carbon credits will be audited to see if they conform with a registry program's requirements and methodologies. In addition, most carbon registries will require forest carbon projects to be certified for sustainable forestry practices.

While a number of strategies for generating carbon credits are presented below, implementation of a forest carbon credit system would present challenges for public and private landowners. One is that the project must have "additionality", meaning that the resulting carbon sequestration is more than business as usual. Forest carbon credits assume that the project would not occur without the carbon financing incentive. For example, many of the possible carbon credit project types are already business-as-usual for state forest land, due to the bureau's commitment to ecosystem management and dual SFI and FSC certifications. This limits the scope and impact of potential carbon sequestering projects on state forest land.

In contrast, Pennsylvania has approximately 11.5 million acres of private forest land, with a broad range of conditions and management. These lands likely present the greatest opportunity for carbon sequestration through carbon credit projects such as forest protection, improved forest management, reforestation, and restoration. A new carbon credit program designed specifically for private forest landowners is currently being piloted in Pennsylvania. The Family Forest Carbon program, created by the American Forest Foundation and The Nature Conservancy, seeks to remove the barrier of high upfront costs in typical carbon market programs. By taking a practice-based approach to monitoring and measurement and calculating carbon based on forest stock changes, rather than costly forest carbon inventories, the expense to landowners can be reduced greatly. Because families and individuals own 38% of all forests in the U.S., it is important to ensure these landowners can participate in carbon markets. More information about this program and the pilot in Pennsylvania: https://www.forestfoundation.org/family-forest-carbon-program and https://www.familyforestcarbon.org/ Leakage is another concern. Leakage refers to emissions being simply transferred to another area or industry sector, thereby reducing, or eliminating the impact of the proposed project. For example, timber harvest restrictions in one area result in commercial harvesting shifting to a nearby region, with similar emissions; or wood products are substituted with carbon-intense alternatives (e.g., cement and steel).

div.head: Forest Carbon Credits
div.p: In general forest carbon credits are determined by first establishing a baseline. This baseline is the amount of GHG emissions that would have been removed without the project. The carbon credit therefore is the additional amount of GHG the proposed project will remove over and above the baseline. Forestry carbon credits can be generated in a number of ways, including, but not limited to:

div.head: Reforestation and Restoration
div.p: Carbon credits are gained through afforestation of open or degraded sites. Forest carbon stocks accumulated on the site over and above the baseline conditions count for the credits. Abandoned mine land, fallow agricultural land, industrial brownfields, riparian buffer plantings and poorly stocked/degraded forestland all present an opportunity for carbon credits.

div.head: Extended Stand Rotation
div.p: Longer stand rotations allow additional carbon stocks to be accumulated in a forest stand, thereby increasing the amount of emissions removed from the atmosphere. The applicability of this approach varies with stand age and tree species composition.

div.head: Avoided Ecosystem Conversion
div.p: Carbon credits can be earned by projects that prevent conversion from forest to non-forest or from native grassland and shrubland to a non-native state. This approach includes avoided emissions from planned and unplanned deforestation and degradation, as well as planned conversion (e.g., forest to agricultural land or development) and unplanned conversion.

div.head: Forest Products Industry Workforce
div.p: Lumber and wood products are part of the $21 billion forest products industry in Pennsylvania, according to recent figures. Forest-related jobs are part of Pennsylvania's heritage and it offers a variety of career opportunities ranging from forestry to production, sales, and management. The sustainable management and use of Pennsylvania's exceptional forests provide good job opportunities across a range of skill and education levels. Maintaining a skilled and knowledgeable workforce in the forest products industry in Pennsylvania is vital to the industry across the country and world, as Pennsylvania is a top producer of hardwood lumber in the U.S. and a leading producer of millwork, flooring, cabinetry, and pallets. With worker's compensation insurance rates on the rise, safety training for forestry professionals is needed. Continued safety education and the transition from hand-felling to more modern mechanized felling will help minimize injuries and reduce the worker's compensation costs to operators. Along with safety training, recruitment of younger generations is needed to ensure a workforce for tomorrow's forest products industry. Falling numbers of graduates from forestry programs, as well as the elimination of some programs, has been a trend over the past decades. The lack of younger people joining the work force in the forestry industries has become an issue. Increased efforts are needed to promote forest products jobs (from logging to manufacturing), which offer valuable and diverse career opportunities. In addition, forestry-related professions should be more widely included in secondary education and included in career counseling for students when they are considering potential career fields. As awareness around Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion expands within forestry and natural resources professions, it has become apparent that there are opportunities to engage more broadly in our outreach and recruitment efforts. There is great potential to engage underrepresented groups and leverage assets that may be valuable to the effectiveness and resiliency of the workforce within natural resources professions. Because statewide programs often have a less-tangible impact than local or regional workforce development "ecosystems", partnerships with such ongoing efforts may be effective in leveraging previously untapped opportunities for recruitment.

div.head: Recreation and Tourism
div.p: Outdoor recreation is an enormous industry in Pennsylvania. The Outdoor Industry Association (OIA) examined the impact of spending on outdoor recreation in 2017. In Pennsylvania, outdoor recreation generates $29.1 billion in consumer spending, $1.9 billion in state and local tax revenue, $8.6 billion in wages and salaries, and sustains 251,000 direct Pennsylvania jobs.

The economic impact of outdoor recreation in Pennsylvania is substantial. Spending by recreationists provides direct earnings, jobs, and tax revenues. In 2017, Pennsylvania ranked 5th in the nation for spending on outdoor recreation. The OIA went on to report that 56% of Pennsylvania residents participate in outdoor recreation each year. Communities across Pennsylvania recognize that outdoor recreation contributes to a high quality of life, and perhaps most importantly attracts and sustains employers and families. Investing in outdoor infrastructure attracts employers and active workforces, ensuring those communities thrive economically and socially.

In 2018, the Center for Rural Pennsylvania reported that the total estimated annual expenditures associated with visits to state forest land alone were nearly $400 million. The major industries associated with the expenditures were lodging, restaurants, groceries, and gasoline, which accounted for 87 % of the total. The estimated total economic contribution to Pennsylvania's economy related to these recreational trips to state forest land was This increased outdoor recreation comes with unintended consequences. There is already much concern over the current condition and maintenance of recreation infrastructure throughout Pennsylvania. If the trend of increased outdoor recreation continues, it will just add to the stress of our already aged recreation-based infrastructure. With more people enjoying the forest, there is also concerns with diminishing the amount core forest available for remote outdoor recreation such as backwoods backpacking and camping. We have already seen an increase with user group conflicts for example equestrian riders using the same roads or trails as dual sport motorcycles. With more forest recreators, the likelihood of search and rescue operation to find lost or injured users increases. Further, the likelihood of tick bites and chances for contracting a tick-borne disease such as Lyme disease also increases. There are also concerns with the number of invasive insects, diseases, and plants that are unintendedly introduced to previously unimpacted areas due to more outdoor recreation.

div.head: Forest Management Challenges
div.p: In order to ensure a healthy and robust forest related jobs and economy, we must maintain healthy, sustainable, and productive forest systems. Threats to forests are covered in detail within the other Issues in this chapter. Below are some highlights as they relate to economy and jobs in forest-related industries.

div.head: Forest Conservation and Sustainability
div.p: Parcelization, fragmentation, and land conversion are true threats to Pennsylvania's forests and forest related economy. A forest conservation easement can be a useful tool, provided it allows timber harvesting as an option on private forest land. Working forest conservation easements can conserve forestland while providing access for sustainable timber harvesting and other forestdependent activities that support jobs.

div.head: Carbon Capture
div.p: Intact, actively managed forests capture more carbon thus reducing threats of climate change. Some of the best ways to do this is to keep Pennsylvania's forest intact, sustainably manage them, and explore emerging carbon offset markets that directly pay forestlands for their forests' carbon sequestration. These payments can help offset forest landowner costs such as property taxes, help pay for good forest management practices, and prevent subdivision that often leads to forests not being commercially viable for timber harvesting.

div.head: Invasive plants/ forest pests
div.p: Over the last 120 years, Pennsylvania's forests have seen an onslaught of invasive forest pests in the form of insects, disease, and plants. These pests have had, and continue to have, a devastating effect on forest ecosystems and forest related industries. For example, the economic losses associated with emerald ash borer alone are expected to reach over $10 billion across 25 states. Healthy, biodiverse forests combat the spread of many forest pests, and timber harvesting is a crucial tool in forest management. Robust timber markets provide more opportunities for active forest management.

div.head: Forest Regeneration
div.p: The capacity of the forest to renew itself through natural regeneration is a key indicator of forest health and a necessary component of a sustainably managed forest. Ensuring desirable and diverse regeneration is a significant management challenge throughout Pennsylvania's forests. Pennsylvania's forest regeneration problems and contributing factors are not uniform across the commonwealth. To ensure Pennsylvania has healthy, resilient forests and quality timber resources, collaborative efforts will be necessary among state and federal agencies, as well as conservation partners and industry.

div.head: Strategies
div.p: These strategies are supported by the following USDA Forest Service Program Areas: Outdoor recreation across the commonwealth is addressed in detail in the federal Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP). Every five years, states across the nation are required to produce a new statewide recreation plan to help guide their recreation policies, programs, and investments. The plan is needed to remain eligible for federal grants from the Land and Water Conservation Fund, Pennsylvania has benefitted from more than $178 million in funding from the Land and Water Conservation Fund for projects across the commonwealth during the last 55 years. These grants are used to:
• Build parks and historic sites • Conserve forests, rivers, lakes, and wildlife habitat • Provide access to recreation, hunting, and fishing

The SCORP is compiled through collaborative efforts between various state agencies and organizations who can bring resources to the planning, funding, and implementation of the plan and that manage outdoor recreation, including DCNR Bureau of Forestry. Extensive public engagement is also key to the development of themes and strategies within the plan. For the most recent SCORP, public engagement processes included online polling and stakeholder/recreation user surveys, as well as focus groups to address targeted issues. More information about these recommendations and actions, as well as the final copy of the 2020 SCORP can be found here: https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/Recreation/PAOutdoorRecPlan/Pages/default.aspx Forest recreation is a component of overall outdoor recreation and as such is covered in detail in SCORP. In this Issue Overview, we focus on forest recreation specifically, and how it is linked to other topics and themes of this Forest Action Plan. Please reference the SCORP for additional details on outdoor recreation in Pennsylvania and the approaches and considerations that are employed to provide recreational experiences to the citizens of the commonwealth.

div.head: Forest Recreation in Pennsylvania
div.p: A sustainable system is an interacting group of things, functioning holistically, in a way that is effective and can continue in perpetuity. Most references identify a sustainable system as existing in a balance of 1.) social, 2.) economic, and 3.) environmental dimensions (Figure 3.10-1). In the book, Outdoor Recreation: United States National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands, Charles Zinser defines recreation as "conscious enjoyment that occurs during leisure time," and explains that a sustainable recreation opportunity is one created by balancing 1.) visitor objectives, 2.) managerial capacity, and 3.) ecological capacity.

div.head: Visitor Objectives
div.p: The ability to pursue individually satisfying recreational experiences in forest lands is an important human dimension for Pennsylvanians. conflict and overcrowding increase. Most user conflicts arise between motorized and nonmotorized activities, or when lands have been set aside for a specific purpose, like hunting. In the 2019 Spring Lion Poll for DCNR's Bureau of Forestry, more than half of the respondents said they use forested landscapes for viewing natural scenery, plants, or wildlife; hiking; and for picnicking, family gatherings, relaxing, or hanging out. Conversely, only four percent use the lands for riding offroad motor vehicles and only one percent ride snowmobiles. As DCNR considers expanding its ATV trail system on state forest land, it must build sustainable trails that minimize the impacts on other activities like wildlife watching, fishing, and hiking.

The SCORP's online public survey indicated that 90% on respondents agree that outdoor recreation is an essential part of their lives, and 80% would like to participate more in outdoor activities. A sustainable system for recreation is one that serves needs of users. In a related survey that targeted outdoor recreationists specifically, participants were asked to indicate their priorities and attitudes regarding different topics related to outdoor recreation. When given the opportunity to share the single most-important thing that parks and outdoor recreation agencies or organizations could do to help them participate in outdoor recreation in Pennsylvania, respondents shared a wide range of suggestions and concerns. Common topics included maintenance, general trail use, motorized trail use, technology, conservation, activities and programming, education, support of sportsmen and nature enthusiasts, access and affordability, communication, ADA compliance, and safety. Of the more than 6,700 open-ended comments received, about 2,600 were related to trails, (38 percent). Of those trail-related comments, about 1,000 related to motorized recreation, most of which were seeking an increase in opportunities for ATV and motor bike riding.

div.head: Managerial Capacity
div.p: The opportunities people have to experience outdoor recreation are largely limited by the resources available to them. For quality outdoor recreation opportunities to be available, there needs to be useable infrastructure, e.g., a road, trail, culvert, bridge, parking lot, rest facility, communication media, etc., and there needs to be a healthy and appropriately-sized forested space in which the activity can be experienced. Infrastructure degrades over time and requires periodic maintenance.

Currently, state forest land and state parks have a greater than $1 billion list of infrastructure and maintenance needs (see PPFF Infrastructure Study). Many managers have not experienced increases in staff complement, nor funding levels, to remain commensurate with rising recreation demands or even to meet maintenance costs of existing infrastructure.

Furthermore, model-based climate change research predicts increasing occurrences of severe weather events, intense flooding, and prolonged warm seasons that will increase the amounts of recreation uses on public lands while threatening infrastructure. Taken together, these factors will increase the weathering/degradation effect on public lands infrastructure, placing public assets at increasing risk.

Public land managers are tasked with providing and maintaining infrastructure and administering the physical spaces in which it exists. The capacity to provide healthful and quality outdoor recreational opportunities is limited by the finite resources that managers have. There currently exists no model for carrying capacity or limits of acceptable change for outdoor recreation managers in Pennsylvania. A sustainable system for outdoor recreation ensures that managerial resources and visitor use are commensurate.

div.head: Environmental Capacity
div.p: Citations too numerous to list illustrate the deleterious effects caused and experienced by humans when carrying capacity of the physical environment has been breached and habitat becomes unsuitable. All activities have an environmental impact to some degree, and outdoor recreation is no exception. Outdoor recreation opportunities should be planned to avoid, minimize, and/ or mitigate negative impacts to the environment. Some negative impacts from various forms of recreation could include: erosion and sedimentation, soil compaction, water pollution, increased fire frequency, unsanitary conditions, noise, and effects to fragile ecosystems and community dynamics of plants, wildlife, fungi, etc.

For many, the relative health of the environment in which they recreate is a key dimension of the experience. When asked about recreational funding priorities in the Penn State 2019 Spring Lion Poll, respondents indicated that four of the top five priorities were to:
1. protect wildlife and fish habitat 2. restore damaged rivers and streams 3. provide environmental and conservation programs 4. acquire and protect open spaces as undeveloped, i.e., conserved land.

Likewise, a top answer to a different question in the same survey indicated that almost 50% of Pennsylvanians think it is important for government to invest in sustainable park practices, like recycling, native plants, rain gardens, and solar energy.

Vast, undeveloped areas are rare in Pennsylvania and throughout the northeast region of the United States; thus, they are extremely valuable. Pennsylvania bears a custodial responsibility for some key forested lands.

Human beings are vectors for the spread of invasive plants, animals, and diseases into novel ecosystems that, over time, have become a major problem in Pennsylvania. The influx of recreational activities can increase this vector intensity, but proper management can help to control it. It is incumbent upon managers and visitors alike to account for environmental dimensions in their planning. A sustainable system for recreation is one where activities are performed within environmental constraints and the capacity of the land to renew itself.

div.head: Resource Management Stewardship
div.p: To participate in outdoor recreation, people need places that are accessible, protected, and safe. Millions of acres of local, state, and federal lands have been set aside to provide areas for healthful recreation to all Pennsylvanians and visitors to the commonwealth, with many dollars invested each year to ensure that these facilities meet that goal. Budget restraints and growing maintenance backlogs challenge providers' ability to meet citizen demand. Due in part to a centuries-old hunting and fishing heritage, Pennsylvanians believe strongly in their natural resources and taking care of what we have so these precious lands and waters can continue to be the setting for recreation for generations to come.

div.head: Funding and Financial Stability
div.p: At the heart of delivering outdoor recreation programs and services is the ability to fund and sustain them for the benefit of all. Recreation and conservation initiatives have several long-standing state and federal funding sources, and new sources such as the Marcellus Legacy Fund of 2012, have helped to meet more demand. However, demand outpaces the total funding available for projects, usually 2:1. Implementing recommendations and best practices will require innovative and more permanent funding solutions.

Funding is needed to maintain and promote forest recreation in Pennsylvania, but forest recreation also generates billions of dollars in revenue for the commonwealth. Motorized and non-motorized recreation have significant impacts on rural economies, especially those near public land. The SCORP outlines funding and economic development as one of the five key themes and provides detailed recommendations to support and promote outdoor recreation in Pennsylvania as well as build cooperation and enhance appreciation of community benefits of outdoor recreation and its economic contribution.

div.head: Health and Wellness
div.p: Outdoor recreation is key to helping address some of today's pressing health care issues. Creating opportunities for forest recreation and making improvements to infrastructure and facilities can encourage active living. An increased focus by the health care community on recreation and opportunities for new partnerships and coordination can lessen our obesity and chronic disease crisis. Getting people of all ages -including the growing population of active seniors -connected to the outdoors and nature can have a positive effect on the health and wellness of our citizens.

During the COVID-19 crisis in 2020, forest recreation increased tremendously across the nation. In Pennsylvania, state parks and forests saw record visitation for spring months during the social distancing period. These trends reiterate the essential linkage between human health and forests and provide renewed opportunities to strengthen society's connection to forests and conservation ethic.

Conversely, threats to health exist for forest recreationists and employees in forest-based professions. Most prominently for Pennsylvania is the tick-borne illness Lyme disease. Cited in several public surveys as a barrier to forest use/recreation, fear of such hazards can represent an obstacle to connection to the forest resource. Visitors and workers must take precautions to prevent these illnesses. To ensure visitors feel confident and safe to enjoy forest recreation, education about methods to protect oneself are a critical part of promotion and advancement of responsible forest recreation across the commonwealth.

div.head: Issue Discussion
div.p: Water is one of the critical components needed for life. Soil is the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems and influences the vegetation that occurs in a given area. It could be said that water and soil together are the two most important physical aspects of an ecosystem. Therefore, water quality and soil health are vitally important to sustainable forest ecosystem management.

div.head: Sub-Issue: Water
div.p: Pennsylvania's abundant water resources have historically been, and will continue to be, key factors in the economic development, community health, recreational opportunities, and ecological wealth of the state. These resources include roughly 86,000 miles of streams; 4,000 lakes, reservoirs, and ponds; 80 trillion gallons of groundwater and over 400,000 acres of wetlands.

Pennsylvania is a headwaters state and is connected through our rivers to the Great Lakes, Gulf of Mexico, and Delaware Estuary and Chesapeake Bay drainages. Land management choices impact not only Pennsylvania's citizens, but thousands of downstream communities as well. Pennsylvania has committed to Chesapeake Bay enhancement goals for stream buffer planting, urban tree canopy expansion, wetland restoration, streambank stabilization, conservation landscaping, and forest land conservation that will benefit millions of people downstream.

div.head: Background/Issues
div.p: Pennsylvania began protecting water resources over 100 years ago, when the legislature passed an act authorizing the purchase of lands for forest reservations in the headwaters of each of the main rivers of the commonwealth, including the Delaware, Susquehanna, and Ohio rivers. Since its formation in 1866, the PA Fish & Boat commission has sought to maintain healthy aquatic systems and species. This foresight, along with subsequent legislation, helped to acquire and establish the current, publicly-owned state forest system, which today serves as a 2.2 million-acre source of clean water for Pennsylvania. This protection, however, does not extend to the commonwealth's private forest lands.

div.head: Conversion of Forestland
div.p: As forest land development and impervious surface area increases, infiltration, recharge and buffering capabilities decrease. Further, the demands for clean water, and the costs of stormwater management and water treatment increase for communities within the developed landscapes.

div.head: Erosion and Sedimentation
div.p: Soil erosion from large-scale forest clearing for agriculture in the years following European settlement resulted in large quantities of sediment entering into Pennsylvania's streams. After forest clearing, poor land use practices added increased sedimentation into Pennsylvania's waterways. At the same time, hundreds of mill dams were constructed across the state, trapping tons of sediments behind these barriers. As centuries-old mill dams were removed, these deposits became a legacy of unstable sediment and contributed to bank erosion, flowing down tributaries into other downstream waterbodies, such as the Chesapeake Bay, the Ohio River, and the Delaware River, among others. This sediment produces scouring effects, reduces water clarity, and smothers shellfish and spawning beds.

Other factors, such as unfenced streams with no barriers to control livestock, a lack of streamside forest buffers, and/or excessive surface or stormwater runoff all lead to destabilized banks, erosion, sedimentation, and nutrient contamination of streams in agricultural as well as developed lands.

While floodplain restoration of impacted streams is one way to address siltation, it is often costly. Multiple research studies conducted at the Stroud Water Research Center in Avondale, PA suggests that by fully restoring riparian forests buffers at least 50 feet wide, even without changes to existing point and non-point pollution source runoff or collected legacy sediments, Pennsylvania would significantly decrease the overall levels of stream pollution.

div.head: Stream Connectivity
div.p: Stream-road crossings and dams can be found throughout the state of Pennsylvania. Many stream crossings can be undersized or installed incorrectly, resulting in a vertical drop at the outlet. The resulting conditions can limit aquatic organism passage by exceeding the swimming or jumping ability of fishes. The North Atlantic Aquatic Connectivity Collaborative (NAACC) has established a stream crossing assessment protocol to evaluate crossings for aquatic organism passage (AOP). Pennsylvania now has a state NAACC coordinator and is implementing this protocol state-wide. DCNR, Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission, PennDOT, and the State Conservation Commission's Dirt, Gravel, and Low Volume Roads program have all worked toward addressing AOP at stream crossings. Dams also drastically limit the connectivity of a stream. Pennsylvania has removed more dams than any other state in the country, but many un-breached, regulated dams remain in the commonwealth.

In addition to well-known aquatic organisms like Brook Trout, less-appreciated organisms, like freshwater mussels, and migratory fish, like American Eels, require unobstructed fish passage to find suitable habitat to carry out various life history needs. In addition, designing infrastructure to accommodate aquatic organism passage often simultaneously benefits the road owner, as the practices can also lead to more resilient infrastructure.

div.head: Acidification from Acid Deposition
div.p: Many of our watersheds and their streams have been impacted by acid deposition from coal-fired powerplants to the west. Ridges received the brunt of acid deposition. The acid deposition has altered the soils and waters, transforming the ecosystems of each. Common impacts include reduced pH, reduced base cations such as calcium, and reduced buffering capacity, along with the mobilization of aluminum, iron, and magnesium. The streams within these watersheds often receive this aluminum which can be toxic to fish and other aquatic life. Acidified streams often have reduced populations of benthic macro-invertebrates and fish, which in turn lead to larger territory sizes of predators such as the Louisiana waterthrush. Acid precipitation, defined as having a pH of less than 5.6, has impacted Pennsylvania since the 1950s, with most of the base cation loss occurring in the 1970s. Even with cleaner air today since the implementation of the Clean Air Act, Pennsylvania still has a legacy of watersheds with reduced levels of base cations, mobile aluminum, and reduced buffering capacity. The reduced buffering capacity has led to many streams being labeled as not attaining their designated use, often referred to as impaired. The watersheds lack available calcium (i.e. buffering capacity), and the streams are acidic due to past pollution.

Another source of acid that has an impact on streams comes from acid mine drainage. The exposure of coal and associated rock layers to air create acids that can release toxic amounts of aluminum, magnesium and iron into the water leaching from these mines. Thousands of miles of streams have been impaired due to this industrial practice. To restore stream health and remediate these impacts, Pennsylvania has allocated funds to the Abandoned Mine Drainage Abatement and Treatment Program (AMDATP). More information about preventing additional impacts and remediating past impairment can be found here: https://dced.pa.gov/programs/abandoned-mine-drainageabatement-treatment-program-amdatp/

div.head: Aquatic Invasive Species
div.p: Pennsylvania is host to many invasive species. Some species that are particularly threatening in aquatic systems include Zebra/Quagga Mussels, Rusty Crayfish, Red Swamp Crayfish, Didymo, Northern Snakehead Fish, invasive riparian vegetation, such as Japanese knotweed or Phragmites, and aquatic invasive plants, such as Hydrilla, Eurasian Water Milfoil, and Water Chestnut. These species disrupt the natural function of the ecosystem and can have drastic negative impacts.

div.head: The Importance of Riparian Forests
div.p: Riparian forest buffers, also known as streamside forests, are critical to the health of the waters of the commonwealth. Riparian forest buffers help to intercept pollution that would otherwise flow into streams and rivers as it is picked up in stormwater runoff. Pollutants that seriously threaten Pennsylvania's waterways include excess phosphorus, nitrogen, and sediment. The impact of these pollutants on our streams and rivers can be greatly reduced through the planting of streamside buffers.

Further, streamside forests provide woody material and leaf litter to aquatic systems, which forms the basis of the aquatic food chain. Stroud Water Research Center scientists have discovered that this debris produces a mixture of dissolved organic matter or "watershed tea." This "tea" nourishes riparian communities and provides the basis for communities that are uniquely adapted to the local "blend." These "teas" are so distinctive that migrating salmon in the Western US use them to navigate when spawning. A healthy aquatic system also means that streams are better able to process nutrients already in the water, which further reduces harmful levels of nitrogen and phosphorus. Without streamside forests, streams are less able to handle these excess nutrients.

Riparian forests reduce flooding by improving infiltration of rainwater and slowing stormwater flow. Tree roots hold soil, trap debris, and create deep holes that shelter fish and mammals alike. Trees shade and cool streams to the benefit of cool and cold-water fisheries and provide habitat for aquatic communities ranging from bacteria and macroinvertebrates to otters and beaver. Streamside forests also provide critical migration corridors for terrestrial wildlife, as well as habitats for many animal species that prefer to nest in riparian areas. Finally, forested streams are valued by human visitors for the myriad of recreational and aesthetic benefits they offer.

Forest cover across the landscape, not just along streams, is valuable for increasing on-site infiltration rates (which in turn reduces stormwater runoff going into streams), reduces scouring, improves water quality, and serving to filter airborne pollutants. Forests allow localized groundwater recharge and promote slowed release of rainwater into watersheds. Recharge and consistent stream flows help to neutralize chronic water quality problems like air-depositional nitrogen, abandoned mine drainage, and the impact of combined sewerage overflow. Reducing impervious surfaces by enhancing or restoring vegetative cover (in either urban or rural areas) is one way to help reduce and mitigate stormwater runoff that carries nutrients and pollutants.

The TreeVitalize Program and Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2) grants, funded by DCNR, now include components for funding riparian buffer plantings to encourage the replanting of streamside forests, particularly in urbanized areas.

Despite these benefits and the efforts Pennsylvania has made toward retaining and expanding streamside forests, significant threats remain, and great progress is still needed to help reach statewide forest buffer implementation goals. Introduced insects such as the hemlock woolly adelgid and the emerald ash borer will further impact ash and hemlock riparian forest ecosystems. The spotted lanternfly will also impact various riparian tree species. Land clearing for development, agricultural field expansion, or aesthetic preference threatens to diminish both existing and newly planted and long-established buffers. The current funding streams for riparian forest buffer implementation are making a difference, but significantly increased funding from a variety of sources will be needed in order to plant additional acres of streamside forest buffers to improve the water quality in streams and rivers across the commonwealth.

div.head: The Impact of Stormwater Runoff
div.p: Even if riparian buffers are carefully protected during land development, natural infiltration and groundwater recharge is reduced when upland forests are converted to impervious surfaces.

Traditionally, the approach to stormwater management in urban areas has been to collect and channelize runoff, moving it as quickly as possible away from the developed area and into the nearest waterway. However, this often leads to increased flooding downstream, as well as a gradual depletion of the water table beneath the impervious development. Additionally, sediments and pollutants from roadways are washed directly into waterways and result in significant degradation of surface water quality. The majority of rain events in the state are small, producing less than an inch of rainfall. Such small events would rarely result in flooding and yet contribute the majority of non-point source pollution from urban areas. If small rain events were handled differently, drastic reductions in non-point source pollution could result. Yet, there are an increasing number of extreme precipitation events. In forested situations, trees have the capacity to intercept and take up vast quantities of water, reducing stormwater runoff, filtering out pollutants, and recharging ground water. Practices that would assist with combating these impacts include increasing urban tree canopy cover, establishing rain gardens, and reducing impervious cover. Incorporating green infrastructure into new development and retrofitting existing development with plant and soil features can aid in stormwater management and provide many community benefits .These can result in tremendous improvements to water quality.

div.head: Watershed Protection and Land Conservation
div.p: Water quality in any watershed is closely tied to the forests within the watershed's boundaries. Forests have historically been the dominant natural cover throughout most of Pennsylvania, and watersheds are healthiest with abundant forests to stabilize and replenish the soils, improve infiltration rates, and cool the waters. Forest canopies temper hard rainfall, alleviating erosion. Forest litter protects the soil surface, and forest soils develop good porosity that allows rainwater to infiltrate and to recharge aquifers and streams. Forest buffers filter pollutants from stormwater runoff before it enters waterways. Although forests in Pennsylvania have changed over the centuries as a result of altered land use, climate, fires, and storms, forests across the commonwealth continue to function to provide abundant and excellent quality water.
Because of these benefits, forests are a critical element of the "green infrastructure" that produces clean water without expensive treatment

div.head: The Chesapeake Bay
div.p: Pennsylvania is comprised of six major river basins as shown in the map below: 1) Susquehanna River Basin, 2) Ohio River Basin, 3) Delaware River Basin, 4) Potomac River Basin, 5) Genesee River Basin, and 6) Lake Erie Basin. Numerous initiatives, collaborations, and other efforts have evolved around these major river basins or the larger water bodies into which they drain. Although it is not contiguous to the Chesapeake Bay, Pennsylvania provides an estimated 50% of the Bay's fresh water supply through its Potomac and Susquehanna drainages and comprises over 35% of the total Chesapeake Bay watershed acreage.

In 1967, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation (CBF) formed to help address the looming concerns of more boats, more people, more houses, poor sewage treatment, and dirty industrial discharges that were affecting sailors, waterfowl, and the fisheries within the Chesapeake Bay region. CBF adopted the motto "SAVE THE BAY". (Source: https://www.cbf.org/)

The Chesapeake Bay Executive Council, including Pennsylvania's governor, has signed three directives that relate to forestry and are designed to improve water quality in the Bay. These directives include a riparian forest buffer goal, a forestland conservation goal for priority watersheds, and an urban tree canopy expansion goal, among other goals.

The Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement of 2014 calls on federal agencies and states in the Bay watershed to better prioritize and target resources to protect the Bay and its tributaries, including implementation of stronger storm water management practices, addressing climate change, expanding access to waters and open space, and better protection of Bay living resources. Pennsylvania plays a key role in defining its state priorities and practices, which can and should include funding and programs to conserve and enhance forestland for water quality, wildlife habitat and interception of airborne pollutants.

Chesapeake Bay Program partners incorporated the TMDL into the goals of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement, reaffirming the formal deadline of 2025 for all Chesapeake Bay Watershed jurisdictions to reach their reduction goals. In 2019, Pennsylvania submitted its Phase III Watershed Implementation Plan (WIP) to the EPA, which outlined how the commonwealth will meet its pollution reduction goals required by the mandated Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) set by EPA in 2010.
Pennsylvania's Phase III WIP set goals for the following practices in the Forestry section of the Plan:
i. Riparian Forest Buffers: implement 83,000 new acres of forest buffers on agricultural lands, and an additional 3,100 acres on developed lands.
ii. Urban Tree Canopy: plant 50 new acres of Urban Tree Canopy at 300 trees/acre.

iii. Turf and Lawn Conversion: implement 5,000 acres of Conservation Landscaping (or converting turf areas to managed native meadow); implement 5,000 acres of Urban Forest Expansion (or converting turfgrass areas to forest cover).
iv. Wetland Restoration: implement an additional 400 acres of Nontidal Wetland Restoration annually.
v. Stream Restoration: implement 60,000 linear feet of stream restoration projects on agricultural or developed lands annually.
vi. Land Conservation: conserve an additional 20,000 acres of natural lands annually.

Due to these goals and the short timeframe for meeting final load reductions, it is necessary that funding to Pennsylvania to implement these practices and other practices outlined in the Phase III WIP increase between 2019 and 2025 from local, state, and federal sources.

div.head: Needs
div.p: If Pennsylvania is to meet current water quality commitments and continue to provide abundant water to meet today's and future water demands, DCNR's Bureau of Forestry and its partners must work strategically to promote and educate communities on the need for watershed forestry.

Connections must be strengthened between DCNR and its partners, state and federal agricultural agencies, and communities to both maximize funding for private forestry practices and to promote forestry education and programs.

The Department must continue to work with federal and state agencies that regulate stormwater runoff and fund infrastructure improvement projects. Tree planting has been shown to be among the simplest and most cost-effective measures that communities can undertake to reduce urban nonpoint source pollution. It is critical for research verifying the importance of urban forestry to be effectively communicated to EPA at the national level and DEP at the state level.

Many variables contribute to the effectiveness of stormwater uptake by trees: tree species, age, growing space, soil type, quantity of rainfall, and surrounding impervious cover. Unlike engineered solutions, precise measurements of expected results are more difficult. Continued research is needed to provide data needed for this purpose, and increased communication between scientists and regulators is needed.

div.head: Sub-Issue: Soil
div.p: Soils are the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems. Plants, the primary producers, depend on soils for nutrient and water uptake. Soils contain a diversity of bacteria and fungi needed for nutrient cycling. Soil chemistry, texture, and structure strongly influence the vegetation that can thrive in a location. The importance of soils cannot be stressed enough.

Some main stressors to the soil ecosystem include compaction, a lack of soil organic matter, altered soil chemistry, and accelerated erosion. Each of these stressors provides opportunity for soil restoration and management. Another issue concerning soils is the lack of information pertaining to the forest soil ecosystem in Pennsylvania.

div.head: Compaction
div.p: Soils that are compacted have reduced capability to supply water and oxygen to plant roots. Some compacted soils also resist normal root growth. Common causes of compaction include the use of heavy equipment, intentional compaction for development, and compaction of trails from use. Areas of compacted soils can be found on forest roads, haul roads, log landings, recreational trails, areas of oil and gas development, and abandoned mine lands (AML).

There are practices that can reduce or eliminate compaction in soils. Compacted soils such as retired roads, log landings, AML sites, and oil and gas restoration areas can be deep ripped to loosen the soil. Deep-rooted vegetation such as native warm season grasses, trees, and shrubs planted on these sites can reduce the chances of the loosened soil becoming compacted again. In some cases where soil stock piles are present for use on the site, techniques that utilize dumping of soil back onto the site with minimal grading can provide a loose substrate for vegetation growth (see Appalachian Regional Reforestation Initiative (ARRI)).

div.head: Soil Organic Matter
div.p: The presence of soil organic matter (SOM) improves infiltration rates, water holding capacity, nutrient cycling, and can help reduce compaction. Typical healthy forest soils have about 5% SOM. Reduced amounts of SOM can lead to less productive vegetative communities and less soil biota, along with the negative impacts on infiltration, water holding capacity, nutrient cycling, and compaction potential. Sites where SOM may be reduced or lacking include AML sites and areas of oil and gas development.
Many options are available for improving SOM content of soils. During restoration, the use of soil amendments such as wood chips, engineered soil media, and mulches can add organic material.

div.head: Soil Chemistry
div.p: The chemistry of soils is normally determined by the parent material from which soil develops, along with the climatic factors of the area. Soil chemistry can be altered due to past use such as agriculture and mining, along with pollution events such as acid deposition. The soil left on AML sites are often nutrient poor, low in pH, and high in aluminum and other metals. Soils impacted by acid deposition are lower in pH, have reduced base cations such as calcium, more available aluminum, poor calcium to aluminum ratios, and reduced nutrient availability due to the reduced pH. Calcium to aluminum ratios below 1.0 are normally considered harmful, while aluminum is more soluble and toxic at a pH below 5.0.

Opportunities exist to remedy soil chemistry issues. Soil amendments such as lime, gypsum, and fertilizer can improve or help restore soil chemistry factors. Lime is often used to increase pH and provide calcium to soils, while gypsum is utilized to provide calcium without increasing the pH.
Fertilizers can be used to provide lacking nutrients to soils. Improving the pH of a soil also may result in improved nutrient availability.

div.head: Accelerated Erosion
div.p: Human induced accelerated erosion results in a loss of soil from the site along with increased sediment making its way into water bodies. Areas where accelerated soil erosion are common include agriculture fields, pastures, roads, trails, and unforested stream banks.

Opportunities exist to reduce accelerated erosion. The Center for Dirt and Gravel Roads has a BMP manual for use on roads with practices to reduce erosion and sedimentation. The DEP Erosion and Sedimentation Control Plan also has BMPs to reduce erosion on disturbed sites. Projects can also be designed and implemented to stabilize streambanks and reduce accelerated erosion. Establishing and maintaining healthy riparian forest buffers will also reduce the impacts of erosion and sedimentation.

div.head: Soil Data
div.p: There is a general lack of baseline and current soil data, and information about the soil biotic community for Pennsylvania.

Opportunities to improve soil data in Pennsylvania include implementing a soil monitoring program on state forest land and testing of soils prior to certain forest management and restoration projects. Continued research pertaining to soil issues and management is also needed.
