How to r ar"ticipate? The ability of families in Adams County to enroll local forests as Forest Legacy Areas will be a valuable tool in maintaining the unique features of our community. The nature of our community is certainly changing and anything that can be done to preserve and protect the forests from development and other non-compatible land uses will be of benefit to the community.

We support your application for designation as a Forest Legacy Area. The birds not only add to our enjoyment of life but are important additions to the biologic diversity of nature. Birds reduce insects and rodents, distribute seeds, and pollinate plants.

Bird watching is a major economic force. A 2001 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service study revealed that nationally $32 billion was spent on bird watching. This had an economic ripple effect of$85 billion for the nation and a realization of$13 billion in tax revenues, and additionally resulted in the creation of 863,406 jobs. It is estimated that in Pennsylvania 27% of the population is involved in bird watching. Second to back-yard bird watching, the most popular setting in which to observe birds is in forests.

Adams County has been identified as the third most rapidly growing county in Pennsylvania. This rapid development is a threat to loss of habitat and increased fragmentation for nesting birds. There are a number of bird species of concern identified in Pennsylvania; birds not yet threatened with extinction but which are showing a decrease in numbers. Included in these species are the Scarlet tanager, Wood thrush, Cerulean warbler, and Broad-winged and Sharp-shinned hawks. These bird species are particularly affected by fragmentation of forests and loss of riparian habitats. Wayne County has seen a steady increase in population growth over the last five years and future projections indicate that the county is expected to grow during the next ten years. Wayne County's population has increased from 39,944 in 1990 to 47,722 in 2000, or an increase of nearly 20% in the lastten years (Data is from Wayne County's "Population Growth and Projection" based on data from the US Census). Compare this with the state-wide increase from 1990 to 2000 of just 3.4%. This same data projects Wayne County growth to increase to 50,000 by 2010. But with the 2004 population estimate at 49,561, it appears likely that the population will surpass 50,000 before 2010. Census 2000 data indicates that Wayne County is the 12 1 h fastest growing county out of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. The number of real estate transactions has risen steadily over the past five years. In this time period, the Wayne County Planning Commission reviewed approximately 964 subdivision requests. In Wayne County's history, forestry and agriculture have both played important roles. In 1953, the U.S. Census reported that there were 2,299 dairy farms, the primary type of agriculture in Wayne County. But due to the growth and development and change in the dairy industry, there are now only 130 dairy farms in the whole county. Less than 16% of the county is used now used for agricultural purposes. Forested land is being developed as well. With such a dramatic increase in the number of people moving to Wayne County, forested land is being subdivided and developed at a steady rate.

div.head: How does the proposed area meet each Eligibility Criterion?
div.p: The proposed area meets the eligibility criteria in the following manner:

div.head: Parcelization/Fragmentation
div.p: Wayne County is threatened by parcelization that will result in conversion to non-forest use, loss of traditional recreation use and the area's environmental integrity. A massive amount of land has already been converted to residential and other uses. In 2000, over 8,380 acres or approximately 18% of the county's land area was developed with housing sites, mainly single family units on lots of 1 acre or larger, or commercial or industrial development. Between 1991 and 2000, residential land use in Wayne County has increased from 226,995 acres to 240,390 acres. The industrial acreage of Wayne County increased from 528 acres to 978 while the commercial acreage increased from 9,762 to 14,254 acres. As the population is expected to increase even more over the next decade, the parcelization and fragmentation of the land will only become more severe.

div.head: Environmental Importance
div.p: Wayne County includes mountains, lakes, streams, woodlands, wetlands, clean water, bogs and barrens; habitat for the black bear, river otter, and other important species can be found throughout the County. Its vegetation is distinctive to Northeast Pennsylvania. These features comprise a fragile ecological system unique on the American Continent. Ecological diversity is not confined to a particular section or district of the County. Exceptional natural features extend throughout the entire 751 square miles (466,560 square acres), from Township to Township and even to the more developed boroughs of Bethany, Hawley, Honesdale, and Waymart.

According to the "Natural Areas Inventory Draft, Wayne County": "Wayne is a county rich in scenic and natural resources. However, these very characteristics, in combination with its proximity to major metropolitan centers, have made Wayne County an attractive place to live and vacation. As a result, southern Wayne County is experiencing a primary-and secondary-home surge much as Pike and Momoe Counties to the south, and Northern Wayne is gaining many new vacation homes. The scenic and natural environments that have attracted so many people to the county are quickly being degraded or lost because of increasing development. If these natural environments and the plants and animals associated with them are to be maintained, wise planning is required. A balance is necessary between growth and the natural resources of the county, and this can only be accomplished by guiding development away from the most environmentally sensitive areas."

The inventory describes the sites of Wayne's wealth of unusual natural areas, and many of the sites support plant and animal species considered rare in the state or even globally. Many of the signif1cant natural areas identified in the Inventory have been well protected, but some of the most unusual areas are only partially protected or not protected at all.

div.head: Opportunities for Traditional Uses
div.p: Forest/Recreation Management-Forest-based recreation in Pennsylvania is a large component of tourism, the state's second-largest industry. Preservation of forested areas in Wayne County will support aesthetics for both the tourism industry and residents alike. It will result in maintenance of wildlife habitat for nnique species such as black bears and river otters, protection of water resources, enhancement of fishing opportunities via maintenance of stream canopies, and many other benefits to the forested areas and tourism industry.

Timber Harvesting-Nationally, Pennsylvania ranks number one in hardwood production. Nearly 60% (17 million acres) of Pennsylvania's 28 million acres is forested. In Wayne County, 66% of its 466,500 acres are forested, some 306,700 acres.

Contributing to Wayne County economics, forestry has traditionally exceeded agriculture in total value. Today, the annual value of Wayne County's timber harvest is $3.61 million. The Forest Legacy Program will provide continued opportunities for forestry activities.

Other Commodity Use-Forests provide many other environmental and economic goods and services such as recreation, wildlife, water quality protection, biodiversity, carbon sequestration, and aesthetics. Use of Wayne County's forest lands for other commercial commodities currently occurs on a small scale use by individual artisans and craftsman. The maintenance of these opportunities is important, and specialty silviculture products and use of these materials by local artisans remains an important part of the County's economic development.

div.head: Description of each important forest area.
div.p: Wayne County is 66 percent forested and this percentage is growing due to abandoned farmland reverting to forestland. The next largest land use is farmland, mostly hay land and pasture. Natural glacial and man-made lakes and ponds makes up a smaller percent.

Most of the forestland is privately owned. Only 6 percent is public property controlled by Pennsylvania Game Commission, Pennsylvania Fish commission, DCNR-State Parks, and local municipalities. The Pennsylvania Game commission controls the vast majority ofthe public land. Most of the PA Game Commission tracts are concentrated in several large tracts.

Most of Wayne County is part of the Appalachian Plateaus Physiographic Province. In turn, the Glaciated Low Plateau section of this province encompasses the majority of the county. The Glaciated Pocono Plateau Section of this province is located in the southern end of the county. There is also a small section of the Appalachian Mountain Province, Ridge and Valley Section located on the Moosic Mountain range. This is the only section in Wayne County that does not have a glacial history.

The general topographical features of Wayne County are rolling hills separated by narrow stream valleys. The slopes are sometimes very steep and the soil surface is usually very rocky. The southern end of the county is dominated by a relatively flat plateau region, which coincides with the Glaciated Pocono Plateau Section. The other exception is the meandering Delaware River Valley with high ridges and sometimes very steep slopes. Along the Delaware River, the forest type can change from Northern Hardwood to Mixed Oak to Hemlock in a matter of a few I 00 yards, depending upon the compass aspect the slope is facing. The Moosic Mountain also differs greatly from the rolling hills and narrow valleys covering most of the county. The glacial topographical features, climate, and soils are very conducive to presence of the Northern Harwood forests.

The vast majority, 79 percent of the forestland in Wayne County is classified as a Northern Hardwood forest type. Sugar maple, red maple, American beech, sweet birch, white ash, black cherry, American basswood, bitternut hickory, and yellow birch make up the majority of the species in this forest type. Understory tree species include hophornbeam, hornbeam, and serviceberry. The Mixed Oak/Oak-Hickory forest type makes up 14 percent ofthe forest. The Mixed Oak type is concentrated along northeastern edge of Lake Wallenpaupack, along the Wayne-Pike County border, areas along the Delaware River, and the Moosic Mountain range. Red oak, white oak, chestnut oak, red maple, bitternut hickory, shagbark hickory, and white pine are the primary species in Wayne County's Mixed Oak forest type. The Hemlock-White Pine type only encompasses 7 percent of the forestland. Actually most of the Hemlock-White Pine type can be classif1ed as Hemlock. Except for sections along the Delaware River and the Wayne-Pike County border, white pine is a very small component of Wayne County's Hemlock forests.

The most common understory shrubs are witch hazel, mountain winterberry, and mountain-leaf viburnum. In specific sites there are mountain laurel, rhododendron, spicebush, and Japanese barberry. The abandoned agricultural fields typically revert to arrowwood, highbush blueberry, multiflora rose, and in some locations silky dogwood.

The character oftoday's forest has been heavily influenced by the past agricultural land clearing and by clearcutting the forests for timber. Much of the land clearing and clearcutting was completed around 1900. Many of the clearcut forests regenerated to an excellent mix of sugar and red maple, white ash, black cherry, hickory, and red oak because of the low deer population and the vast amount of acreage cut over a short period of time.

The upland forests of Wayne County are interlaced with many forested wetlands of various types. The most common are spring seep forests, which have no particular forest type, associated with them. Vernal ponds/pools are also very common. Active and inactive beaver ponds with the associated forest wetland dot the landscape. With the many High Quality Streams and Tributaries, streamside wetlands are common too. Due to the nature of Wayne County soils, shrub/forest wetlands can be found in many locations.

One of the most interesting and most uncommon ofthe forested wetlands are the bogs. They are composed of mostly red maple and hemlock but have a more northerly species component. Tamarack and black spruce are the most common northern species, with an occasional balsam fir. The Thousand Acre Swamp in southern Wayne is a good example.
The natural glacial lakes/ponds also support these forests around the edges.
Another interesting forest is the Northeastern Pitch Pine/Scrub Oak Barrens found on the ridge top of the Moosic Mountain.

The most noteworthy of an individual forest is the Damascus Forest, owned by Damascus Township. It has an old growth Hemlock/White Pine/Oak forest and long abandoned agricultural fields that have reverted to white pine, red maple, and oak. There is also an active beaver pond, which features live and dead trees and shrubs. This forested wetland provides excellent habitat for wood ducks and other duck species.
5. Summary of the important traditional forest uses and environmental values and how they will be conserved in the FLA.

In 2002 approximately 6% of the land and water area in Wayne County was protected open space (public property, conservation, or scenic easements, or fee simple ownership by conservation groups). With the addition of Act 319 tracts and common open space of homeowners' association, the total climbs. This is a good beginning, but much of the tax relief acreage is vulnerable to development pressures, and other important areas including a large amount oflands owned by private hunting and fishing club establishments are still altogether unprotected.

Wayne County has historically had a vibrant timber industry with numerous sawmills, pallet mills, and logging operations. The heritage of logging and milling is vitally important to this area and must be preserved.

Participation in the Forest Legacy Program is a natural "next step" in the efforts to preserve the natural features which make Wayne County unique. Designation of the County as a Forest Legacy Area will complement the above noted efforts and environmental values, which have been endorsed by a broad cross section of the community.
6. Describe how conserved tracts in this FLA will result in a positive cumulative impact or improved benefits.

Tracts conserved through the Forest Legacy Program will complement other land preservation efforts and result in significant masses of open space being retained. This enhances the preservation of wildlife habitat and corridors, enhances groundwater recharge and aquifer protection, promotes silvicultural activities and economic benefits and helps to maintain the County's essential character, which has attracted new residents and visitors for over 200 years. These tracts will also be beneficial in maintaining Wayne County's forest industries.

div.head: List of Public Benefits derived from Wayne County Forest Legacy Area.
div.p: According to the Wayne County Comprehensive Plan: "Wayne County's woodlands are important resources from numerous standpoints. Their environmental benefits in terms of reducing noise and air pollution are the beginning. Also valuable are their contributions offal! foliage and scenic vistas to the tourism industry. Finally, wood products industries are integral parts of the local economy. Loggers, sawmill operators and other wood products manufacturers ... directly employ or provide sources of income for hundreds of residents." In order to protect such an important resource, the plan goes on the recommend that the community "Encourage the preservation of woodlands and open spaces to the maximum extent possible". The Forest Legacy Program will promote the protection of these important areas through the purchase of conservation easements on open forest land. A system of protected, highly diverse, open land and water areas is essential to Wayne County's economic well-being, public image, fiscal balance, and overall quality of life.
8. Governmental entity that will hold the lands or interests in lands enrolled in Wayne CountyFLA:
The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources will hold and monitor the conservation easements on the land emolled in the Wayne County Forest Legacy Program.

div.head: Estimated Timber Volume and Primary users in Wayne County.
div.p: Wayne County has an estimated 531 million cubic feet of standing timber. The value of standing timber is approximately $257,500,000 and the annual timber harvest has a value of approximately $3,610,000. As for privately owned properties, Delaware Highlands Conservancy holds conservation easements on over 1,360 acres in Wayne County and negotiating easements with for more than 1000 additional acres. Other major land trusts have extensive holdings in Wayne County, totaling well over 5,500 acres. This makes for about a total of26,000 acres of public and private protected land.

Unfortunately, there are many important forested areas that are still unprotected. This includes 6,370 acres of summer camps, 16,600 acres of hunt clubs, and 1,500 acres of lands held by homeowners associations. Most of these areas have little or no protection from development.
Of Wayne County forestland, 6% is publicly owned land while 94% is privately owned.
11. How Delaware Highlands Conservancy will promote and administer the Wayne County Forest Legacy Program:

The Conservancy will promote the Forest Legacy program by speaking to select groups with an interest in land use planning, and with forest landowners, professional foresters and loggers, etc. The availability of these programs will be advertised and coordinated with Wayne County Conservation District, Wayne County Planning Board, the Wayne County Forester's own programs, and in other Wayne County media. The Conservancy will also set up booths at other regional events, and talk with interested landowners individually.

The Conservancy's priorities for selecting lands to recommend to the program will be based on the Forest Legacy Program's stated priorities: Threat of development or parcelization; environmental importance; and opportunities for continuing traditional uses will be the criteria.

Appropriate tracts ofland will be identified through the process of public education and applications received by interested landowners. The Conservancy will help landowners gain an understanding of the program, and will walk the landowners through the application process. Applications from landowners will be accepted during an advertised time frame and ranked and rated according to established criteria.

The Conservancy will build on its experience in the program in Pike County, to provide Wayne County residents with the best information about their options. Wayne County has long been known for its forest land and fOrest industry, working farms, and natural resources. This, combined with its proximity to major metropolitan areas, especially New York City, has attracted a steadily increasing number of full-time residents and tourists. As a result, Wayne County is now one of the fastest growing counties in the Commonwealth. In order to temper this grnwth and development, it is vital that we protect some of the important forest land which is part of the County's rural working landscape and adds both to the local forest industry and the County's recreation appeal.

div.head: COMMISSIONERS OF WAYNE COUNTY
div.p: For this reason, we fully endorse the effort to make Wayne County eligible for the Forest Legacy Program (FLP). Through the FLP, some of Wayne County's most precious forest land and natural resources can be preserved, ensuring that this area will always retain a viable forest industry and the rural character that has attracted so many people.
The Commissioners believe that Delaware Highlands Conservancy is a fitting sponsor for the Wayne County

div.head: Summary of 2009 FLP Review Findings and Recommendations
div.p: The previous Pennsylvania Forest Legacy Program Review was conducted on April 27-29, 2009. During the review, three findings of deficiency were identified with the implementation of the Pennsylvania FLP. The following is Pennsylvania's actions to the 2009 FLP Review findings.

div.head: Pennsylvania FLP Review Findings and Objectives 2014 Update
div.p: Finding 1: The required Title VI information is not posted on the DCNR website, and the "And Justice for All" poster is not displayed. b. Ensure that the "And Justice for All" poster is posted in an area visible to the public. c. Link to NA website which contains the required language and information on Cooperative Forestry programs. 2014 Final Update: a. The required language is posted on the DCNR website. b. "And Justice for All" poster was located on a bulletin board near the elevator. c. The DCNR website that contains information about the PA FLP has a link to the U.S. Forest Service. a. Take all possible actions to ensure that grants are closed within the initial two-year grant period. b. When the period must be exceeded due to circumstances outside the control of Bureau of Forestry Staff; Bureau Staff will ensure timely submittal of requests for extension and ensure that required reports adequately explain the obstacles to closing in the two year time frame. 2014 Final Update: a. All prior FLP project grants have been closed. Pennsylvania currently has one FLP project grant that was awarded in FY2013 and is less than 2 years old.

div.head: Finding 3:
div.p: The Behr donation cannot be accepted into the Forest Legacy Program until it is certified as a donation. State Forester must determine that the donation meets the requirements of the program. The guidance for making this determination can be found on page 17 of the FLP implantation guidelines.
Objective 3: Assure a donated conservation easement is credited to the FLP and can be counted as cost share.
a. The State Forester documents that the donation conforms to guidance laid out in Guidelines, thereby certifying the donation and accepting it into the Forest Legacy Program.

2014 Final Update: a. The value of the donation was not needed to make any grant cost share requirements and will not be reported as FLP cost share in FLIS Pennsylvania currently has two FLP Administration Grants that total $77,651 in unspent funds. FLP administration grants are intended to be spent in one year but are awarded for two years to allow for some overlap and allow for submissions for reimbursement. Having large unspent balances in FLP grants accumulates to large sums of money across the country and it gives a negative perception that the States are not spending the money they already have and could lead to the question why should more FLP funds be sent to the States.

div.head: Possible Actions:
div.p: • The Pennsylvania FLP could spend FLP administration grant funds in the year they are awarded and close the grant out the following year. • The Pennsylvania FLP should budget for due diligence activities into the request for project funds request and reduce the amount of admin grant requests to a level that is likely to be spent. ☐ Contains a mix of species/biodiversity (be sure to elaborate on this element as much as possible)

recreational participation and facilities Pennsylvania forests have long been a destination for recreation, contributing immensely to our overall quality of life and the economy of the commonwealth. According to recent surveys (see citations in SCORP 2020-24), more than 90% of Pennsylvanians participated in a wide variety of outdoor recreational activities at both public and private park and recreation areas. Public ownership protects over 5 million acres of forest land open for recreation including State Forests, State Game Lands, the Allegheny National Forest, 121 State Parks and hundreds of county and local parks. These publicly-owned forest lands provide a variety of opportunities for many types of recreation. Pennsylvanians are fortunate in that most of the commonwealth's residents live within 25 miles of a State Park. Total state park attendance in 2018 was estimated at 38 million. The Poconos, Laurel Highlands, and Pennsylvania Wilds are historically well-known regions attracting significant recreational visitors to a variety of outdoor, historical, and cultural attractions. From a private land perspective, landowners consistently cite recreation as a top reason for owning their forestland.

Code, Chapter 102 Erosion and Sediment Control regulation, under authority of the Clean Streams Law, mandates an erosion and sediment control plan and measures for certain timber harvesting activities and other disturbance activities. Timber harvest operations are also governed by DEP's 25 Pa. Code, Chapter 105 Dam Safety and Waterway Management regulations and the Fish and Boat Code, Act 175, which govern stream crossing and other impacts to water courses and wetlands. Water use and withdrawals are governed by major river basin commissions such as the Susquehanna and Delaware River Basin Commissions.

To restore degraded forested ecosystems. concerns about the changing nature of forest resources in the United States, Congress, in 1990, initiated the Forest Legacy Program (FLP). In 2000, the Governor of Pennsylvania designated the Department of Conservation and Natural

newly elected President Franklin D. Roosevelt created the US Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), a work program for able bodied, unemployed males. This peacetime "army" was recruited to battle the destruction and erosion of the nation's natural resources. Approximately 93 resident work camps, each consisting of 174 to 200 young men, were built on Pennsylvania's state forestlands. State forestry personnel planned and supervised work projects for the CCC. Work projects included construction of roads, fire trails, workshops, park and picnic area development, tree planting, and fire suppression. Most of the CCC camps in Pennsylvania were closed by 1942. In the 1940's, some of these abandoned camps housed conscientious objectors, draftees who were excused from bearing arms during World War II and later, as the war progressed, the sites were surrounded with high barbed wire fence and used again by the Army, this time to house German prisoners of war.

Over a three-year period beginning in 1998, the State Forest Stewardship Committee, representing 28 statewide conservation organizations, provided input into the development of the original AON. Then beginning in 2013 and lasting through the fall of 2014, the Forest Legacy Program subcommittee of the Stewardship Committee met to review the AON and decide what information should be updated and added. Both in 1998 and 2013/14, the committee considered the various statewide programs that can help to conserve and establish forests in Pennsylvania. The major programs that affect forestry are: Pennsylvania's Growing Greener I Program: initiated in 1999 and reauthorized in 2002, this program has broad parameters that can include conservation or enhancement of forest resources. The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) manages the Community Conservation Partnership Program (C2P2), which links DCNR and various private/non-profit organizations. DCNR provides assistance in the form of grants and technical assistance to organizations in the following areas:

Forest Health Management provides expertise necessary to sustain the health and productivity of trees, forests, and forested watersheds in urban and rural areas. Includes forest health monitoring, insect and disease suppression and eradication. Assists landowners in development of management plans in the area of identifying non-native species invasion and pest assessment and management.The U.S. Department of Agriculture operates several programs that may encourage forest growth on agricultural lands. The funding for the programs listed below is in the form of cost/share for the implementation of technical practices.  Agricultural Conservation Easement Program (ACEP)  Conservation Innovation Grants (CIG)  Conservation Reserve Program (CRP)  Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP)  Conservation Stewardship Program (CStP)  Emergency Watershed Protection Program  Environmental Quality Incentive Program (EQIP)  Healthy Forest Reserve Program (HFRP)  Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP)  Small Watershed Program The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Non-Point Source Program can assist with farming, riparian buffers, and treatment of abandoned-mine drainage. PA Stream ReLeaf Program is funded through a cooperative effort with the Department of Environmental Protection and the EPA. The restoration of riparian forest buffers is a major component of this program.

Currently there is no program that has accomplished what the FLP is designed to do. The Federal government has given Pennsylvania a unique opportunity to address current forest conservation needs.The Bureau of Forestry is the lead agency that administers Pennsylvania's participation in the Federal FLP. Pennsylvania's FLP has three major elements consisting of the selection of local Forest Legacy sponsors, designation of Forest Legacy Areas, and conservation of important forest lands within Forest Legacy Areas through development of landowner multi-resource management plans and the voluntary acquisition of forest conservation easements (or fee simple purchase) on these lands.

Assessment: The group also states that there have been conflicting comments and verbiage defining the purposes and priorities of the program. They also state that differences of opinion on the true threat of development, the current status of forest protection, and other baseline information were prevalent with measurable data absent. The group stated a list of items that should be completed prior to implementation of Forest Legacy. The goals of the Forest Legacy Program are clearly stated in the Guidelines. At the previous Stewardship Council Meetings, members were given the right to comment on the Forest Legacy Program Guidelines and Assessment of Need (AON) on behalf of themselves and the organizations they represent. The comments have been taken into consideration and the appropriate changes have been made to the program. The committee approved the Guidelines and the AON at the June 29, 2001 meeting.

group stated that the Stewardship Committee was created to advise the Bureau on the implementation of the Stewardship Program. They have said that the committee has been fairly non-controversial in the past and was structured to be inclusive and participatory. However, the structure, make-up, and format of the committee, and subcommittees, are not appropriate to deal with a controversial issue such as the FLP and are not an effective forum for producing a collaborative outcome. Federal Law states that the Forest Stewardship Committee of each state is the organization charged with the development and implementation of the Forest Legacy Program. The State Forester appointed 28 statewide organizations to the Stewardship Committee over the last ten years. Each of these organizations has an interest in the stewardship of Pennsylvania's forest resources. Committee Make-Up: Concerns exist regarding membership, defined voting rights, and other procedures of the committees, which should ensure fair and effective deliberation and decision-making regarding the program. These concerns exist for deliberations and decisions concerning Legacy Areas, sponsors, and the inclusion of individual parcels in this program.

group was concerned that the proponents of the FLP have repeatedly assured individuals and groups who were skeptical of the program that the FLP would ensure working forests for the future. They also stated the Legacy Program has been modeled after the Farmland Preservation Program. They also state that although language is included to allow and promote timber harvesting, the Bureau has made it clear that they are unwilling to require enforcement language in the easement that will ensure land accepted into the program remain working forests. They believe this to be a large obstacle to support the program.

Parcels: The group was also concerned that other states have erred when enrolling larger parcels of land into the program. They felt that large forest landowners, mostly corporations, would use the program to lock up vast areas of own use while pocketing considerable sums of public money, the net effect would then be to create a shorter supply of timber for smaller operators, a correspondingly higher price, and an increased and concentrated level of harvesting on remaining lands. The group was convinced that larger parcels are likely to be industrially held and located in parts of the state where development pressure is prevalent.Nationwide the forest industry has embraced this program. To date, 50 percent of the Forest Legacy funds have been used to create easements on forest industry owned land. Several large PA forest industry landholders are interested in this program.Previously Protected Lands: The group was concerned that the documents fail to address another issue in the implementation of the program and the selection of lands for easement protection. The group was concerned that the program permits acquisition of easements on lands that have been previously protected with public funds. Their view was that the FLP should be focused on lands genuinely threatened by development and conversion to non-timber uses. They felt land that have already been acquired and protected, in whole or in part, through the use of taxpayer funds are no longer threatened and should not be eligible for the program.

The State Stewardship Steering Committee discussed the program for several hours and subsequently decided to table the AON until a time when questions could be answered concerning the program. Conversations with the forest industry and the Forest Service ensued during the next 12 months. The AON was revised to meet the requirements of the Forest Legacy Program. During this time frame the Conemaugh Valley Conservancy proposed the Kiski-Conemaugh Watershed as a Forest Legacy Area. This Legacy area was accepted by the full committee and is included in the AON. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania has received several letters of support. Local policymakers and landowners are very interested in working with the Forest Legacy Program to conserve forestland in the watershed. A conference call hosted by Bill England, Appleton Papers was held on May 31 st , 2000 involving the PA Bureau of Forestry, the timber products industry in both Maine and Pennsylvania, and Penn State University. Participants included: Gene Odato, Chief, Rural and Community Forestry, DCNR, Bureau of Forestry, Mark and Dave Krumenaker, Bill England, Edwin Fosterm, Jay Brittom, Bill Robie from the Hardwood Lumber Manufacturers Association, Alan Hutchinson, Chip Bessey, Jim Robbins of Robbins Lumber from Maine, and Jim Finley, Penn State School of Forest Resources. Much of the conversation revolved around Robbins' placement of 20,000 acres in the Legacy program. Selling the development rights allowed the Robbins family to retain land without the necessity of conducting intensive high grading (a non-sustainable practice) harvests just to offset the taxes. The land remains a working forest owned by the family and managed for white pine. All of the participants from Maine emphasized the need to craft the easement carefully, stating upfront that the easement expressly preserved the forest as a working forest. Any rights which are retained, such as access to a gravel pit or other resource need to be clearly expressed. Chip Bessey of Maine was asked by Bill Robie (HLMA) of Pennsylvania if he would put his own lands in Legacy, and he said no, at least not right now, because he wanted to retain all rights. HLMA has taken the position that this is proof that Legacy was a bad program. HLMA has voiced their opposition primarily based upon what they refer to as government control of the resource because the landowner must comply with the easement and a forest management plan.

Be environmentally important, exhibiting one of the following values: Scenic Resources Lands bordering scenic roads and trails, and lands visible from public places. Scenic resources also include riverfronts, lakes, streams, ponds, open fields and town centers. Landscapes with outstanding features such as lakes, rivers, rock outcrops and significant topographic or geologic features are also considered scenic resources. Public Recreation Opportunities Lands with established and potential recreation opportunities. Examples include areas where recreational opportunities are proposed, such as hiking trails and areas that contain a significant portion of public open space or access points to public areas.

Threatened: A threatened forest is an area of forestland that exhibits potential for loss of traditional use (land use change) or loss of environmental value due to fragmentation and parcelization. Examples of threats include areas already zoned for commercial or residential development or where actual subdivision and building plans are proposed. Threatened forests may exhibit extensive land transfers, be proximal to newly developed/proposed transportation corridors or in areas where second home and resort development are actively proposed.

figure.figDesc: SILVAH USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station developed the SILVAH (SILViculture of the Allegheny Hardwoods) program that is widely-used across PA and beyond. SILVAH is a software program to generate silvicultural prescriptions in hardwood stands of the mid-Atlantic and upper Appalachian region. Using an objective set of research-based standards and constraints, it recommends appropriate treatments based upon land manager objectives and overstory, understory, and site data provided by the user. SILVAH also contains a wildlife attributes report, forest stand growth simulator, provides the ability to test alternative harvest strategies, enables development of a forest-wide inventory database, and facilitates other forest management planning functions.

Educators include the PA Bureau of Forestry Service Foresters, PSU Forestry Extension, the SFI of PA program, Game Commission Wildlife Diversity Biologists, landowner associations, and conservancies or other non-profit organizations. For example, WeConservePA (formerly the Pennsylvania Land Trust Association) provides a library of resources for navigating conservation programs and issues (www.conservationtools.org). The Center for Private Forests at Penn State was created in 2011 to ensure a continued focus on education, research, and outreach to private woodland owners , resources, educational opportunities, and by engaging the natural resources professional community. The Center manages the Pennsylvania Forest Stewards (PAFS) program that creates woodland ambassadors who provide outreach in their communities. Additionally, the Center coordinates the Private Forest Landowners Conference, the first of which was held in 2013 and continues to occur every 2 years.Educational opportunities for forest management professionals are also important and such resources as the Roach Bauer Forestry Forum, Pennsylvania Consulting and Industrial Forester Conference, Society of American Foresters training opportunities, Penn State Extension Annual Forest Health Briefing, and various SFI workshops and logger certification exist. SFI Professional Timber Harvester Training Program is designed to educate Pennsylvania's logging workforce and give them the tools they need to operate safely and efficiently, in accordance with all applicable rules and regulations, and to sustainably manage Pennsylvania forests for generations to come.

The Bureau of Forestry, Game Commission, and Allegheny National Forest all have management plans and demonstration sites serving as models for forest and habitat management. Numerous guidelines and management consideration documents are created on a subject or species basis (Invasive Species Management Guidelines, Brook Trout Management Guidelines, Biomass Guidelines, etc.).For municipalities and community residents, a partnership exists including Penn State Extension Urban Foresters, and a number of other valued partners represented on the PA Urban and Community Forestry Council (also known as TreePennsylvania). Of special note are the TreeTenders program (a registered trademark of the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society) and the Correctional Conservation Collaborative (CCC). TreeTenders trains citizens in basic tree biology, planting techniques, and tree care. The CCC is a collaborative effort that is helping to teach re-entrants skills in arboriculture and related professions in order to create additional job opportunities and reduce recidivism rates.

figure.figDesc: The four jurisdictional agencies of the Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program (PHNP) review submitted project proposals to determine if there will be any impacts to special concern species and resources. Depending on special concern species and resources, the agencies that review are PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (Bureau of Forestry), PA Game Commission, PA Fish & Boat Commission and US Fish & Wildlife Service. In 2017, Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program developed a tool to allow easier access to the Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory called the Pennsylvania Conservation Explorer. Conservation Explorer is a one stop shop for conservation planning and environmental review for threatened and endangered plants and animals. The Explorer provides conservation information on biological diversity, protected lands, streams, and other natural resources for planning purposes. It allows users to screen a project area for potential impacts to threatened, endangered, and special concern species, even without going through the formal PNDI review. PNDI reviews and use of PACE are not mandatory except in certain projects in which streams may be impacted. Certain permitting processes trigger this review. On public lands, such as state forest land, PNDI reviews are conducted as a matter of procedure for all projects that could potentially impact sensitive resources.

Considering all this feedback as well as internal expertise of ongoing and emerging issues, an interdisciplinary Forest Action Plan workgroup within the Bureau of Forestry developed the structure of this plan and drafted the bulk of the text and summaries. The 11 "Priority Issues" in this chapter include eight from the 2010 PA Forest Action Statement: Maintaining the forest land base is critical to ensuring functional ecosystems and providing various resources and values. Although the forested acreage in PA is vast and net acreage has been stable for decades, these forests are threatened due to several factors that convert forest to non-forest and fragment existing forestland. The threats and intensity of land use changes differ by region. In addition to the net acreage of forestland, the composition, distribution, and character of the forests are important to consider, as forests possess differing features and may not contribute equally to ecosystem services and functions and the spatial arrangement of forests has important implications for diversity and connectivity.

note.p: Plan, as well as three additional topics (i.e., Forest-related Economy and Jobs, Forest Recreation, Water and Soil). These "new" Priority Issues were covered in the previous Forest Action Plan but were embedded within other topics and various sections. These issues are broadly prioritized in forest conservation and have substantial efforts underway, therefore, a focus, priority discussion, and specific strategies within this Forest Action Plan seemed warranted. Allegheny County and the city of Pittsburgh dominate the region in terms of urban land use and population. Davis.

figure.figDesc: Many counties in the northcentral, central, and northeastern regions indicate an overall gain in forest land as open land reverts to forest. Losses in forest land at the county level are prevalent in counties within or surrounding urban areas. Many counties that show a net loss of forest land are located near urban centers or major connecting highways. These areas are characterized by large cities, e.g., Philadelphia, with little forest land. Surrounding areas often include development patterns that have led to small patches of highly fragmented forests.

note.p: Historical data suggest that forest once covered more than 90 % (27.3 million acres) of Pennsylvania's land area in the pre-European settlement era (1630s). By the early 1900s, industrial timber harvesting, urbanization, and agricultural land clearing had diminished acreage of forests to only 32 % (9.2 million acres). Following this period of extensive reduction, forest land increased steadily as it reclaimed former sites.

figure.figDesc: Smaller parcel sizes are more challenging for natural resource professionals to manage and less conducive to maintenance of ecosystem functions. Subdivision of forestland into smaller acreages and subsequent increases in the number of private forest landowners have profound implications for the future of Pennsylvania's forestlands, complicating outreach and assistance efforts. Education and incentive-based programs will have to continue to adapt and will likely become more resource-intensive to encourage forest stewardship among a growing number of private forest owners and across increasingly subdivided forests. Financial incentives and funding mechanisms that target opportunities at the time of land transfer could be vital in ensuring sustainable practices and management options for landowners during property transferences.FragmentationOne important consideration in the conservation of forests of the commonwealth is maintaining core forest conditions and minimizing and managing the potential effects due to forest loss and forest fragmentation in order to maintain the health, viability, and ecosystem function of forest habitats. Forest fragmentation is defined as the division of contiguous or adjoining forest land into smaller patches. These disturbances can be natural (e.g., forest fire, windfall, or flooding) or human-caused (e.g., road construction, pipeline right-of-way clearing, wellpad construction). Disturbances, whether natural or anthropogenic, can vary in scale and intensity. The consequences of a fragmented forest vary by scale, species, and forest community type, but are generally due to one or more of the following: reduction or change in forest area (forest loss), increased vulnerability of smaller forest patches to further disturbance and degradation (edge effects), or increasing separation between forested areas (loss of connectivity). Fragmentation can be caused by urbanization, or as in Lancaster, Lebanon, and York counties, agriculture can be a cause of fragmentation of forest land, as farm protection programs displace development pressure onto remaining forests, or strapped farmers sell off woodlots to keep their agricultural operations intact. Road and pipeline construction associated with increased shale gas development has the potential to further accelerate forest fragmentation in the state.

note.p: In addition to increasing numbers of forest landowners, the demographic composition of these landowners has implications as well. With the average age of Pennsylvania forest landowners at 61 (an increase of two years from the previous analysis; Butler et al. 2020), it is likely that private forestlands will, of necessity, change hands over the next two decades. Anecdotal evidence indicates that most harvesting and parcelization takes place during ownership exchanges, making further subdivision, and perhaps development, very possible.

figure.figDesc: such easement program is the Forest Legacy Program which is administered through the USDA Forest Service and its state partners. In Pennsylvania, DCNR has been designated the state lead agency. The mission of the program is to protect working forestland threatened by development through fee simple acquisitions or conservation easements. Since entering in 2002, Pennsylvania has completed five projects, for a total of five conservation easements, and two fee simple acquisitions for a total of 10,596 acres protected. The shaded areas of the map below are Pennsylvania's current Forest Legacy Areas (FLAs). Only properties located within FLAs are eligible for funding through the program. New FLAs can be added through the state's application process, with support from county government and a sponsoring conservation organization. The Forest Legacy Program allows DCNR to acquire and protect private forestland in perpetuity, to the benefit of all residents of Pennsylvania.

figure.figDesc: recently enacted program that provides additional opportunities to conserve forests within the commonwealth is the Community Forest and Open Space Conservation Program (Community Forest Program). Created in 2014, this program offers a unique opportunity for communities to acquire and conserve forests that provide public access and recreational opportunities, protect vital water supplies and wildlife habitat, serve as demonstration sites for private forest landowners, and provide economic benefits from timber and non-timber products. There are not currently any projects funded within PA under this initiative.

Forest insects and diseases, invasive plants and animals, inadequate forest regeneration, and over-
abundant deer populations are the major factors affecting forest health in Pennsylvania. Wildland fire
Non-native invasive species are very serious threats and can have significantly devastating impacts on
the long-term health and sustainability of Pennsylvania's forests. Diseases, such as chestnut blight
and Dutch elm disease, and insect pests, such as gypsy moth, hemlock woolly adelgid, and emerald
ash borer have already significantly changed the forests and urban landscapes of Pennsylvania. Many
of the invasive insects and pathogens in the United States have initially become established in urban

Descriptions of the National Insect & Disease Riskmap (NIDRM) program from the USDA Forest
NIDRM is a nationwide strategic assessment and database of the potential hazard for tree
mortality due to major forest insects and diseases. The goal of NIDRM is to summarize
landscape-level patterns of potential insect and disease activity, consistent with the philosophy
that science-based, transparent methods should be used to allocate pest-management
resources across geographic regions and individual pest distributions. In other words: prioritize
investment for areas where both hazard is significant and effective treatment can be efficiently
From USDA Forest Service, regarding the 2018 update to the 2012 riskmap:
Since 2012, significant tree mortality events from fire, forest pest outbreaks, and broad scale
forest harvesting operations have reduced or in some cases eliminated hazard. For the 2018
NIDRM update, we adjusted the composite 2012 NIDRM by subtracting major disturbance
events, thus accounting for reductions in hazard due to previous and ongoing tree mortality. The
update does not account for increases in hazard due to tree growth, which can make additional
trees susceptible and vulnerable to new forest pest attacks. Also, the update does not account
for new pests on the landscape such as the Flathead fir borer, a wood boring beetle that
primarily attacks stressed or weakened Douglas-fir, true firs, and western larch in Region 6.

The extent and quality of forest regeneration has far-reaching impacts on forest health and the suite
of values the forest provides to society. The natural replacement (regeneration) of forests helps
maintain and enhance Pennsylvania's nearly 58 % forest land base that recharges water within
watersheds, stores carbon, and provides incalculable ecological services. The habitat structure that
Eradicated young forests provide is essential to many wildlife species, such as American woodcock, golden-Not Present after 1 Treatment
winged warblers, and Appalachian cottontails. The species mix in these regenerating forests impacts
the future availability of wood products. Some of today's commercially valuable timber species, for
example -such as oak, black cherry, and sugar maple -are not strongly represented in the
regeneration component of today's forest. Ecologically, declines in regeneration from species such as
cherry, beech, oak, and hickory lead to loss in both plant and wildlife diversity within the landscape

The National Forest Inventory and Analysis Program of the USDA Forest Service has been in continuous operation since 1930, based initially on authorities in the McSweeney-McNary Forest Research Act of 1928. The FIA Program conducts and continuously updates a comprehensive nationwide inventory and analysis of the status and trends of America's forest resources. Information collected and analyzed under this Program are the primary source of ecological data on the conservation and sustainable management of forests across all ownerships in the United States. The latest report for Pennsylvania, Pennsylvania Forests 2014, is available online at https://www.fs.fed.us/nrs/pubs/rb/rb_nrs111.pdf.

note.p: FIA conducts the nation's continuous forest census, collecting, analyzing, and reporting information on the status and trends of America's forests. The quality of this information will not be attained, as Congress intended, without full funding. Information provided by FIA on how much forest exists, where it exists, who owns it, and how it is changing (growth, mortality, removal, and successional trends) have many uses for SAF members, partners, policy makers, and research analysts. Data collected and analyzed by FIA on insects, diseases, and other types of forest damage help characterize current health and potential future risks. Such information serves as the foundation for landscape-level policy decisions and economic and ecological management decisions and offers substantial utility to land managers in devising better forest management plans and developing an understanding of future ecosystem changes.DCNR -Bureau of Forestry's Continuous Forest Inventory (CFI)

note.p: Project Learning Tree https://www.plt.org/ USDA Forest Service Conservation Education https://www.fs.usda.gov/main/conservationeducation/home Issue 6: Energy Management & Development Highlights Issue Statement: Reliable energy sources are key to our society. Extraction of energy resources must be carefully managed and continually adapted to ensure protection of common natural resources while responsibly extracting or harnessing energy to power our communities. In PA, shale gas infrastructure and utility and pipeline rights-of-way have substantial overlap with forests of the commonwealth, and coordination across ownerships is essential to ensure that these industries are managed responsibly and in a way that avoids, minimizes, mitigates, and monitors impacts wherever possible. In addition, seeking and promoting use of renewable energy sources and minimizing energy consumption is a shared responsibility of all Pennsylvanians, but resource management agencies such as the DCNR have the unique opportunity to provide a model for these efforts. Threats • Fragmentation of forests from infrastructure due to the rapid expansion of shale gas development (over 13,000 wells drilled statewide since 2010) • Introduction of invasive species through development • Irresponsible management of development and infrastructure • Water quality concerns related to extractive processes, increased traffic and disturbance, and loss of forests due to energy development • Air quality concerns with increased traffic and industrial activity • Noise pollution and soundscape alteration with development, traffic, and extraction activity Opportunities reclamation, abandoned mine land restoration, etc.)

figure.head: Forests and ROWs Legislation affecting state forest land addresses utility ROWs
figure.figDesc: The program aims to inform and improve shale gas management efforts and provide objective and credible information to stakeholders. The DCNR Bureau of Forestry's Shale Gas Monitoring Program is an interdisciplinary team designed to assess and communicate the environmental and social effects of natural gas development on state forest lands. A comprehensive and systematic program to track, detect, and report on these impacts is critical for the continued sustainable management of the state forest system. Understanding the effects of shale gas development will aid in the development of improved policies, guidelines, and best management practices.To help guide its monitoring program, DCNR identified a suite of "monitoring values." These values, developed in 2010 with input from its Ecosystem Management Advisory Committee, help focus monitoring efforts on values that relate to the sustainability of the state forest system; the effects of natural gas drilling on state forest to stakeholders and communities; and DCNR and the bureau's Introduction Utility Rights of way (ROWs) have crossed Pennsylvania for more than a century. Many were developed as the national power grid was assembled in the early 1900s, to transport electricity via support towers and transmission lines. ROWs have also been developed in the state for the purpose of utilities or energy transmission such as gas pipelines, water lines, sewer lines, and buried fiber optic cable lines. The number of gas pipeline ROW requests in the state have accelerated due to the aging of existing pipeline infrastructure, additional shale formation development, and increasing transport of liquified products. Efforts to modernize and expand capacity of National Interstate Electric Transmission Corridors (NIETC), including the Mid-Atlantic NIETC that crosses Pennsylvania, have added pressure for new or expanded ROWs. Pennsylvania connects power plants in the Midwest to concentrations of users in New York and New Jersey. Upgrades to existing facilities are also increasing, to ensure reliability and to accommodate projected increased demands.In recent years, as demands for rights-of-way have increased, various stakeholders and citizens have voiced concerns regarding the impacts of ever-increasing ROW networks. As evident in Figure3.6-4 below, Pennsylvania is a crossroads for many transmissions corridors and has many overlapping transmission routes. Environmental advocates are focusing on forest conversion and fragmentation impacts of new ROW routes that target undeveloped lands. State forest land contains many ROWs. One of the first -and now largest -terminals for natural gas in the nation was located in the middle of the Sproul State Forest at Leidy Hub in Clinton County PA in the 1950s. As demand for ROWs increases and specifications become more impactful, careful placement planning and strategic utilization of existing corridors will be necessary to minimize the environmental impacts from Pennsylvania's status as a hub of transmission and distribution.

figure.figDesc: Special Protection Areas: • ROW development within Wild Areas, Natural Areas, and State Parks is predominately incompatible with management objectives. • Corridors should avoid exemplary geologic formations, sensitive habitats, and known occurrences for rare, threatened, or endangered flora and fauna species. • Impacts to water resources including wetlands and vernal pools should be avoided. Route Planning: • A clear need for the right-of-way should be established and alternative routes should be investigated and included in the proposal, as well as a justification for why the preferred route was chosen. • Proposals should minimize further forest fragmentation by paralleling existing rights-ofway and roads. • Routes should work within topographical constraints to minimize aesthetic impacts. • Proposed corridors should consider potential recreational impacts and existing DCNR operations. Design and Construction: • Companies with existing rights-of-way should work within that right-of-way to increase available capacity versus requesting additional acreage to site additional infrastructure. • Corridor widths should be minimized to include only the width necessary to ensure safe and adequate working conditions. • Companies with adjacent right-of-way interests should work cooperatively in the management of the corridor and the siting of necessary infrastructure.ROW projects that remain within state boundaries (e.g., non-storage gathering gas pipelines, distribution electric lines, etc.) or cross state boundaries (e.g., hazardous liquid gas pipelines) are within the jurisdiction of the Pennsylvania Utilities Commission. Certain electric transmission lines, gas storage pipelines, or natural gas transmission pipelines come under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and must adhere to federal regulatory guidelines standards and certifications. In terms of gas transportation, DCNR currently recognizes two different types of pipelines on state forest land: gas gathering pipelines and transmission pipelines. More complete information about how to apply for a ROW can be found on the Bureau of Forestry's ROW website. -term change in land use that can limit or prevent other uses (such as recreational access) and can have a variety of impacts on habitat. Linear corridors dramatically increase edge habitat within the forest. While this can benefit several species of flora and fauna, it decreases critical habitat for interior forest-dependent species, increases competition for limited resources, and fuels the potential for introducing undesirable invasive species and diseases.

note.p: Invasive PlantsROW projects across lands managed by DCNR or others have the potential to disturb sizable acreage. Careful and well-planned revegetation efforts following ROW construction can help restore wildlife habitat, suppress soil erosion, and improve aesthetics. Strategically designed and incorporated native seed mixes applied during site rehabilitation can work to compete against or control the advancement of invasive plant species. DCNR's 2009 ROW revegetation plan addresses these issues and provides guidance.

figure.figDesc: Given trends in ownership and parcel size, many areas of the state will require new, innovative approaches if access is to be maintained. Harvesting operations for biomass must consider approaches appropriate for small properties and respect private forest landowners' preferences (i.e., most do not want to see clearcuts or unsustainable harvesting). Forest landowners, local policymakers, and the timber industry must work together to address access in the context of an increasingly parcelized forest. January 8, 2019, Governor Wolf signed Executive Order 2019-01 on the subject of Commonwealth Leadership in Addressing Climate Change and Promoting Energy Conservation and Sustainable Governance. This Executive Order set a target of 26% reduction of net greenhouse gas emissions statewide by 2025 from 2005 levels, and an 80% reduction of net greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 from 2005 levels. It also set various emission and energy performance goals for commonwealth agencies and re-established the GreenGov Council. Various aspects of this Executive Order have a bearing on forests of the commonwealth and Bureau of Forestry operations.

figure.figDesc: According to the Pennsylvania Fire and Emergency Services Institute, the number of volunteer firefighters in Pennsylvania has shrunk from 300,000 in the 1970s to about 60,000 in the early 2000s, then to 38,000 in 2018. Pennsylvania has 2,462 fire companies, of which more than 90 % are volunteer-staffed. Additionally, the number of volunteer Forest Fire Wardens in Pennsylvania has reduced from approximately 2,000 in the early 2000s to about 1,100 in 2019.Additional support to volunteers is provided through the USDA Forest Service Volunteer Fire Assistance grant program. The VFA program is administered by State Forestry agencies through 50-50 cost-sharing grants to local fire departments located in rural communities. The program's main goal is to provide Federal financial, technical, and other assistance in the organization, training and equipping of fire departments in rural areas, defined as having a population of 10,000 or less. These grants are a valuable avenue to provide funding to volunteers specifically for wildland fire and should be maintained going forward.

note.p: Support to volunteer wildland firefighters is provided by DCNR through several avenues. First, the Federal Excess Personal Property Program and the Department of Defense Firefighter Property programs allow DCNR to obtain excess equipment from the federal government to provide to volunteer fire organizations. The Federal Excess Personal Property (FEPP) program refers to Forest Service-owned property that is on loan to State Foresters for the purpose of wildland and rural firefighting. The Firefighter Property Program (FFP) refers to one of the Department of Defense's (DoD) special programs where firefighters can acquire excess DoD property to be used for firefighting and emergency services. Both of these programs provide significant support for volunteer fire organizations; however, the Bureau of Forestry has not had any personnel dedicated to these programs on a full-time basis in several years. Revitalizing these programs by dedicating a full-time staff member within the Division of Forest Fire Protection to the centralized management and coordination of these efforts would provide much needed support to volunteers.CooperatorsDCNR leverages cooperative relationships with multiple wildland fire agencies and organizations at all levels. The specific terms of these relationships are outlined in formal, written agreements that are vital to the operation of the wildland fire program. Cooperative agreements are in place with the following agencies and organizations for wildland fire:Additionally, cooperative agreements are signed between DCNR and local fire departments involved in the FEPP and FFP programs.DCNR is an active member of the Pennsylvania Prescribed Fire Council, allowing the DCNR to collaborate with agencies from across the state in this important work.One other especially important cooperative endeavor is the Middle Atlantic Interstate Forest Fire Protection Compact. The Middle-Atlantic Interstate Forest Fire Protection Compact (MAIFFPC) is authorized by public law and is comprised of seven states and associate partners from the U.S. Forest Service, National Park Service and Fish and Wildlife Service. The seven states are Ohio, West Virginia, Virginia, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and Maryland. The purpose of the Compact is to promote effective fire prevention and the control of wildfires in the Mid-Atlantic region.

figure.figDesc: used to support most costs for logistics, travel, instructors, and training materials.After the fire season of 2016, DCNR identified a need to make wildland fire training more inclusive and accessible for all of the commonwealth's wildland firefighters. For the past two years, DCNR has conducted a Summer Wildfire Academy. Over 300 students have attended each year. Most courses are 100 and 200-level NWCG courses, with a mixture of classes offered both during the work week for DCNR employees and over the weekend to accommodate volunteers. This training event has been a positive change and should be sustained in the future.DCNR also continues to support the Mid-Atlantic Wildland Fire Academy and provides additional support to its cooperators when requested and available. Qualifications are essential to any wildland fire program to establish baseline position competencies and behaviors needed for individuals to fulfill needed roles in response to wildfires, prescribed fires, and other emergencies. Without individuals in these roles, requests for resources may go unfilled or need to be filled by partners or cooperators, often creating a greater delay or stress on the incident.

note.p: 2018, DCNR provided over 100 classroom training sessions that trained approximately 1,800 students. Additionally, about 300 students completed online training. This training is completed to National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) or National Incident Management System (NIMS) standards. Most all of this training is provided at no cost to the students. State Fire Assistance (SFA) grant funds are The national standard in the United States is established by NWCG. DCNR currently utilizes NWCG standards for wildland fire qualifications. This allows DCNR resources to work as seamlessly as possible with our partners. NWCG qualifications are obtained by firefighters through a combination of training and experience. Experience is documented by completing a position-specific task book (Table3.7-1).

figure.figDesc: The Division of Forest Fire Protection manages a State Fire Cache at Halifax, in Dauphin County. This facility is co-located with the Weiser Forest District -Haldeman Tract maintenance and fire facilities. The State Fire Cache is responsible for storage, maintenance, and inventory of tools, supplies, and equipment needed to support wildland fire operations throughout the commonwealth. The Cache is a centralized storage and distribution point for the myriad items needed to support the wildland fire program.

With almost 13 million residents, 29 million total acres, and 16 million acres of forestland, Pennsylvania has a relatively high number of acres that are classified as Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI). The research map NRS-8, The 2010 Wildland-Urban Interface of the Conterminous United States, published by the US Forest Service in 2015 identifies Pennsylvania as one of four states with the largest WUI area. As of the 2015 study, WUI covers about 10.3 million acres in Pennsylvania. Public safety and awareness in wildfire prevention are enhanced through education and focused outreach in areas of risk to wildfires. A key component of public education on wildfire prevention is accurate and timely determination of wildfire danger and subsequent communication of that information to staff and the public. Another important component is Smokey Bear, who has been the symbol of wildfire prevention in the United States for over 75 years. The Smokey Bear program is administered by the USDA Forest Service and remains a viable component of wildfire prevention efforts. Forest Fire wardens conduct many programs across the commonwealth each year.

note.p: Many homes throughout Pennsylvania are constructed near wildlands. These areas often have fuel types that are susceptible to ignition, and consequently there is an increased risk of human-caused wildfires. Wildfires occurring in the WUI can quickly transition to burning residences or structures. Additionally, most WUI areas in Pennsylvania are served by volunteer fire departments, which have documented challenges with staffing, finances, and equipment. Planning is critical to determine wildfire risk and strategies and capabilities to mitigate these risks. A comprehensive, statewide wildfire risk assessment is needed for decision support and to prioritize and identify target areas for addressing these challenges.

figure.figDesc: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) founded the Natural Heritage network in the early 1970s, with the first program established in South Carolina in 1974. With funding from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources (DER), the single department precursor of today's DCNR and DEP, Pennsylvania established its Heritage program, called the Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory (PNDI) until the early 2000s. A database was established and two offices; one in the west, run by WPC, and one in the east run by TNC. The program began the process of collecting records for species occurrences. Slowly the program added staff biologists and data managers and in the late 1980s began the County Inventory program. With additional funding from DCNR's Bureau of Recreation and Conservation, the County Inventory Program (see below) began to grow rapidly and by the late 1990s had completed projects in more than half of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. By this time, the program was known as a partnership between WPC, TNC and DCNR, with the PFBC and PGC as active cooperators with the program. With a change of its name to the Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program, the previous name, PNDI, was reserved for the database itself and today often refers to the environmental review process.In 2005, TNC decided to leave the partnership and a major planning effort was undertaken. The result was that WPC's role expanded to cover all of Pennsylvania, and all TNC PNHP employees were transferred to WPC. With the addition of the PGC and the PFBC as full partners, the program evolved into the four-way partnership that it is today. While not a formal partner, the Pennsylvania Field Office of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service also works closely with PNHP. With a new strategic and operating plan, the newly restructured program officially went into operation onJuly 1, 2006.

Many populations of Pennsylvania's rarest plants are found on private lands. These locations generally do not receive the same amount of active management as populations found on statemanaged lands. Many plant species need specific conditions to thrive, such as an open canopy, reduced competition, or removal of invasive species. The Pennsylvania Plant Conservation Network (PPCN) program addresses those issues through a collaborative approach. The PPCN is a new program that will leverage statewide partnerships to coordinate on-the-ground stewardship, outreach, and education efforts about native plants. The goal is to collaborate on projects across the state, building partnerships to meaningfully advance native plant conservation in Pennsylvania. This initiative is coordinated by DCNR and seeks to bring together the following groups:• Botanists, ecologists, and other environmental professionals • Researchers and students • Citizen scientists and botanical clubs • Horticulturists, growers, and gardeners engaged in native plant conservation • Anyone who has an interest in plant conservationPennsylvania Invasive Species Council to the GovernorThe Governor's Invasive Species Council of Pennsylvania (PISC) is a multi-agency advisory panel made up of seven state agencies and non-governmental agencies with the common purpose of identifying invasive species of concern that currently or could potentially threaten the commonwealth's natural and agricultural resources and the industries they support.Initially enacted in 2004 by Executive Order No. 2004-1, Governor Tom Wolf reenacted the Council on December 20, 2017 with Executive Order No. 2017-07. The Council's main purpose is to develop the commonwealth's invasive species action plans, advise the Governor on invasive species policy development, and coordinate interagency response to invasive species threats.

Identify species most at risk from climate change • Reintroduce river otters and osprey to the commonwealth • Understand management needs for rare plants and animals, including species like American ginseng and hellbenders Pennsylvania Wildlife Futures Program This program is a new partnership program between the Pennsylvania Game Commission (PGC) and the University of Pennsylvania's School of Veterinary Medicine (Penn Vet) to integrate comprehensive disease surveillance and mitigation expertise into a single, unified effort to combat the numerous wildlife diseases. This program was launched in 2019 and hopes to: • Establish new statewide, innovative research and surveillance programs to identify diseases • Develop and maintain a comprehensive wildlife health information system • Facilitate communication across agencies, to the science community, and to the public • Enhance technical and staff capacity through a comprehensive training programThe Wildlife Futures Program is research-oriented and is, therefore, comprised of a vast network of scientists, veterinarians, and conservationists from across the commonwealth. By combining the expertise and resources of the PGC and Pennsylvania's only veterinary school, the WFP implements a forward-thinking approach to safeguard the commonwealth's wildlife resources for current and future generations.

This report is very telling of the economic impact state forest land recreation has on Pennsylvania's economy. Considering PA State Forests only comprise 2.2 million acres of Pennsylvania 17 million acres, the Center for Rural Pennsylvania report only tells part of the story.It is evident that outdoor activities are increasingly popular across Pennsylvania. In many cases communities have taken advantage of this trend to revitalize city centers. By conserving forests and other natural lands and making them available for outdoor recreation, small towns can boost air quality and water quality and focus development downtown. Promoting outdoor recreation can also create jobs in unlikely remote locations and offer new opportunities for people to connect with the natural world. "Trail Towns" or "Outdoor Towns" programs provide framework for communities to promote nature-based tourism to reap the economic, social, and environmental benefits of wellmanaged recreation and tourism opportunities.

figure.figDesc: Besides the increasing total demand, most sources indicate that the types of demand, i.e., individual activities practiced by users, have experienced increasing diversification. That is, visitors have been experiencing public lands in more different ways, and/ or visitors expect more varied recreational opportunities to be available. For example, while traditional opportunities have included playgrounds, hunting, and hiking, the 2018 Lion Poll results overwhelmingly indicate that novel uses like kayaking and rock climbing are on the rise(SCORP 2020-24). Furthermore, the Preliminary Report for the Bureau of State Parks strategic planning process indicates an increasing demand for new avenues like adventure activities and dark sky opportunities. Motorized recreational opportunities, such as snowmobiling and ATV-riding are increasingly in demand by users of Pennsylvania's forests.

note.p: According to the 2017 Pennsylvania Outdoor Recreation Economy Report by Outdoor Industry Association, 56% of Pennsylvanians participated in outdoor recreation, generating $29.1 billion in spending. According to the Penn State Center for Survey Research's Spring 2019 Lion Poll, 79% of Pennsylvanians agree that the commonwealth should increase its permanent source of funding for outdoor recreation. Additionally, forest landowner studies, such as the National Woodland Owner Survey, indicate that recreation is often a major reason for owning forestland.
