figure.figDesc: regional model for forestland protection of interest to Pennsylvania is Woodnet, developed by government and nonprofit partners in New York State's Catskills region. This innovative program recognizes the value forests play in protecting water quality and invests funding that would have gone toward expanded water treatment plant capacity into preserving the forested watershed region where drinking water originates and flows through. The program also recognizes the importance of preserving a working forest landscape and integrating local timber operations, furniture making, and other wood products industries to develop economic incentives for forestland preservation. Pennsylvania has introduced the program to two pilot areas of the state, South Mountain and the Poconos, although it currently lacks a funding mechanism similar to the New York model.

Forest Legacy Program (FLP) is a partnership between individual states and the USDA Forest Service to identify and help conserve environmentally important forests from conversion to nonforest uses. The tools used for protecting these important forests are conservation easements and fee purchases. Participation in FLP is entirely voluntary and limited to private forest landowners. To be included in the Forest Legacy Program, a property must lie partially or entirely within a designated Forest Legacy Area. To qualify, landowners are required to prepare a multiple resource stewardship plan as part of the conservation easement acquisition. The Federal government may fund up to 75% of program costs, with at least 25% coming from private, state, or local sources.

figure.figDesc: Delaware is the longest undammed river east of the Mississippi, flowing freely for 330 miles from lower New York State through Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware to the Atlantic Ocean. The Delaware's 13,539 square mile watershed drains about four percent of the continental United States land area and provides drinking water for 13 million people in four states. The river meets tide-water at Trenton, NJ and constitutes the entire boundary between New Jersey and Pennsylvania, most of the boundary between Delaware and New Jersey, and part of the boundary between Pennsylvania and New York.

note.p: The Delaware Bay Estuary is the tidal portion, or the lower half, of the Delaware River Basin. The area surrounding the estuary stretches as far west as the Schuylkill River's headwaters near Pottsville, PA, and to the east near Fort Dix, NJ. The vastness of this watershed makes the Delaware Bay Estuary one of the largest estuaries in the country, approximately 6,800 square miles in size. Within these boundaries are over 200 species of fish, the continent's second-highest concentration of shorebirds, and over 400,000 acres of wetlands.Land use, fragmentation, forest health, and water quality are major issues within the Delaware River watershed, providing significant opportunities for partnership. The Delaware River Basin Conservation Act was signed into law in December 2016 and established the Delaware River Basin Restoration Program. The program is supported by diverse partners and collaborators seeking to improve ecological integrity, and therefore, communities and quality of life throughout the basin. The program will support conservation, stewardship, and enhancement projects focusing on 4 areas: coordinating conservation and restoration activities. The program will leverage collaborative efforts to obtain funding for common goals and identify gaps, with grant-funding mechanisms for projects that support shared priorities and complement existing efforts.

figure.figDesc: Appalachians are among the oldest mountains on Earth. They extend almost 2,000 mi from the Canadian provinces of Newfoundland and Labrador in the northeast, southwestward to Alabama in the U.S. They include the White Mountains in New Hampshire, the Green Mountains in Vermont, the Catskill Mountains in New York, the Allegheny Mountains primarily in Pennsylvania, the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia and North Carolina, the Great Smoky Mountains in North Carolina and Tennessee, and the Cumberland Plateau extending from West Virginia to Alabama. Their highest peak is Mount Mitchell in North Carolina.The Appalachian Region in this plan focuses more on the Mid-Atlantic States and south, than the Appalachians that extend into the New England region. The region (see map below) is a 205,000square-mile area that follows the spine of the Appalachian Mountains from southern New York to northern Georgia.

figure.figDesc: The Department of Conservation and Natural Resources' Bureau of Forestry is soliciting comments on the draft Pennsylvania Forest Action Plan. We are fortunate to live in a state containing nearly 17 million acres of forest. These forest ecosystems provide valuable benefits and services, including clean air and water, recreation opportunities, wood products, habitat for native species, and carbon storage and sequestration. This Forest Action Plan is part of a coordinated, nationwide forest planning effort. As mandated by the 2018 Farm Bill and coordinated by the USDA Forest Service, a Forest Action Plan is completed for each state and territory every 10 years. Completing this effort also makes Pennsylvania eligible for continued federal funding for its private lands, urban and community forestry, wildland fire, and forest health programs.

note.p: The Forest Legacy Program (FLP), established by the 1990 Farm Bill, was created by Congress to identify and conserve "environmentally important forest areas that are threatened by conversion to non-forest uses, through the use of conservation easements and other mechanisms, for promoting forest land conservation." The Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act of 1996, (P.L. 104-127:stat.888), authorized the Secretary of Agriculture, at the state's request, to award grants for the state to carry out the FLP, including the acquisition of land and interests in land.

figure.figDesc: In 1933, newly elected President Franklin D. Roosevelt created the US Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), a work program for able bodied, unemployed males. This peacetime "army" was recruited to battle the destruction and erosion of the nation's natural resources. Approximately 93 resident work camps, each consisting of 174-200 young men, were built on Pennsylvania's state forestlands. State forestry personnel planned and supervised work projects for the CCC. Work projects included construction of roads, fire trails, workshops, park and picnic area development, tree planting, and fire suppression. Most of the CCC camps in Pennsylvania were closed by 1942.

In 1902, Rothrock established the first State Forest Nursery, and in 1903, founded the Pennsylvania State Forest Academy in Mont Alto. These institutions were designed to provide the trees and the trained foresters necessary to begin the reforestation of Pennsylvania. The public interest in conservation gained momentum and in 1905, the first of Pennsylvania's State Game Refuges was established in Clinton County. It was not until 1919 that the State Legislature passed a law authorizing the Game Commission to purchase lands. figure.figDesc: Today, in Pennsylvania, approximately 2 million acres of land is in State Forest Lands, 1.4 million acres is in State Game Lands, and 500,000 acres is in the Allegheny National Forest. The location of these public lands is shown in Figure2. County and Municipal forestland holdings comprise nearly 250,000 acres, statewide. Of the nearly 17 million forested acres in Pennsylvania, 15,894,129 are classified as commercial forestland. Commercial forestland is defined as land capable of producing 20 cu.ft./acre/ year, excluding reserved areas (natural and wild). Private landowners hold the largest portion of forestland in Pennsylvania. These private lands account for 12.5 million acres. FLP will help to conserve these private lands from conversion to non-traditional forest uses.Although 59% of Pennsylvania is forested, 55% of the state is currently covered by commercial forestland capable of producing a sustainable yield of forest products. Of this 55%, almost three-quarters or 12.5 million acres are privately owned. While northwestern, southwestern and northcentral Pennsylvania are the most heavily forested sections of the state, forestland is the dominant land cover in most of Pennsylvania. However, the state of the forest is changing. Today's forests are adversely affected by air pollution, insect and disease infestations, and conversion to non-forest uses.

figure.figDesc: see Appendix p 69) and was accepted by the full State Stewardship Steering Committee. The original AON included a large Forest Legacy Area in north central and northeastern PA. It was agreed to accept a large area and allow local conservancies to concentrate their efforts in small areas within the larger area. DCNR, as well as, the Governor's office received several negative comments on the Forest Legacy program the day before the meeting in September 1999. The State Stewardship Steering Committee discussed the program for several hours and subsequently decided to table the AON until a time when questions could be answered concerning the program. Conversations with the forest industry and the Forest Service ensued during the next 12 months. The AON was revised to meet the requirements of the Forest Legacy Program. During this time frame the Conemaugh Valley Conservancy proposed the Kiski-Conemaugh Watershed as a Forest Legacy Area. This Legacy area was accepted by the full committee and is included in the AON. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania has received several letters of support. Local policymakers and landowners are very interested in working with the Forest Legacy Program to conserve forestland in the watershed.

Conservation Message: Public ownership of forestland affords a long-term sustained yield of forest products and
benefits. Conservation easements will also serve in a similar capacity. History indicates
that most lands change ownership every 10 years. In most areas of the state it takes
more than eighty years to grow a sawlog-size tree. This means that a tree will have
several owners, each with his/her own objectives. Multiple objectives over the long-term
can lead to non-sustainable management of forest resources.
The Forest Legacy Program is designed for the landowner to enter his/her land into a
conservation easement. The program is based on a willing seller/willing buyer basis and
the landowner retains the title to the property. Only the development and recreation
rights can be purchased under this program.

figure.figDesc: Federal, State and Local governments own 21 percent of the total forestland in Pennsylvania. Public forestland is managed for forest products, as well as water resources, recreation and aesthetics. The DCNR pays in lieu of tax payments to local governments on every acre of state forest. The Federal Government contributes 25 percent of the timber revenues to the local schools. Pennsylvania's State and Federal lands are some of the best managed forests in the world. Corporate, Industry and other private concerns hold 24 percent, and farmers and private landowners hold the remaining 55 percent. Therefore, fully 79 percent of the forestland in Pennsylvania is privately held.

figure.figDesc: a first step, conservancies/land trusts and other non-profit groups can apply for sponsorship. After certification as a sponsor, they can nominate potential FLAs. FLAs are defined by the sponsor. Sponsors are encouraged to use county boundaries. The County, Township, State and Federal governments must approve the Legacy Area prior to property inclusion in the FLP.FLA Sponsors must be willing to address public relations for the FLP; to work with landowners toward understanding; and to help potential landowners complete the application and acquisition process. The FLP is a cost-share program run by the USDA Forest Service. The Federal government pays no more than 75 percent of total program costs for each FLP easement. The local cost-share may include cash contributions, lands or interests in lands, or In-Kind Services. The FLA Sponsors will assure that 25 percent of program cost-share funds are from non-Federal sources.Property assessments are normally based on Market Value; however; when individual interests are sold or the property is enrolled in the Clean and Green Program, the assessments may be reduced. A landowner may request a property reassessment after the sale of development or recreation interests as a result of selling an easement. A county or township may raise tax assessments on other properties to compensate for the shortfall created by enrollment in land conservation programs. Lands enrolled in the Pennsylvania Clean and Green Program, a preferential property tax program, are also eligible for enrollment in the FLP. Lands protected solely under the Clean and Green Program may be removed from the preferential tax treatment, while lands entered into the FLP will remain working forests in perpetuity.

figure.figDesc: ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________Timber prices in Pennsylvania are currently very high. Many landowners who had not considered harvesting timber previously are now receiving unsolicited offers for their timber. The money may sound tempting, but you'll want to be certain, if you do harvest, that it's in your best interest to do so now. If your timber is immature you may be cutting it just as it begins to increase most in value. You may not have a pressing need for income at the present time, but may anticipate a need in the future-say when your children are college aged or once you've retired and are on a fixed income. Not every woodlot has the potential to produce salable timber within the owner's lifetime. You should consider whether it is important to you to obtain income from your land now or in the future, and let your plan writer know so that he/she can develop a plan to try and meet those needs. For what kinds of activities? Are there other benefits you'd like to get from the land? Do you plan to keep the land in forest or to change the land use within your lifetime-perhaps develop all or part of it? What are your hopes/plans for the land for the next 10 or 20 years? What do you hope will happen to the land after your death? a commitment of time, labor, and sometimes money. Think carefully about how often you (or others in your family) spend time in your woods and how much time you'd be able to commit to doing the actual work involved. What kind of equipment do you have available? How experienced are you at working in the woods? It is easy to underestimate the amount of skill and labor involved in completing a Forest Legacy Area. Are you willing to expend funds toward the management of your land to hire professional equipment operators? Some cost-share assistance is available to help; let your plan writer and Service Forester know if you'd want to apply for assistance. If you have little time or other resources available at present for managing your land, be sure to make that clear so that your plan can focus on only the most cost effective activities for your land.

Management Plan: All forestry and forest management activities shall be performed in accordance with a current Multi-Resource Management Plan that meets the purposes of this easement as defined in Section I. Natural forest areas cannot be converted to plantation forestry. Plantation forestry may only occur in areas that are currently plantations or on previously non-forested areas within the conservation easement area. The Grantee shall review and act to approve or disapprove Multi-Resource Management Plans submitted by the Grantor within sixty (60) days of the Grantee's receipt of each such plan. The Grantee shall also act on amendments to such plans within sixty (60) days of receipt, excepting that the Grantee shall act within thirty (30) days on any amendment which proposes a different forest stand treatment to a single treatment unit. The Grantee shall approve any management plan or amendment so long as such plan or amendment is consistent with the purposes set out in Section I of this Easement and complies with the requirements of Paragraphs II.A and B above. For the purposes of construing this Easement, "forestry" shall include the science, art, and practice of creating, managing, using, and conserving forests and associated resources for human benefit and in accordance with best management practices, including the production of specialty forest plants or plant and timber products for domestic or commercial purposes.

Except as expressly provided in Paragraph IV.C., hereof, there shall be no building, structure or other improvement of any kind, temporary or permanent, constructed or placed on the subject land, including, but not limited to, any houses, towers, satellite dishes, windmills, wind turbines, sheds, barns, silos, tanks, mobile homes, dams, impoundments and communications equipment. Existing stone walls, fords, culverts, drains, power lines, poles, towers and trails, which are noted in the Easement Inventory and Baseline Documentation attached hereto, may be maintained in their current state or condition.C. Mineral Development: Mining and mineral development may be conducted in, under or upon the subject land provided that no more than ten (10) percent of the surface acreage thereof is disturbed at any single point in time by such activities, and not to exceed the maximum 25 percent non-forested cover requirement in the Program. Having reached the ten(10) percent acreage limitation, or the 25 percent non-forest cover, whichever is the lesser of the two, no further mining or mineral development shall be permitted unless the Grantor first restores, reclaims, remediates and reforests according to program guidelines, effective as of the date of this easement, the affected area. To the protection of traditional forest uses any such mineral development must meet state and federal regulations. Reforestation is defined as land currently growing forest trees of any size with a total stocking value of at least 16.7 percent, or lands formerly forested, currently capable of becoming forest land, and not currently developed for non-forest uses. Oil and gas development may not occur in, under or upon the subject land. In cases where the oil and gas rights are owned by a third party, and these rights would not impact the surface of the subject property (e.g. if the land is subject to forced pooling for extraction of oil or gas), then it may be acceptable if the exploitation of the existing reserved oil and gas is unlikely to negatively impact the property. The State Forester or designee will determine the acceptability of these impacts. Except as permitted under Paragraph III.C. above, no removal, filling, or other disturbances of soil surface, nor any changes in topography, surface or subsurface water systems, wetlands or natural habitat shall be permitted unless such activities are approved by the grantee; and are commonly necessary to the accomplishment of the forest management plan; and are not detrimental to or inconsistent with the purposes of this Easement or any and all other activities required and approved by the grantee; and prior to commencement of any such activities, all necessary federal, state and local permits and approvals shall be secured. No portion of the subject land shall be used for any dumps, landfills, or the storage, deposit, burning or other destruction or elimination of waste materials of any kind, hazardous or otherwise. Disposal of any waste materials generated by on-site forestry or forest management activities shall be permitted on the subject land provided that such disposal shall comply with all then-applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations. Except for the forestry and forest management activities allowed under Section II herein, and the more intensive land development practices allowed under Section III herein, use of the subject land for industrial, commercial or residential development of any kind is prohibited.

figure.figDesc: For purposes of this easement, harvesting operations are defined in the accompanying Multi-Resource Management Plan or approved Forest Stewardship Plan. The Grantee must be notified of all upcoming timber harvests. The Grantee will in no way interfere with the harvesting of timber unless that harvest is not intended to be conducted in accordance with the corresponding Multi-Resource Management Plan or approved Forest Stewardship Plan. Recreational use by the Grantor or Grantor's invitees are permitted within the subject land in accordance with all federal, state and local laws and regulations. Such recreational use shall be conducted in a manner consistent with the purposes of this Easement. For purposes of this Easement, recreation is defined as non-developed, dispersed, recreational activities such as, camping, hunting, trapping, fishing, hiking, snowshoeing, skiing, biking and horseback riding. Grantor is also permitted to enter into fee-paid arrangements for recreation privileges on all or part of the property provided that the terms of such leases or licenses comply with the purposes of this Easement." Commercial and/or intensive use by Off Highway Recreational Vehicles (OHRV) is prohibited. Grantor reserves the right to exclusive possession of the subject land and to prohibit trespass, subject to Grantee's rights of access and enforcement as set out in Paragraphs VI.A below. Grantor may permit public access and use of the subject land for recreational activities, such as those outlined in Paragraph IV.A above. The construction of roads or other access ways for the purpose of removing forest products from the subject land shall be permitted. In furtherance of and to facilitate the type of recreational activity permitted under Paragraph IV.A. above, Grantor may construct and maintain, unpaved paths and trails incidental to such recreation. Road and trail construction and maintenance shall be carried out in accordance with applicable Best Management Practices in a manner that is consistent with the purposes of this Easement and the forest management requirements of Section II. Subject to the limitations and restrictions of Paragraph III.G. above, Grantor may erect, maintain and periodically replace such signs as the Grantor or Grantee may deem necessary or desirable for the achievement of the purposes of this Easement. For safety purposes, Grantor shall post signs to restrict or close public access to areas involved in active forestry operations. Grantor may continue to farm existing agricultural fields as noted in the Easement Inventory and Baseline Documentation and may preserve and maintain other appropriately noted open or semi-open areas for wildlife and habitat diversity. Agricultural activities, shall not exceed ten percent of the entire property and must employ conservation tillage and pest and nutrient management practices recognized at the time of such activities as consistent with the purposes of this Easement.

figure.figDesc: No amendment of this Easement is permitted that is inconsistent with the purposes of the Easement set out in Section I. No amendment may affect the Easement's perpetual duration or its prohibitions on residential, commercial, or industrial development. The affirmative forestry obligations of Section II shall also not be altered by amendment. If circumstances in the future should arise so as to render the purposes of this Easement impossible to accomplish, this Easement may be terminated or extinguished. Such action, whether applying to the entire subject land or only to some part thereof, may only be affected by judicial proceedings in a court of competent jurisdiction, applying the statutory and regulatory provisions of the Forest Legacy Act (Section 1217 of Title XII of the Food, Agriculture, Conservation and Trade Act of 1990). Such court will determine whether conditions exist for termination and extinguishment of the Easement and shall, in consultation with the United States Secretary of Agriculture, decide the appropriate method for disposal of the subject land. The Grantee understands and acknowledges that this Easement was acquired, at least in part, with federal funds under the Forest Legacy Program and the interest acquired cannot be sold, exchanged, extinguished, or otherwise disposed of except as provided for in that Act. In the event of any sale, exchange, or other disposal as ordered by a court of competent jurisdiction, the United States government must be reimbursed the market value (at the time of disposal) of that percentage of the subject land acquired with federal funds. The United States Secretary of Agriculture may, in the exercise of his or her discretion, and in consultation with said court, consent to such sale, exchange, or disposal upon the Grantee's tender of the required reimbursement funds or of some other, equal-value consideration acceptable to said Secretary and court.

In the event of a disagreement or dispute between the Parties concerning any of the provisions of this Easement, the Parties may submit the issue(s) to either mediation or arbitration and shall participate in such proceedings and discussions in good faith. The Parties agree that mediation or arbitration shall not operate to stay any proceeding that either party may institute in a court of competent jurisdiction. Any arbitration determination shall not be binding upon the Parties unless they have agreed to be so bound in advance of such determination. Arbitration shall be conducted by three(3) independent arbitrators qualified to act as such and knowledgeable concerning local forest management and conservation practices. The Grantor shall select or name one(1) of the arbitrators, the Grantee shall select or name one(1) of the arbitrators and the final arbitrator shall be selected or named by the two arbitrators already named by the Parties. Nothing in this paragraph shall act to bar or stay either of the Parties rights to initiate or have any disputed issue determined by a court of competent jurisdiction. Grantor acknowledges that he/she/it has been represented by legal counsel of his/her/its own selection or has had the opportunity to be so represented. Grantor understands fully that he/she/it is committing himself/herself/ itself to the ongoing and perpetual practice of forestry on the subject land and is relinquishing certain rights that he/she/it would otherwise have to the full use and development of the subject land. It is expressly understood and agreed that this Easement has been acquired and granted pursuant to and in furtherance of federal law and, notwithstanding any provision of state law, that this instrument shall be construed to effect the purposes of the federal Forest Legacy Program (Forest Legacy Program Implementation Guidelines, Part 1, Section 2) extant on the date this Easement enters into force. With the exception of the preceding rule, any other general rule of construction notwithstanding, this Easement shall be construed so as to preserve, protect, and further the purposes set out in Section I to the fullest extent possible. If any provision in this Easement is found to be ambiguous, an interpretation consistent with the Easement's purposes that would render the provision valid and enforceable shall be favored over any interpretation that would render it invalid or unenforceable. For purposes of construing this Easement, neither of the Parties shall be deemed to be the drafter thereof. Except where necessary to discern the specific intentions of the federal Forest Legacy Act (Section 1217 of Title XII of the Food, Agriculture, Conservation and Trade Act of 1990), the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania shall govern the interpretation and performance of this Easement. Nothing in this Easement shall be construed to permit or authorize any activity by either of the Parties, individually or jointly, which is otherwise prohibited or circumscribed by any federal, state or local law or regulation.I. figure.head: have the population trends been for the last 5 years? Future projections? Provide the growth rate and population density for each county in the proposed Forest Legacy Area. Compare these figures to statewide average.
figure.figDesc: Adams County is currently the third fastest growing county in Pennsylvania and is facing growth pressure from Washington, D.C., Baltimore, Frederick, Harrisburg and York. Adams County has experienced a 5.7% population increase over the past five years(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005) with a current population of 96,456 and a 16.6% population increase between 1990 and 2000, while Pennsylvania's population has only increased by 0.7% over the past five years. Adams County is projected to grow by 8.9% to 97,059 people by 2010, and by 6.6% to 103,475 people by 2020, while Pennsylvania is projected to grow by 1.4% to 12,407,523 people by 2010, and by 1.3% to 12,569,017 people by 2020. At the time of the 2000 census, the population density in Adams County was 175.6 people per square mile ofland, and Pennsylvania's population density was 274 people per square mile of land. 2.

figure.figDesc: Between 1990 and 2003, 60% of Adams County's new development was located within designated growth areas. But with little land remaining for new development in the boroughs, several large scale housing developments(1 ,000 homes or larger) have been proposed or built in locations outside of designated growth areas. The majority of development and subdivision being proposed in Adams County has changed from the local farmer subdividing off a lot or two for his kids to large out-ofcounty developers who purchasing and building large (1 00+ units) residential developments on land parcels of200 acres or larger. In general, most new residential development has been proposed for locations in Southern and Eastern Adams County. Over the last five years, approximately 3300 new homes were constructed in Adams County, the majority being single-family residential units with a smaller portion comprised of mobile homes. Adams County has seen an increase in sales volumes of homes of approximately 8% a year since 2000, and a little more than 5,000 homes were sold in the county over the past five years. The average price for a single-family detached dwelling has increased by nearly 50% over the past five years, from approximately $120,000 in 2000 to approximately $180,000 in 2004. The size of proposed new residential lots varies from year to year, with higher density units appearing to be proposed in three to five year cycles. The number of proposed lots over 10 acres has been steadily declining. Approximately 1 ,230 subdivision and land development requests were made in Adams County from 1998 to 2002, proposing the creation of 5,100 new lots/residential units; and 2,472 new residential lots/units were proposed on3,924 acres in 20033,924 acres in . Between 19953,924 acres in and 2003, 9, 9,900 acres of Adams County fannland was proposed for new residential development, equaling 2.94% of the total county acreage.

figure.figDesc: For FLA eligibility, the forestland must: o Contain lands threatened by significant evidence of parcelization or likelihood of fi'agmentation: 83% of Adams County's forestland is privately-owned, and thus has no penn anent protection from parcelization or fragmentation. As the third fastest growing county in Pennsylvania, Adams County is seeing an increase in large residential subdivisions on its farmlands, and increasingly, its forestlands. A large portion of the privately-owned forestland in Adams County is located in townships that have outdated or no zoning regulations that could control the residential development and subdivision of the forestlands. In 2004, 3,000 acres of land was proposed for residential development in Adams County. Over the past 20 years, several dense 1 00+ unit residential subdivisions have been built on remote forestland that is surrounded by or adjacent to Michaux State Forest and large privately-owned forest tracts. In the 2005 USDA's Forest Service report "Forests on the Edge: Housing Development on America's Private Forests" a portion of Adams County is projected to have housing density increases to occur on private forests across 5% to 20% of its land by 2030. This conversion of land to non-forest use disrupts the natural functions of the forestlands due to increased and polluted stonnwater runoff and erosion from an increase in impervious surfaces and resulting decrease in water quality, decrease in available wildlife habitats, disruption of connected forests for movement of wildlife, altered hydrology, and increased susceptibility to forest fires. With the loss of Adams County's forestlands, also comes the loss of available timber to support the county's forestry, wood products and paper industries, forcing these businesses to find available timber in other counties and states, and possibly shut down all together. o Be environmentally important: • Scenic Resources-Route 30, as it passes through Adams County's forestland heading west from Gettysburg, is included in the scenic Lincoln Highway Heritage Corridor, designated as a Heritage Park by the Governor in 1995, due to its history as the part of the first transcontinental highway. Also, scenic views of Adams County's forestlands are afforded from the Appalachian Trail as it winds through Michaux State Forest and Route 234 as it winds through picturesque areas such as Buchanan Valley and the Conewago Narrows, a water gap formed by Co new ago Creek that has a maximum relief of 698 feet and numerous large outcrops of gray-green metarhyolite. • Public Recreation Opportunities-A portion of Adams County's forestlands are within the boundaries of Michaux State Forest and Caledonia State Park, both owned by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and managed by the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which provide many recreational opportunities including: small game and deer hunting, primitive camping, hiking (including the Appalachian Trail), horseback riding, bicycling, rock-climbing, picnicking, fishing, swimming, canoeing, and snowmobiling. • Riparian Areas-The headwaters of many tributaries of the Potomac and Susquehanna Rivers that eventually flow into the Chesapeake Bay, including Conewago Creek and Marsh Creek, are located in the forestlands of Adams County. Many of these limestone spring fed streams have been identified as High Quality Cold Water Fisheries or Exceptional Value Streams with exceptional trout habitat and water quality. Without any water flowing into Adams County from surrounding areas, all of the county's water originates here and flows out of the county, these streams provide the water source for many townships and boroughs, including Gettysburg Municipal Authority, Fairfield Municipal Authority, Possum Valley Municipal Authority, and Arendtsville Municipal Authority. The Waynesboro Reservoir, the water supply for the town of Waynesboro in neighboring Franklin County, is also located in the forestlands of Adams County. • Fish or Wildlife Habitat-The forested spring-fed streams of western Adams County provide exceptional habitat tor Brook and Rainbow Trout and other aquatic organisms. The majority of the western Adams County forestlands are located in the South Mountain Important Bird Area, as identified by the Pennsylvania Chapter of the Audubon Society, which provides habitat tor interior forest bird species including Hooded Warbler, E. Pee-Wee, Canada Warbler, Hermit Thrush, Kentucky and Worm-eating Warbler, and Whippoor-wills and habitat at the reservoirs tor waterfowl and wading birds including Wood Duck, Common Loon, Pied-Billed Grebe, Common Merganser, Great Blue Heron and Green Heron. • Known Threatened or Endangered Species--The Pennsylvania Chapter of the Nature Conservancy found many threatened and endangered species in the forestlands of Adams County when completing the Natural Areas Inventory. The names of the species are kept confidential, but include: a !'A-Endangered plant species and !'A-Rare plant species characteristic of barrens habitats found on Big Flat Barrens, several !'A-Endangered and Federally-listed Endangered plant species found in seep-derived wetland and forested swamp communities within Michaux State Forest, a globally rare animal species found in a portion ofConewago Creek, a !'A-Endangered plant species found in Caledonia State Park, a globally rare and P A-Endangered animal species found in several small forested wetlands and small stream tributaries, several !'A-Endangered plant species found on the forested diabase ridgetops in central Adams County, and several PA-Rare plant species and !'A-Endangered plant species found in forested riparian areas along Marsh Creek tributaries. • K11own Cultural Resources -The forestlands of Adams County contain many cultural resources, including the capture site of Mary Jemison, known as the White Squaw, who was captured by invading Shawnee Indians and French soldiers in 1758 and adopted into the Seneca tribe and lived the remainder of her life in their society; the Carbaugh Run Rhyolite Quarry Site, listed in the National Register of Historic Places due to the 40-50 prehistoric quarrying pits used by prehistoric inhabitants and Native Americans as a source of metarhyolite since Paleoindian times for the production of chipped-stone tools; several original pre-Revolutionary War iron fumaces that processed iron ore; and the Tapeworm Railroad, laid out by Congressman and abolitionist Thaddeus Stevens in 1836 to connect the iron furnaces of South Mountain to Baltimore. Also, on their march to battle in Gettysburg from Chambersburg during the Civil War, many soldiers passed through the gaps in the forested hills of western Adams County. • Other Ecological Values-Many vernal pools formed by snow melt and spring rain that provide habitat for mole salamanders, fairy shrimp and wood fi•ogs, species that only breed in such pools, arc found in the forestlands of Adams County. Also, portions of the Big Flat Barrens, a fire-maintained Pitch pine-scrub oak barren habitat that is a unique and diminishing forest type in the East Coast, are located in Adams County. o Provide for continued traditional uses: • Forest Management-The timber resources of Michaux State Forest are managed by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to produce a variety of wood products. The sale of timber products from state forests returns money to the Commonwealth and provides a stable resource base for the forest products induslly. But the majority of Adams County's forestlands arc owned by private landowners, including 20 forest stewards, who manage their properly's forest resources with the help of consulting and service foresters. • Timber Harvesting-The forestlands of Adams County have a net volume of 157.9 millions of cubic feet of growing-stock trees on timberland (142. 7 Oak/HiekOiy, 8.0 Oak/Pine, and 7.2 Elm/Ash/Maple) and a net volume of 477.8 millions of board feet of sawtimber trees on timberland. 34 forestry and wood product establishments that employee I ,953 people are located in Adams County, and the estimated value of the county's standing timber is $95.56 million with an annual county timber harvest value of$3.05 million. 4.

figure.head: Description of each important forest area.

figure.figDesc: Potomac River Basin; this area contains the Strawberry Hill Nature Preserve, a 2500-acre forested parcel owned and managed by Glatfelter Pulp Wood Company, and numerous I 00+ acre privately owned forested parcels. o South Mountain, including MichmLr State Forest, Caledonia State Park, Big Flat Barrens and Carbaugh Run State Forest Natural Area: Part of the Blue Ridge Mountain Range, South Mountain is characterized by pronounced ridges dissected by deep valleys with a relief of generally several hundred feet fom1ed on metavolcanic and quartzite rocks. The area is mainly covered by mixed oak forest, including white, red, scarlet, and black oaks mixed with tulip poplar, red maple, and an understory of ericaceous shrubs (blueberries, mountain laurel and rhododendrons); with drier ridgetops characterized by shallow nutrient poor soils that supp01t chestnut oak, black gum, red maple, other oaks and ericaceous shrubs and some areas of fire-maintained Pitch pine-scrub oak barrens. Michaux State Forest and Caledonia State Park, both owned by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and managed by the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, provide many recreational opportunities including: small game and deer hunting, primitive camping, hiking (including the Appalachian Trail), horseback riding, bicycling, rock-climbing, picnicking, fishing, swimming, canoeing, and snowmobiling. The timber resources of Michaux State Forest are managed to produce a variety of wood products. The sale of timber products from state forests returns money to the Commonwealth and provides a stable resource base for the forest products industry. South Mountain also contains an abundance of water resources, including valuable potable water resources for municipal water supplies in the form of reservoirs and limestone spring fed streams with exceptionally high water quality and vernal pools and seeps. o Piney Mountain: An area of mixed oak forest (including white, red, scarlet, and

figure.head: Describe the estimated timber volume and primary users in the proposed Forest Legacy Area and its dependence upon the forest resources in the area.
figure.figDesc: 9. Adams County has a net volume of 157.9 millions of cubic feet of growing-stock trees on timberland (142.7 Oak/Hickory, 8.0 Oak/Pine, and 7.2 Elm/Ash/Maple) and a net volume of 477.8 millions of board feet of sawtimber trees on timberland. The primary users of Adams County's forestlands are its 34 forestry and wood product establishments that employee 1,953 people, including: 2 consulting forestry companies, 2 veneer log buyers, 3 logging companies, I 0 sawmills, 2 timber companies, 1 forestry and timber equipment supplier and several retail lumber stores; including Glatfelter Pulp Wood Company. Adams County depends upon its forest resources for their economic contribution and employment opportunities. The standing timber in Adams County was estimated by Penn State University to have a value of$95.56 million. The annual value of Adams County's timber harvest is $3.05 million. Adams County's forestry sector has a $17.34 million annual economic contribution, and the wood products and paper sector has a $63.95 million annual contribution.

figure.head: Please outline how the Organization will promote and administer the Legacy Program in their area. This includes: o
figure.figDesc: The organization's priority/or selecting land to recommend to the program: The six scoring criteria (development threats, forest resources, water quality, habitat, scenic/cultural/recreational opportunities and proximity to preserved land) and weights as established by DCNR for ranking state applications, will be used to score the applications received for Forest Legacy Program acquisition in Adams County and make recommendations to the state of priority lands. o How tracts of/and will be identified and recommended to the program: All landowners eligible for the Forest Legacy Program in Adams County (determined by GIS assessment of I 0-acre or larger parcels with 80% woodland coverage) will be notified of the availability of applications for the program by personal letter and/or press releases after initial Forest Legacy Area designation. On an annual basis, the Land Conservancy of Adams County and the Adams County Commissioners will advertise the availability of applications for the program, in order to reach new forestland owners. When the applications are received, they will be scored using the six scming criteria and weights developed by DCNR for ranking state applications, and these scores will be forwarded to DCNR. The applications will be kept on file with the Land Conservancy, and updated and rescored upon changes to the property. The existing applications will be resubmitted annually to the state upon landowner indication of continued interest in the program. o How program promotion and landowner outreach will be conducted: A public meeting was held by the Adams County Commissioners and Land Conservancy of Adams County on Thursday, August 18 to receive public comment on the proposed designation of Adams County as a Forest Legacy Area and to explain how the Forest Legacy Program operates. A letter was sent to all Adams County township supervisors, borough councils, municipal planning commissions, landowners of forestland of 200+ acres eligible for the program, timber and wood product companies, and relevant county government agencies and organizations.

div.head: Forest Health Priority Landscape Analysis
div.p: The Forest Health Analysis aimed to identify forest and young forest areas at risk to invasive species and damaging agents. Layers used in the analysis:
• Mature Forest Areas (Derived from 2016 National Land Cover Database (NLCD) -US Geological Survey)
• Shrub/Scrub Areas (Derived from 2016 NLCD)
• Percent Basal Area Loss (US Forest Service National Insect and Disease Risk Map)
See Appendix B for detailed methodology of analysis.

div.head: Urban and Community Forest Priority Landscape Analysis
div.p: The Urban Forest Analysis aimed to identify areas of dense population with tree cover and impervious surfaces intermixed. Layers used in the analysis:
• Population Density (derived from 2010 Census information)
• Percent Canopy Cover (derived from 2016 NLCD)
• Percent Impervious (derived from 2016 NLCD)
• Environmental Justice Area (2015 census blocks)
See Appendix B for detailed methodology of analysis.

div.head: Wildland Fire Priority Landscape Analysis
div.p: The Wildland Fire Analysis aimed to identify areas at risk of wildfires depending on multiple factors and the history of wildfire occurrence over the past 10 years. Layers used in the analysis:
• LANDFIRE data (from US Forest Service and US Dept. of Interior)
• 2010 Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) data (from US Forest Service)
• Wildfire points from 2009-2019 (internal bureau data)
• Slope of land (derived from digital elevation model)
• Aspect of land (derived from digital elevation model)
See Appendix B for detailed methodology of analysis.

div.head: Ecological Priority Landscape Analysis
div.p: The Ecological Analysis aimed to identify areas of high value for forest connectivity and species habitat. Layers used in the analysis:
• Important Bird Areas (from Audubon Pennsylvania data)
• Forest Patch Analysis output (derived from 2016 NLCD)
• CNHI (County Natural Heritage Inventory) Areas (from Western PA Conservancy data)
• ER (Environmental Review) Data (from internal bureau data)
See Appendix B for detailed methodology of analysis.

div.head: Water Priority Landscape Analysis
div.p: The Water Analysis aimed to identify areas that contain public water sources, restricted streams, and high value riparian buffers. Priority for afforestation for water quality would be roughly the inverse of this map. In other words, this map illustrates resources that should be prioritized for conservation.
Conversely, prioritization can also focus on areas that are the most in need of intervention or assistance, which would be areas lacking streamside buffers, for example. Layers used in the analysis:

• Watersheds containing restricted streams (derived from bureau stream data and PA Dept. of Environmental Protection stream classifications) • Forested watersheds containing public water resources (water source data from PA Dept. of Environmental Protection, and from 2016 NLCD) • Stream buffers (derived from bureau stream data) • Agricultural land in stream buffers (extracted from 2016 NLCD) See Appendix B for detailed methodology of analysis.

div.head: Major Watersheds and River Basins
div.p: Watersheds are an important planning unit as water quality is highly dependent on land use and particularly the amount of forest cover within the watershed. Many government and non-profitbased efforts are tied to watershed boundaries. Watersheds also help to provide a sense-of-place and sense of responsibility for down-stream impacts.
Pennsylvania contains five major watersheds as shown in the map below:
• Susquehanna (Chesapeake Bay)
• Potomac (Chesapeake Bay) • Delaware River • Ohio River • Genesee • Lake Erie

div.head: Priority Areas Summary
div.p: Pennsylvania's landscapes are highly diverse and variable. While statewide policies and program objectives are critical for working toward a shared vision, acknowledging regional differences, and targeting specific landscapes allows managers to customize program delivery. Many regional and landscape-based programs have been functioning in Pennsylvania for years and have proven effective. The bureau intends to continue to support these efforts while looking for new opportunities, such as those identified in the GIS Priority Area Analysis.

div.head: Overview
div.p: This appendix describes the methodology used for Pennsylvania's Priority Landscapes GIS Analysis. This methodology defines seven spotlighted perspectives that depict priority landscape areas: (1) Forest Pests, (2) Wildfires, (3) Ecological, (4) Water, ( 5), Urban and Community, (6), Working Forests and ( 7), Climate Change. For each, a priority landscape map was produced that classifies all 28 million acres of the state into high, medium, and low priority categories based on the maps theme.
This document describes the methodology used for each of the seven spotlighted perspectives. A description of the map's results, data used, model components, and weights are included.

ArcGIS Pro 2.3.1 with the Spatial Analyst Extension was used to perform all analyses. ArcMap 10.6 was used to create all PDF map outputs for use in the Forest Action Plan. A description of all datasets used in the analyses can be found in Appendix C. The raster grids computed (priority landscape outputs) have a resolution of 30 meters and cell values computed between zero and 1. Cell values near zero are low priority, and cell values near one are high priority. The climate change priority landscape analysis is the only output that does not follow this format.
mid-late succession forest (not both). As such, these components are independent, and a given area cannot receive the weight of both components.

The output for the forest pest priority landscapes model is shown below. Most high priority areas are found in relatively small patches within the Ridge and Valley region, Pocono mountains, and the north central part of the state. Medium priority areas represent other forest areas that have lower tree mortality risk due to insect and disease agents. The southeastern region contains the largest amount of low priority due to increased amounts of agriculture and other non-forest land uses in the region.
Forest pest priority landscape output results

div.head: Wildfire Priority Landscapes
div.p: The wildfire priority landscape analysis identifies area where wildland fires are predicted to occur and become problematic, especially areas prone to extreme fire behavior, have potential to cause extensive property damage, or could threaten the safety of the Commonwealth's citizens.

Five dataset we used as inputs: (1) The WUI classifies areas where homes and other human development meet or intermingle with undeveloped land. LANDFIRE characterizes the land's vegetation into fuel models that predict different fire behavior intensities. The PA wildfire point origins are records of wildfire origins that have been reported, as well as their total acres burned. Percent slope aids in determining fire behavior from the terrain. Aspect, or the direction a slope faces, helps determine how much radiated heat it will receive from the sun. Slopes facing south to southwest will receive the most solar radiation. As a result, this slope is warmer than slopes facing a northerly direction. The warmer slope results in lower relative humidity, higher temperatures and rapid loss of moisture. The fuel will tend to be dryer, flashy-type that ignites and burns readily. The period that fires will ignite and burn will also be longer on southfacing slopes.

Five components were created as input for the wildfire priority landscapes model. These components were derived from the datasets listed above. Developed areas with intermixed vegetation received increase weights. Shrub-type vegetation (fuel models 4 -7) received greatest weights; the timber (fuel models 8 -10) received moderate weights; and grasses (fuel models 1 -3) received lowest rates in the model. A spatial clustering of wildfire "hotspots" was computed using the fire point origins to identify where large fires have been occurring and where numerous occurrences of smaller fires have been reported. Steeper slopes were given higher weights than flat areas because of risk of extreme fire behavior increases in steep terrain. Southern facing slope aspects (SW, SE) were given higher weights, while northern facing aspects (NW, NE) were given lower weights.
Appendix B: Priority Landscapes GIS Methodology

The output for the wildfire priority landscapes model is shown below. Most high priority areas are found in the Poconos, lower Ridge and Valley region, and in the center of the state. These regions have favorable fuels, steeper slopes, intermixed areas of vegetation and development, and "hotspots" of past wildfire occurrences. Most medium priority areas exhibit favorable fuels, but do not have a history of wildfire occurrences or do not have intermixed areas of vegetation and development. The southeastern region contains the largest amount of low priority area due to unfavorable fuels and a lack of wildfire occurrences -a significant amount of agriculture and other non-forest land uses are found within this region.
Wildfire Priority Landscape Output Results

div.head: Ecological Priority Landscapes
div.p: The ecological priority landscapes analysis identifies areas that contain critical biodiversity areas, specially designated habitats for birds, large/contiguous forest patches, and habitats for species of special concern.
Five datasets were used as inputs:

(1) Pennsylvania County Natural Heritage Inventories (CNHI) (2) Pennsylvania Environmental Review (ER) Layer (3) Important Bird Areas (IBAs) (4) Major Pennsylvania Roads (5) 2016 National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD)

The CNHIs are areas with special biodiversity importance. The ER layer contains known locations of species of special concern. IBAs are specially designated areas for birds. Major roads include interstates and other major roadways that fragment forested areas (rural and woods roads are not included). The NLCD classifies land into 16 different land cover categories such as agriculture, forests, developed areas, wetlands, and barren lands.

Four components were created as inputs for the ecological priority landscape model. These components were derived from the datasets listed above. Areas designated as IBAs or designated biodiversity areas (CNHI) were given higher weights than those areas that not designated. Large forest patches (greater than 100 acres) unfragmented by major roads were given higher weights than fragmented forest patches. Higher weights were also given to areas that have known populations of species of special concern.

The output for the ecological priority landscape model is shown below. Most high priority areas occur in South Mountain, the Laurel Highlands, the mountains of the Ridge and Valley region, the Kittatinny Ridge, and the north central part of the state. The largest forest patches in the state are found in the north central and contribute to the high priority classification of this area. Other high priority areas are those specially designated for some type of important area. Many specially designated areas also contain known populations of species of special concern. Medium priority areas may be forest patches that meet the 100-acre large forest patch size requirement, but may not be a specially designated area or do not contain species of special concern. Low priority areas in the result are small forest patches not specially designated as important and do not contain species of special concern. The southeast region contains the largest portion of low priority.
Ecological Priority Landscape Output Results

div.head: Water Priority Landscapes
div.p: The water priority landscape analysis identifies important areas for maintaining or improving water quality.
Five datasets were used as inputs:

(1) Pennsylvania Streams (2) Small Watersheds (3) 2018 Public Ground Water Supply Points (4) 2018 Public Surface Water Supply Points (5) 2016 National Land Cover Data (NLCD) Some stream watercourses have special designations (exceptional value, high quality, wilderness trout, etc.) that are given higher weight in the analysis. The geographic land areas that drain into different watercourses are defined by the small watersheds dataset. Public drinking water supply sources (surface and ground) are integrated in the water model as there are especially critical places to maintain clean water. The NLCD classifies land into 16 different land cover categories such as agriculture, forests, developed areas, wetlands, and barren lands.

Four components were created as input for the water priority landscapes model. These components were derived from the datasets listed above. Agricultural land along streams with no buffer or filter strip has the potential to contaminate water through fertilizing, tilling, spraying pesticides, and other farming practices. As such, agricultural lands within 300 feet of a watercourse were included as places to promote reforestation and were given higher weight in the model. Forestland in watersheds containing public water supply sources were given higher weight in the model as these areas are important to keep forested. Higher weight was also given to watersheds containing a stream with a special designation. All riparian corridors (300 feet around streams) were given higher weight than other areas in the model.

div.head: Appendix B: Priority Landscapes GIS Methodology
div.p: The output for the water priority landscape model is shown below. Most high and medium priority areas are found along waterways in the Poconos region, Laurel Highlands, and the central part of the state. This is where many of the streams with special designations are found to overlap forests that protect public water supplies. Many of the medium priority areas are also found in smaller patches along riparian stream corridors across the state. Low priority areas are lands outside of riparian corridors and not in critical watersheds.

div.head: Urban & Community Priority Landscapes
div.p: The urban priority landscapes analysis identifies important urban areas to advocate the role of trees as a critical part of the urban infrastructure.
Four datasets were used as input:

(1) Environmental Justice Areas (2) Percent Urban Tree Canopy (3) Percent Impervious Surface (4) 2015 Census Information Environmental Justice areas are census blocks where 20% or more of individuals live below the poverty line, and/or more than 30% of the population is a minority. Urban areas that need the role of trees advocated as a critical part of the infrastructure are those with a lower percentage of tree canopy coverage, high population densities, and higher percentage of impervious surfaces.

Four components were created as input for the urban and community landscapes model. These components were derived from the datasets listed above. Environmental Justice areas were created with the consideration of vulnerable communities. These communities are granted enhanced public participation in permitting processes in relation to certain major permit applications, in addition to the normal course of public involvement. The percent of each area that lived below the poverty line was considered, with higher percentages given higher weights in the model. Due to the importance of tree canopy in urban infrastructure, areas with a lower percentage of tree canopy cover were given higher weights in the model. With impervious surface areas creating more runoff and reducing the amount of water flowing back into the ground, areas with a higher percentage of impervious surface areas were given higher weights in the model. Population density was derived from census information, with higher density populations receiving higher weights in the model.

div.head: Appendix B: Priority Landscapes GIS Methodology
div.p: The output for the urban and community landscapes model is shown below. Philadelphia, Pittsburg, Harrisburg, Allentown, Erie, and Reading are a few of the larger urban areas that stand out as high priority. Medium priority areas are urban areas having higher tree coverage percentages, lower population densities, lower percentages of impervious surfaces, or coincide with the environmental justice areas. Most of the state is classified as low priority because it is not in an urban environment.

div.head: Working Forest Priority Landscapes
div.p: The working forest priority landscapes analysis identifies areas to maintain in "working" forest conditions for the purpose of providing community and economic values. Such values include supply of wood products, carbon sequestration, recreation, an aesthetic landscape, and many other services that forests can provide.
Eight datasets were used as inputs:
(1) Percent Slope (2)

div.head: Climate Change
div.p: The Climate Change landscape analysis identifies climate corridors that are important links to facilitate species movements, as well as resilient areas that have populations of biodiversity that are more likely to maintain function as the climate changes

This data was created by The Nature Conservancy and provided to DCNR. There were no input layers or analysis. The original dataset was split out into 3 categories: The original dataset did not cover the whole state. Anywhere outside of those 3 categories was blank.

Since each priority landscape analysis involves including the whole state, some grouping and resymbolizing was done to achieve that. Both categories 1 and 2, since they are prioritized networks, were grouped in high priority areas. The non-prioritized resilient areas, since they are still resilient areas, were grouped into medium priority areas. The rest of the state, which had no data associated with it, was reclassified as low priority areas.

The output results of the Climate Change priority landscapes is shown below. High priority areas are concentrated in the north central region of the state, as well as mountain ridge and valley corridors, especially the Kittatinny Ridge corridor and the Allegheny Front.

div.head: Section I INTRODUCTION
div.p: The FLP was enacted in recognition of the fact that the majority of the nation's productive forestlands are in private ownership. These landowners are facing increasing pressure to convert their forestlands to other uses. Growing population density and user demands are placing increasing pressures on private lands to provide a wide variety of products and services, including fish and wildlife habitat, aesthetic qualities, timber and recreational opportunities. Inherent in the establishment of the FLP was the understanding that good stewardship of privately held forestlands requires a long-term commitment that can be fostered through a partnership with federal, state and local governments.

div.head: Section II PENNSYLVANIA'S FOREST LEGACY PROGRAM PURPOSE
div.p: The overall purpose of the FLP in Pennsylvania is to help protect and sustain working forests while maintaining private ownership of the land. The FLP will work to develop and sustain partnerships with landowners, communities, non-profits and other organizations to conserve forestland.

div.head: PENNSYLVANIA'S FOREST LEGACY GOALS
div.p: Seven goals were established as part of the Forest Legacy Program. These goals were established as a result of extensive discussion by the SFSC; they take the wide variety of interests involved into consideration. The goals will be achieved through voluntary easements protecting forestland from development and through planning and promoting forest stewardship. The seven goals are stated below:
1. To maintain traditional forest uses, emphasizing commercial timber harvesting following Best Management Practice (BMPs) and secondary recreational activities.
2. To maintain productivity of forests for future generations.

3. To reduce the trend towards forest parcelization. 4. To conserve significant tracts of contiguous forest. 5. To conserve water resources and riparian zones. 6. To conserve important habitats for plants, fish, and wildlife. 7. To restore degraded forested ecosystems.

div.head: Section III FOREST LEGACY SPONSORSHIP SPONSOR REQUIREMENTS
div.p: All organizations must meet specific requirements prior to receiving approval by the Bureau to be official FLA sponsors. Entities seeking to become sponsors are required to meet one of the following designations: County Commissioners or their assigns, prequalified land trust, or appropriate/authorized organization. Appropriate/authorized organizations are entities involved in research, restoration, rehabilitation, planning, acquisition, development, education or other activities that further protection, enhancement, conservation or enjoyment of this Commonwealth's forest resources.

Upon sponsorship approval by the Bureau, organizations must be willing to enter an agreement with the Bureau to carry out the following responsibilities:  Provide information and assistance outreach to landowners and other interested parties.  Help potential FLP landowners through the easement application process.  Package matching funds to make up the 25 percent non-Federal share required for easement purchases.  Conduct public participation and prepare necessary information required for approval of FLA designation.

div.head: REQUEST FOR SPONSORSHIP APPROVAL
div.p: Interested sponsors must fill out the Forest Legacy Area Sponsor Application (Form I, Appendix III). This form will provide the Bureau with information about the organization including a list of board members and their affiliations, staff list, charter, organizational chart, organization mission statement, geographic service area, IRS 501 (c) 3 status letter, contact information, and proof of involvement with conservation easements or similar procedures for at least three years. This form will be used to determine whether organizations are eligible to serve as sponsors and are able to adequately carry out the responsibilities necessary to implement the program.

div.head: NOTIFICATION AND APPROVAL REQUIREMENTS
div.p: Organizations seeking status as a sponsor must send a letter of intent to counties within the potential FLA. The prospective sponsor must then send the completed Form I to the Bureau with the appropriate attachments, including a copy of the letter of intent. The Bureau will review the submission. When a sponsor is deemed eligible (fitting all the necessary requirements), the Bureau will send a letter to each county within the proposed FLA indicating that the prospective sponsor has met the eligibility requirements for sponsorship. Each county will have 60 days in which to respond to

div.head: Section V MULTI-RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PLANS
div.p: After approval of the FLA, sponsors can begin working with interested landowners. Each landowner must have an approved Multi-Resource Management Plan developed by an approved plan writer before the easement can be filed at the Recorder of Deeds Office.

Good stewardship is the key to the success of the FLP goals. When a landowner decides to sell the development rights to a tract of forestland, good forest stewardship becomes paramount. Applying BMPs to the management scheme of the property can help landowners realize a good return on their investment, which, in turn, benefits the community while improving the health and productivity of the forest.

All Forest Legacy properties require a Multi-Resource Management Plan prior to acquisition of the easement. Multi-resource management plans shall be prepared by a natural resource professional in accordance with landowner objectives. These plans describe actions to protect and manage soil, water, range, aesthetic quality, recreation, timber, fish, wildlife resources and other conservation values identified on the tract (See Appendix VIII and IX for assistance in developing a plan). Approvals of new plans must occur prior to the closing of a FLP acquisition.

Multi-resource management plans, including revisions, must be approved by the landowner acknowledging that the plan meets their objectives. Evidence of their approval can be a signature on the signature page in a plan. A multi-resource management plan shall be reviewed by the landowner and the easement holder at a minimum of every 10 years, and updated as needed. If there is a change in land ownership, then the multi-resource management plan shall be reviewed and updated. It will also be updated if the landowner objectives change. The easement holder shall document in writing that a multi-resource management plan has been reviewed and approved.
FLA Sponsor employees are prohibited from preparing Multi-Resource Management Plans for proposed Forest Legacy properties within the boundaries of their FLA.
The Bureau, as the lead agency for the Pennsylvania FLP, requires that landowners select an approved plan writer to develop their multi-resource management plan.

The Service Forester will supply the landowner with a list of approved plan writers. A listing of the Bureau's District Office contacts are located in Appendix I. A flowchart diagramming the Landowner Process from announcement to the implementation of the easement can be found in Appendix VII.

Reviews shall occur on multi-resource management plans that have been accepted into the State Forest Stewardship Program prior to the involvement of the FLP. Written evidence of this review and approval on existing plans must accompany the multi-resource management plan and be provided to the Forest Service. This would include updates to a signature page or a letter of approval that the existing planned activities do not conflict with the FLP purposes.

div.head: Section VIII FUNDING
div.p: After the Multi-Resource Management Plan and conservation easement are submitted and approved, funding will be available through the USDA Forest Service. The maximum Federal contribution for the total program costs may not exceed 75 percent.

The remaining 25 percent of these costs may be matching funds or In-Kind Services from non-Federal sources, including states and non-profit organizations. Non-Federal contributions may include direct and indirect costs associated with any of the planning, acquisition, capital improvement, management or administrative activities and the value of fee-simple acquisition of lands by the Commonwealth, county, township or land trusts, as long as these lands conform to the objectives and priorities of the State Forest Legacy Program.

div.head: COST-SHARE
div.p: Eligible non-cash cost-shares include those services directly tied to the program's development and implementation that can be properly documented, and would otherwise have to be contracted for cash payment. For proposals using non-cash services for some or the entire required local cost-share, contact your Program Coordinator to discuss requirements prior to submission of the application. If this tract is selected for funding, DCNR reserves the right to negotiate the values submitted for the non-cash cost-share and will not provide official approval to proceed with the procurement process until the Bureau approves the grantee's noncash services plan. The types of non-cash services that can be used in an FLA as local cost-share are limited to the following:

 In-Kind Services Services and labor provided by the paid staff of the sponsoring organization to perform all or part of the Bureau-approved FLA scope of work. The allowable value of In-Kind Services to be paid by the grant or provided as a non-cash cost-share for the grant may include direct and indirect personal fringe benefit costs such as employee insurance, retirement benefit costs, vacation time, holiday time and sick leave time.

General organizational operating costs such as utilities, general operating supplies and services, amortized costs or rental costs for buildings and equipment used for the general operation of the organization, and general property and liability insurance costs may be included in the hourly rate.

The allowable value for In-Kind Services may not include expenses for food, drinks, gifts, other hospitality items, lobbying of governmental officials related to the general promotion of the organization, or the promotion of any FLAs in which the organization is involved.

In-Kind Service value shall be calculated using an hourly rate for the personnel position performing the work multiplied by the number of hours of Bureau- Conservation Easement An interest in land (such as development rights or recreation rights) that a willing property owner grants voluntarily to ensure the conservation of specific natural resources located on his/her land. The landowner retains the title and all remaining land rights not specifically conveyed or prohibited in the easement.
Cost ShareThe non-Federal portion of the easement or fee simple costs. Can be made up of cash contribution, lands or interests in lands, or In-Kind Services.

Exceptional Value StreamA stream requiring the highest level of protection; a stream in which the water quality is to be maintained. Surface water that meets one or more of the following conditions can be designated as an exceptional value stream: the water is located in a National wildlife refuge or a State Game propagation and protection area; the water is designated as a "wilderness trout stream" by the Fish and Boat Commission; the water is located in a designated State Park Natural Area or State Forest Natural Area, National Natural Landmark, Federal or State wild river, Federal Wilderness Area or National Recreational Area.

The water can also be considered an exceptional value stream if it is an outstanding National, State, or regional or local water resource; is surface water of exceptional recreational significance; or is surface water of exceptional ecological significance.

Federal Appraisal StandardsStandards contained in the publication entitled "Uniform Appraisal Standards for Federal Land Acquisitions: Interagency Land Acquisition Conference, 2000." These standards are available for purchase from the Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington D.C. 20402-9328 (ISBN 0-922154-66-X) or available online at http://www.justice.gov/enrd/land-ack/Uniform-Appraisal-Standards.pdf.
Federal Acquisition ProceduresSteps to be followed when Federal funds are used in any part of the acquisition of lands or interests in lands.
Fee-simple purchaseA land conveyance where a vendor conveys all rights, title and interest in a property to a purchaser.

Forest Legacy Area (FLA)Forested area with important environmental values, that satisfies identified eligibility criteria and has been delineated, described, and mapped in a State's Assessment of Need for the FLP.
