APPENDIX VI Pennsylvania's Forest Legacy Program Summary Sheet
div.p: The A timber harvest occurred in this stand in the late 1940s by the previous owners. The present owners have harvested some firewood from the stand since 1985, removing mostly dead oaks.

div.head: Management Unit Description:
div.p: This is a well-stocked forested stand (basal area 95 square feet) containing mostly small sawtimber 10" to 14" dbh. It occupies the crest of a small flat-topped hill; much of the unit is level to very gently sloping. This management unit provides the best opportunity for producing high value hardwoods. The soil is Berks Shaley Loam considered very good for growing trees.

A good mix of species is present. Sixty-five percent (65 percent) of the growing space is occupied by the combination of red oak, black oak, and red maple. Also present (in decreasing order of growing space they occupy) are tulip poplar, white oak, white ash, hickory, black gum, white pine, and black walnut.

Tree regeneration is spotty, very sparse in some areas, more dense where openings in the canopy exist. Shrub growth of any kind is sparse, but species noted were mountain laurel, flowering dogwood, tartarian honeysuckle, maple leaf viburnum, black haw viburnum, and witch hazel. Grape vines are a problem in some parts of the stand, where they are well established in the canopy layer.

Cavity trees are few and far between; cavities of 5" or larger are nonexistent. There is an abundance of hard mast from oaks, hickory, pine, and black walnut, but the only soft mast available is from black gum and the sparse shrub growth present. The few white pines and mountain laurel provide very sparse evergreen cover, but this is not of concern since cover is abundant in Units 1 and 2. Pileated woodpeckers, screech owls, and barred owls have occasionally been heard and a flock of turkeys has occasionally been seen in this stand.

The gypsy moth has not been a severe problem on this site, but there are occasional pockets of gypsy moth killed oaks. Access to the stand currently exists only from the north off of Route 10 via the farm road through the field.

div.head: Management Objective for the Unit:
div.p: Manage this stand for maximum production of high quality timber with consideration given to wildlife needs.

div.head: Recommendations:
div.p: The stand should be thinned in the near future to sustain the growth of the better trees. However, before permitting additional light to reach the forest floor you'll need to control the grapevines throughout most of the stand. (See the county Service Forester to apply for cost-share assistance for this work). If permitted to grow up into the crown canopy grapevines can deform and even kill the trees supporting them. Cut the vines once at ground level and a second time at head height. Where grapevine tangles are already too dense, you may wish to simply manage it as a grape arbor supplying food for wildlife.

div.head: Management Unit 4
div.p: Pond & Surrounding Field: 10 Acres Management History: Livestock had free access to the pond and surrounding woods in this area for many years. In the early 1970s the present owner installed fencing and gates to limit access, and a watering ramp from the north pasture. In recent years the owner reduced his dairy herd and now rarely pastures them in this unit.

div.head: Management Unit Description:
div.p: Management Unit 4 contains a deep, 4-acre spring fed pond, surrounded by open grassland on the east side and scattered open grown trees on the south and west sides. It borders an open pasture to the north, separated from this unit by a wooden fence. A second pasture south of the unit is similarly fenced off. Livestock is permitted limited access to the pond from the north field by way of a well-constructed ramp.

div.head: Management Objective for the Unit:
div.p: Eliminate livestock entirely from this unit and improve the area for waterfowl.

div.head: Recommendations:
div.p: Reconfigure the existing fence separating this unit from the field south of it, and construct a new fence segment to create a corridor providing livestock access to the pond. Install a second livestock ramp at that site according to instructions provided in DEP General Permit 6. The species of concern, horned pondweed, might be encouraged to grow more abundantly in the pond if pollution now entering it is entirely eliminated.

Given the fertilizer provided over the years by livestock, herbaceous vegetation will quickly grow back on its own to provide cover along the banks of the pond. Wetland shrubs such as red stem dogwood, buttonbush, spicebush, and basket willow; or trees such as black willow, pin oak, sycamore, green ash, hornbeam, and red maple could be interplanted among the existing trees to enhance what may come up naturally.

In the open area east of the pond, consider planting small grains including millet, sorghum, wild rice, and sunflowers to supplement food available for waterfowl. In grassy areas limit mowing to only once or twice a year as necessary to control weeds. Avoid mowing altogether between April 1 and July 30 to improve the nesting success of ground nesters such as mallards, black ducks, green winged teal, blue winged teal, American bittern, and least bittern. Install two or three large nest boxes for wood duck. Survival of the neotropical migrant the Scarlet tanager is of special concern in Pennsylvania as I 3-17% of its global nesting population occurs within the state, including nesting sites in Adams County. The lowest concentrations of birds arc found in areas with the least tree cover. The species requires woodlots of at least 25-37 acres, and the more fragmentation the greater the negative effect on breeding.

The Cerulean warbler, another neotropical migrant, also nests in Adams County. This species of concern is primarily found in forested areas and requires tracts between 50-75 acres, with some reports as high as 4000 acres; the greater the fragmentation the greater amount of space is needed.

The Wood thrush also nests in Adams County and 8.5% of the world's breeding population breeds in Pennsylvania. Although the Wood thrush is still common its population has been declining since 1966 due to degradation of forest breeding habitat.

Broad-winged hawks nest in the larger deciduous or mixed deciduous-conifer forests throughout PA including Adams County. They are rare in high! y fragmented forests of southeast P A and prefer forests of over 40 acres and larger patches may be needed where continuous forest is not adjacent. The Sharp-shinned hawk is another raptor which nests in woodlands of Adams County. They prefer large undisturbed forests over fragmented or developed woodlots. FAX NO. 717+642+6512

We are almost entirely dependent on groundwater, to the el!tent that more than 80% of our water needs are satisfied by private or public wells. Forests are significant recharge areas that allow precipitation to infiltrate the aquifers. Even more than fanmland or open space, forestt:d areas retain most of the moisture that falls there due to less nmoff.

div.head: Franklin & Cumberland County Forest Legacy Area Addition
Addition of Franklin and Cumberland Counties to the Central Pennsylvania Forest Legacy Area
div.p: Summary of how this FLA meets the eligibility criteria 1. Threatened by Parcelization/Fragmentation a. Factors that contribute to loss of traditional use ("…such as timber harvesting, recreation, and supplying of clean water…") -From April 1, 2000 to July 1, 2007, Franklin County's population has grown 9.6% and Cumberland County has grown 6.7%. These are both well above the growth rate of the state, which is 1.2%. -Projected growth from 2000-2030 in Cumberland County is expected to be 32.4%. Franklin County is expected to grow 22.2% during that same time frame. The statewide population growth for that period of time is project to be 7.4% -In Franklin County, housing unit growth is increasing at a greater pace than its population growth. In the 1980s, housing units increased by 225, while population increased by only 7%. Through the 1990s, housing unit growth (11%) continued to exceed population growth (7%). -Because it is cheaper to live in Pennsylvania than in Maryland, Franklin

County is experiencing much growth due to the adjacent border. b. Loss of Environmental Integrity ("…roads, utility lines and housing developments divide forested areas…") -This area is being fragmented and converted to non-forest uses, primarily due to the infiltration of housing developments. This development brings infrastructure with it, including roads and utility lines that divide forested areas and lead to a loss of environmental integrity. c. Conversion to Non-Forest Use -All of the factors above contribute to the conversion of forests to nonforest use. Forests and agricultural areas, which abound in both Franklin and Cumberland counties, continue to be converted to subdivisions for growing populations. 2. Environmental Importance a. Scenic Resources ("…include riverfronts, lakes, streams, and ponds…lands bordering scenic roads and trails, and lands visible from public places.") -These counties contain scenic trails open for public recreation and provide a viewshed and support portions of the Appalachian Trail. -Route 30 is included in the scenic Lincoln Highway Heritage Corridor, designated as a Heritage park by the Governor in 1995. -The South Mountain is one of a handful of globally exceptional temperate broadleaf forests left in the world. b. Riparian Areas ("…areas that provide groundwater recharge and water quality protection benefiting human water supplies and aquatic organism populations…") -Almost all of Franklin and Cumberland Counties' woodland areas serve as the main source recharge of clean water to the groundwater supply and base flow of the many steams in the counties.

-The South Mountain area alone is the source of water for six public water supplies. -The drainages of these counties flow into the Susquehanna and Potomac Rivers. c. Fish or Wildlife Habitat ("…habitat for fisheries and aquatic organisms… connectivity between distinct forest areas.") -These counties contain forested private property that abuts contiguous areas of State-owned forested land, contributing to connectivity between forested areas. -There are many vernal pools in these counties.

-The headwater streams provide the perfect habitat for brook trout and associated aquatic organisms. -Both the South Mountain and the Kitatinny Ridge are designated as Important Bird Areas by the National Audubon Society. d. Known Threatened or Endangered Species ("… Federal or State-listed Threatened or Endangered species identified as occupying the forested area.") -Several Pennsylvania rare and endangered plant and animal species are located in these counties, including species such as bog turtle, and Allegheny woodrat. Full information on specific species are kept confidential.

div.head: Opportunities for Traditional Forest Uses
div.p: -Traditional forest uses continue in these counties. These uses include such activities as timber harvesting/forest products, recreation, hunting, and fishing. -Recreation is very important in these counties. There are literally hundreds of miles of trails on both public and private land. Hiking, hunting, and bird watching are a few of the many pursuits enjoyed by thousands of visitors and residents. a. Forest Management ("…includes management for aesthetics, fish, recreation, urban values, water, wilderness, wildlife, wood products, and other forest resources.") -Forest Management continues in these counties. There are 34 landowners in Cumberland County and 41 in Franklin County with current Stewardship plans. b. Timber Harvesting ("The felling, skidding, on-site processing, and loading of trees or logs onto trucks.") -90 forestry and wood products establishments exist within the proposed Legacy area. -Forestry and forestry related industries employ 1,802 people -Forestry, wood and paper products contribute $77.9 million annually to the local economy.

div.head: Summary of public involvement
div.p: -Franklin and Adams counties submitted proper notification of their public meeting and submitted press releases to local newspapers. -Notices were submitted to all townships and forest products industries within these counties. The Kittatinny Ridge stretches southwesterly from southern New York and northwestern New Jersey, continuing through southeastern Pennsylvania and terminating near the Maryland border.

The ridge is world renowned as a transportation corridor for migrating raptors and songbirds as well as for the movement of other biota in the northeastern United States. The ridge functions as an interstate greenway, linking many of southeastern Pennsylvania's most biologically important areas with each other. Without this resulting connectivity, these biologically rich areas would become functional islands in a sea of farmland, suburban development and other lands modified by human activity, effectively severing modes of reproductive mingling and dispersal for many species of plants and animals.

The southwestern portion of Cumberland County includes the northern end of the South Mountain, which is the northern terminus of the Blue Ridge Mountains of Maryland and Virginia. Several globally rare plant and animal species as well as rare natural communities and an abundance of high quality vernal pools are found here. Many of the highest priority natural areas identified in Cumberland and Franklin County fall within the South Mountain region. The mountain also supports several outstanding geologic features, such as Chimney Rocks, Hammond Rocks, Lewis Rocks, and White Rocks. Like the Kittatinny, this parallel ridge functions as an interstate greenway, linking Pennsylvania with southern natural areas. Although most of the mountain lies within public lands, the development pressures on the valleys surrounding South Mountain threaten to further isolate, fragment, and encroach on the natural resources found here.

The majority of Franklin County's total land area is undeveloped, with 93 percent devoted to agricultural uses and forested land. A significant amount of the development within the County occurs along the major transportation routes of Interstate 81, U.S. Routes 11 and 30, and PA Route 16. Franklin County has maintained a consistent moderate rate of growth in population and economic activity. The convergence of these major highways and access to rail lines has allowed the county to become a major center of new development activity. Cumberland County's population growth is expected to see a 32.4% increase through 2030 while the state is expected to grow at 7.4%. Franklin County's population growth is projected to be 22.2%.
Franklin County's housing unit growth is increasing at a greater pace than its population growth.
In the 1980s, housing units increased by 22 percent while population increased by only 7 percent.

The pace slowed slightly in the 1990s, still housing unit growth (11 percent) exceeded population growth (7 percent). Additionally, between 1990 and 2000 the average household size in the County decreased by 4 percent, consequently resized households occupied additional housing units.

Franklin County's rate of population change in the 1990s was twice that of Pennsylvania. Franklin County is also experiencing a substantial net migration into the County from Maryland, due to affordable housing and lower taxes. Franklin County sits on the Mason-Dixon Line. While it is known that the amount of land consumed by development has been increasing at a much faster rate than the growth in population, there is no reliable county data on precisely how much farmland and forestland is developed each year.

Roughly, only half of Franklin County's municipalities have zoning regulations. The zoning regulations that are in place, quite often are very basic or extremely permissive. These regulations are ineffective at preserving forest and farmland or directing the location of different types of development.

Of Cumberland County's 33 municipalities, 88 percent (29 communities) have a zoning ordinance in place. There is great diversity in the form and function of zoning ordinances across Cumberland County. The more developed communities in the eastern and central part of the County have more stringent, complex ordinances, while the rural communities in the western part of the County have more basic ordinances governing land use.

3b. Environmentally Important, exhibiting the following values; Scenic: Much of Franklin's and Cumberland's rural woodlands would qualify as a scenic resource. The Cumberland Valley holds court to the majesty of the South Mt. and the Kittatinny Ridge (also known as North Mt.). Rt. 30 is included in the scenic Lincoln Highway Heritage Corridor, designated as a Heritage Park by the Governor in 1995. Also scenic views of Cumberland and Franklin Counties forestland are abundant from the Appalachian Trail. The South Mountain is one of a handful of globally exceptional temperate broadleaf forests left in the world, on par with the forests of Mongolia and Patagonia. It serves as the main and largest forested watershed for Cumberland and Franklin Counties and is critical for municipal, commercial and residential water supplies.

Public Recreation: There are literally hundreds of miles of trails on both public and private land in both counties . . Hiking, hunting, bird watching are a few of the many pursuits enjoyed by thousands of visitors and residents. World renowned coldwater limestone spring fed streams beckon anglers from all over the globe. Franklin County has 39,780 acres of state forest lands with approximately 15,178 acres as state game lands. Cumberland County has over 53,000 acres of state, county and municipal public lands.

Riparian: Almost all of Franklin and Cumberland County's woodland acres serve as the main source recharge of clean water to the groundwater supply and base flow of the many streams in the counties. South Mountain is the source of water for six public water supplies Two of these use surface water reservoirs from streams originating on the South Mountain, while four others depend on ground water from wells located in the valley

The drainage of Franklin County consists of two systems, the Susquehanna and the Potomac Rivers. Cumberland County drains into the Susquehanna. Mountain-fed streams drain into these two major rivers, and provide sparkling cold water for people and animals, and provide quality habitat for a good variety of fishes.

Fish & Wildlife: Cumberland and Franklin counties forested ridge tops, open meadows, thick marshes and seepage swamps as well as the spring-fed limestone streams make South Mountain a popular destination for hunters, anglers and wildlife enthusiasts. The headwater streams provide the perfect habitat for brook trout and associated aquatic organisms. Smallmouth bass and associated aquatic life enjoy the clean downstream water. Game animals pursued by thousands are supported by forests-turkey, deer, beer, squirrel and grouse. Forests of Virginia pine and oak provide food and shelter for interior forest birds, including nearly ten percent of the Earth's population of wood thrush and worm-eating warbler and almost a quarter of the world's scarlet tanagers. The South Mountain and Kittatinny Ridge are designated Important Bird Areas by Audubon.

Additionally, both counties boast vernal pools. These pools, due to being ephemeral and virtually free of breeding fish, attract many species of breeding salamanders, turtles, frogs and toads. Some species, like the Spotted Salamander (Ambystoma maculatum), are obligate vernal pool species. This species and other Ambystoma species lay eggs only in vernal pools.

div.head: Air Quality
div.p: With 15,000 to 20,000 trucks traveling on 1-81 in Franklin and Cumberland County daily, air quality is of paramount concern. There are not significant studies to estimate the amount of carbon neutralized through the forest cover in these two counties. At least forty known hazardous substances are found in diesel exhaust, and many of these are carried into the body on fine particles. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is the most significant cause of air pollution in these counties. Because of the high levels of particulate matter in Carlisle, the American Lung Association ranked Carlisle 14th of the 25 most polluted counties in America for short-term particle pollution in 2007. Because Cumberland County has such high levels of diesel PM, the county ranks in the 96 1 h percentile for highest levels of diesel PM in the country. Mountain Creek in Cumberland County is the first watershed in Central PA to be impaired by air quality-acid rain as documented by DEP.

div.head: 3c. Currently available for continued traditional use:
div.p: Although some of Franklin and Cumberland County's landscape has been broken up by sprawl, much remains to be managed for traditional uses especially forest products, recreation, hunting, fishing, aesthetics, watershed and wilderness, wildlife and aquatic habitat. The Department of Conservation and Natural Resources has designated South Mountain as a Conservation Landscape Initiative Area.

div.head: Description of each important forest area
div.p: Of the total land area in Franklin County, 40% is forested and 130,000 acres of that forested land is privately owned. Cumberland County has 30% forests and 64,900 acres is privately owned. South Mountain in Adams, Franklin, Cumberland and York counties is the Pennsylvania name for the northernmost extension of the Blue Ridge. The Blue Ridge is made up of metamorphosed Pre-Cambrian volcanic rocks and early Cambrian sandstones, a bit older than the rocks in the Ridge and Valley physiographic province, which extends west and north from it. Hardwood associates such as Scarlet Oak, Black Birch, Red Maple, Black Gum, Hickories, American Beech and Tuliptree are the major associates within an Appalachian Oak Forest (The Pennsylvania Atlas, 1982). The understory of Appalachian Oak Forests typically consists of Mountain Laurel, Low Sweet Blueberry, Lowbush Blueberry, Black Huckleberry, Witch-hazel, and other species (The Pennsylvania Atlas, 1982). A good example of an Appalachian Oak Forest occurs throughout most of Michaux State Forest. A small part of Franklin County also contains the Oak/Hickory/Pine Forest as the major vegetation type. This forest type typically consists of a medium-tall to tall forest of broadleaf deciduous and needleleaf evergreen trees. Hickory, Virginia Pine, Pitch Pine, White Oak, Scarlet Oak, Chestnut Oak and Black Oak are common species of this forest type. This southeastern forest type reaches its northern limit in Pennsylvania (The Pennsylvania Atlas, 1982). .

Of particular importance in both Franklin and Cumberland Counties is an area known as Bif Flat Pine barrens. This site contains a large example of a "Ridgetop Dwarf-Tree Forest Natural Community", and unknown quality populations of two animal species of concern. It is the large, relatively unfragmented character of this natural community and rarity of this community type at the global level that makes this one of the tops sites for the protection of biodiversity in Franklin and Cumberland County. Additional fragmenting features such as roads and structures will decrease the quality of this habitat. This site is primarily within Michaux State Forest.

div.head: Summary of the important environmental values and how they will be conserved in each FLA:
div.p: If Cumberland and Franklin Counties are designated a Forest Legacy Area, the following environmental values will be conserved:

Fish & Wildlife and their habitat (including threatened and endangered species) When large tracts of forest are conserved through easements that specify and require good forestry practices, all of the above listed environmental benefits are also protected and conserved. Required stewardship plans will help ensure forests will be managed to protect these environmental values.
Because easements require annual inspections, landowners will be made aware of the requirements and intent of the conservation easement especially the forest stewardship plan.
6. Describe how conserved tracts in this FLA will result in a positive cumulative impact or improved benefit:

Through the use of conservation easements and/or acquisitions, the goal is to preserve large areas of existing forests by protecting the lands from development pressures. When large tracts of woodland are kept intact, traditional uses such as timber production and hunting can continue without nuisance complaints and interference of surrounding homeowners. Also, when protected from sprawl development, the environmental values and attributes previously described remain at a high level. Of significant benefit is keeping the valuable water recharge area intact. This is a public safety issue as well as a natural resource protection need-clean, abundant drinking water.

7. List of public benefits that will be derived from establishing each FLA: Tracts of land will be identified by a combination of targeting specific areas based on knowledge and experience of the Planning Office, utilizing the Open Space and Greenways Plan, the Conservation Landscape Initiative and DCNR staff. Advertising the program to the general public will also be used to identify landowners interested in the program.
A public meeting, news releases and newsletters will be used to advertise the program to potential applicants.
Potential applicants will be prioritized using the recommended 100 point scoring system listed in the State Forestry Legacy Program Guideline Manual.

Monitoring wi.ll. be done annually with Planning and/or CPC staff with follow-up visits as needed to ensure compliance with the terms of the easement. A report of findings will be presenied to DCNR on an annual basis. The Forest Legacy Program will focus on preserving woodland in the counties through the use of conservation easements and acquisitions. The program has seven main goals:

1. To maintain traditional forests uses, including recreation and timber harvesting following best management practices. 2. To maintain productivity of forests for future generations. 3. To reduce the trend toward forest parcelization. 4. To conserve significant tracts of contiguous forest. 5. To conserve water resources and riparian zones. 6. To conserve important habitats for plants, fish and wildlife. 7. To restore degraded forest ecosystems.

A public meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, May 20'" at 7pm at Shippensburg University, Rowland Hall-Building 7, Room 200. (Parking is adjacent to the hall.) Please advise any landowner interested in such a program to please attend this meeting. If Cumberland and Franklin County are designated, landowners can voluntarily apply to preserve their forestlands by conservation easement or purchase. The proposal will be available for public review and comments at the meeting.

div.head: Contact:
div.p: Central The purpose of this letter to is inform the Board of Commissioners of our organization's intent to seek enrollment of Franklin County in the FLP and to be the sponsor. The FLP was created with the purpose of ascertaining and conserving "environmentally important forest areas threatened by conversion to nonforest uses, through the use of conservation easements and other mechanisms, for promoting forestland conservation." As a sponsor, we would be responsible for such tasks as providing information and assistance outreach to landowners and other interested parties, helping potential landowner applicants through the easement process, assisting with the federal cost-share process, and conducting public participation. We are currently a sponsor for the FLP in Perry and York Counties.

The FLP will operate through the Bureau. County entities, land trusts, or appropriate/authorized organizations are eligible sponsors. In the proposal, we will provide descriptive information about potential FLAs as well as potential threats as addressed by the FLP goals. The State Forest Stewardship Committee will make recommendations to the Bureau regarding proposed FLAs and Individual Forest Legacy tracts. Pennsylvania will adhere to the approach of willing seller/willing buyer as required by law in all FLP transactions. CPC will hold easements in perpetuity and fee titles will be held by the State.

As you have acknowledged, the South Mountain Conservation Landscape Initiative represents very critical habit, water recharge and forest lands essential to Franklin County's prosperity and quality of life.

We believe that the ability to enroll our local forests in the FLP is a valuable tool to ensure the sustainability and continuity of this unique landscape of our community and respectfully request your endorsement.

We will be submitting our application to the Bureau within the next two weeks. After their review, the Bureau will officially notify you in writing of our potential sponsorship. You will have 60 days to comment on our application. If you choose not to respond, the Bureau may approve our petition to be a sponsor and we will continue to develop the program. We look forward to working with you in the future. The office meeting portion was at Pennsylvania's Bureau of Forestry office in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. An overview of Pennsylvania's program work was presented and the FLP Review Team had an opportunity to inquire about the State FLP future management goals and implementation strategies. In addition, the FLP Review Team also assessed action items from Pennsylvania's FY2009 FLP Program Review and inspected Bureau of Forestry files for the FLP projects in the State. Following the office meeting and field portions of the review, the FLP Review Team held a close-out session to discuss State program commendations, and findings of deficiency.

div.head: FLP Review Commendations
div.p: The FLP Review Team identified the following commendations during the review of Pennsylvania's Forest Legacy Program.
The Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry is commended for:

• The development and implementation of a recordkeeping procedure for conservation easements that sets out what files should be kept, where original and filed copies are stored, and ensures that the Bureau of Forestry meets both Federal and State requirements.
• The continued commitment by Rachel Reyna to the FLP to ensure the program remained a strong and resilient program during the transfer of positions to a new FLP coordinator.

• The scanning and organization of all files on the network drive. Having all copies of mandatory documents in different forms ensures protection against any issues that might compromise a single set of files.
• Acquiring a fireproof safe and storing FLP records at a secondary location.

• The unique and preventive measure to thwart future successor landowner violations and title issues by re-recording the conservation easements every 30 years. In the long term, this policy could prevent future issues with land transfer.
• A robust and functioning FLP subcommittee that addresses big issues on the FLP in the State.
• The District Forester's knowledge of the Tree Farm #1 property and awareness of plans for the multiple uses for visitors of the State Forest and the neighboring Strawberry Hill Nature Preserve.

div.head: 3360-5 Forest Legacy Program Review FY2014 Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
Findings and Objectives Identified by the 2014 FLP Review Team
div.p: During the review, the 2014 FLP Review Team identified one FLP objective for which there is a finding of deficiency. During the course of the review, the FLP Review Team discussed possible recommendations that Pennsylvania could undertake to achieve the identified objective. Two issues were also identified. Issues are items that are not a finding but could lead to difficulty in future management of the FLP if not addressed or could lead to a finding if not addressed..

div.head: Finding:
div.p: The Pennsylvania Assessment of Need was updated without review and approval by the Northeastern Area.

During the review it was discovered by the FLP Review Possible actions identified in the review include: a. Submit any proposed changes to the Pennsylvania Assessment of Need to the Northeastern Area for review and approval before implementing the changes in the FLP.

div.head: Issue 1: Consistency and quality control of record keeping
div.p: Objective 1: All FLP related files be maintained in a manner that ensures consistency with the record keeping policy and high quality control of official records.

While reviewing the FLP files of the projects in Pennsylvania a number of files did not have all of the files listed as required by States to keep as listed in the updated 2011 Appendix G-Forest Legacy Record Keeping. The projects reviewed were all completed before the updated Appendix G was issued so even though the new list of required documents is not in effect for the older projects updating the files to match the new requirement is strongly encouraged.

div.head: State June 2015
div.p: Possible Actions:

• The Pennsylvania FLP could spend FLP administration grant funds in the year they are awarded and close the grant out the following year. • The Pennsylvania FLP should budget for due diligence activities into the request for project funds request and reduce the amount of admin grant requests to a level that is likely to be spent. • The Forest Service could deny any and all requests for grant extensions on FLP administration grants.

div.head: OIL, GAS AND MINERAL RIGHTS:
div.p: Typically the Forest Legacy Program will not enroll properties where the oil, gas and mineral rights have been severed (i.e. not owned by the property owner). However, in rare cases where it can be demonstrated that the amount of oil, gas and minerals is so remote as to be negligible and it would not be economically feasible to extract the oil, gas and minerals from the subsurface given current technologies, lands with severed rights may be eligible for the Forest Legacy Program. Staff input from the Pennsylvania Topographic and Geologic Survey in the form of an oil, gas and minerals assessment report is required in order to determine this eligibility.
